Drop heaped spoonfuls into 180C oil and fry 3-4 min, turning, until deep gold.
Drain, salt, and serve immediately with lemon and hot sauce.
p: The oyster liquor in the batter is what makes these taste of the bay rather than of fried dough. Do not overmix once the oysters go in: they break and weep.

m: Boil the limas in salted water 12-15 min until tender; drain.
Sweat the onion and pepper in the butter until soft, 8 min.
Add the corn and cook 3 min over higher heat to catch a little color.
Add the limas, cream, and thyme and simmer 3 min until the cream thickens slightly.
Season well and finish with parsley.
p: Delaware grows limas by the ton and eats them all summer. Cook the corn briefly and hard: it should still snap; simmered corn goes tired and starchy.

i: 6 ears corn, kernels and scraped milk
m: Cut the kernels from the cobs, then scrape the cobs hard with the back of the knife to collect the starchy milk.
Whisk the eggs with the milk, cream, melted butter, flour, sugar, salt, and pepper.
Stir in the corn and its scrapings.
Pour into a buttered dish and grate nutmeg over the top.
Bake at 175C for 45-55 min until set at the edges with a slight wobble at the center.
p: Scraping the cobs is the difference between corn custard and corn soup: that milky starch is what sets the pudding. Pull it while it still moves; it firms as it rests.

i: 800g rockfish or striped bass fillet, in strips
m: Pat the fish dry and dust lightly with plain flour.
Whisk the flour, baking powder, salt, and Old Bay, then add the cold beer and stir just to combine: lumps are fine, overmixing is not.
Heat the oil to 190C.
Dip the fish in the batter, let the excess run off, and lower into the oil away from you. Fry 3-4 min until deep gold and crisp.
Drain on a rack, salt at once, serve with lemon and tartar.
p: The beer must be cold and the batter must be mixed at the last moment: the carbonation is the leavening, and it starts dying the second it hits the flour.

n: Steamed Blue Crabs with Old Bay
i: Melted butter and lemon to serve
m: Bring the water and vinegar to a boil in the base of a large steamer with a rack set above the liquid.
Layer the crabs in the pot, dusting each layer heavily with Old Bay and salt, heavier than feels reasonable.
Cover tightly and steam 20-25 min until the shells turn bright orange-red all over.
Tip onto a table spread with newspaper and let them cool just enough to handle.
Serve with melted butter, lemon, and mallets; the picking is the meal.
p: Steamed, never boiled: boiling washes the seasoning off and waterlogs the meat. Season between every layer, and reckon on six crabs per person and two hours at the table.

i: 1kg crab shells and bodies for stock, or 1L seafood stock
m: Simmer the shells in 2L water 45 min to make stock, then strain.
Sweat the onion, carrot, and celery until soft, 10 min.
Add the stock, tomatoes, potatoes, Old Bay, and bay leaves. Simmer 20 min.
Add the green beans, corn, and limas and cook 12 min more.
Fold in the crab meat at the very end and heat 2 min only. Season and serve with more Old Bay at the table.
p: A vegetable soup that happens to have crab in it, and the crab goes in last so it stays in lumps. Making the stock from the shells costs 45 minutes and doubles the flavor.

m: Sweat the shallot in the butter until soft without color.
Stir in the flour and cook 2 min to a blond roux.
Whisk in the stock, then the milk, and simmer gently 10 min until lightly thickened and smooth.
Add the cream, Old Bay, and sherry and heat through without boiling.
Fold in the crab, warm 2 min, season with salt and white pepper, and finish with chives.
p: The two Maryland soups are cousins (one tomato and vegetables, one cream) and traditionalists order a cup of each, poured together, called half and half.

i: Paprika and butter for the top
m: Whisk the mayonnaise, egg, mustard, Worcestershire, Old Bay, and lemon into a smooth imperial sauce.
Fold in the crab meat with a rubber spatula in as few strokes as possible: the lumps are the luxury.
Divide among 4 ramekins or clean crab shells.
Dot with butter and dust with paprika.
Bake at 190C for 20-25 min until puffed, set, and golden on top.
p: Fold, never stir. The whole price of jumbo lump is in the size of the pieces, and an enthusiastic spoon turns a special-occasion dish into a crab salad casserole.

i: For the tiger sauce: 200g mayonnaise, 4 tbsp prepared horseradish, 1 tsp lemon juice
m: Rub the roast hard with the salt, pepper, garlic powder, paprika, and cayenne and rest it an hour.
Grill directly over hot charcoal, turning often, so the outside chars while the inside stays rare; 40-50 min to an internal 50C.
Rest 15 min, then slice against the grain as thin as you can manage.
Mix the horseradish into the mayonnaise for tiger sauce.
Pile the beef on a kaiser roll with raw onion and tiger sauce. The roll is a handle, not a sandwich.
p: Baltimore pit beef is charred outside and rare inside: it is grilled, not smoked, and it lives or dies on the slicing. Thick slices eat like a steak nobody asked for.

m: Cream the butter and sugar, add the eggs one at a time, then alternate the dry ingredients with the evaporated milk and vanilla.
Divide the batter into 8-10 thin layers, baking each in a greased 23cm pan at 175C for 8-10 min. They should be pale and thin, barely half a centimeter.
For the icing, boil the sugar, evaporated milk, and butter 5 min, then off the heat stir in the chocolate and vanilla until glossy.
Stack the layers while the icing is still warm and pourable, spreading a thin coat between each.
Coat the top and sides and let the icing set firm. Chill before slicing.
p: Maryland's official dessert, from an island in the Chesapeake: eight to ten layers, and the icing is a cooked fudge that sets hard rather than a buttercream. Thin layers are the whole discipline.

m: Cream the butter and sugar, beat in the egg and vanilla, then alternate the dry ingredients with the milk.
Drop spoonfuls onto lined trays and bake at 190C for 10-12 min until set but pale and cakey. Cool completely.
Warm the cream, pour over the chocolate, then beat in the butter, icing sugar, and corn syrup until thick and glossy.
Let the fudge cool until it holds a mound on a spoon.
Spread a thick dome of fudge over each cookie — the icing should outweigh the cookie.
p: A Baltimore institution since 1835. The proportions are deliberately absurd: the cookie is a soft plain vehicle and the fudge is the reason. Wait for the fudge to thicken or it slides off.

m: Blanch the greens and onions briefly, drain very well, and mix with all the seasonings: the stuffing should be aggressively spicy.
Cut deep pockets into the ham every few centimeters and pack them tight with the greens mixture. Rub any remainder over the surface.
Wrap the ham firmly in cheesecloth and tie it well.
Simmer in a large pot of water at a bare tremble for 4 hours, about 20 min per 500g.
Cool completely in the poaching liquid, then chill overnight. Slice cold, thin, showing the green swirl.
p: A St. Mary's County Easter tradition older than the state fair. It is always served cold and sliced thin so the pattern shows, and the stuffing must taste too spicy on its own: the ham tames it.

i: 450g salt cod, soaked 24 hours with several water changes
Saltine crackers and yellow mustard to serve
m: Simmer the soaked cod 15 min, drain, cool, and flake, checking for bones.
Mash into the potatoes with the egg, parsley, pepper, and Old Bay. The mixture should be stiff.
Form into small flat patties and chill 30 min so they hold.
Dust with cracker meal and shallow-fry 3 min a side until deep gold.
Serve the traditional way: pressed between two saltines with a smear of yellow mustard.
p: Baltimore corner-store food from the Depression, sold two for a nickel. The saltine-and-mustard service is not a garnish; it is the dish, and Baltimore will tell you so.

i: Finely shaved ice, packed into cups
For egg custard syrup: 250ml water, 300g sugar, 2 egg yolks, 1 tbsp vanilla, 1/4 tsp salt
Marshmallow creme, warmed to pouring consistency
m: Boil the water and sugar until dissolved, then cool slightly.
Whisk the yolks in a bowl and temper the warm syrup in slowly.
Return to low heat and cook 3-4 min, stirring, without boiling. Add vanilla and salt and chill completely.
Shave the ice as fine as snow; a snowball is not crushed ice, and the texture is the whole argument.
Pack a cup, douse with the egg custard syrup, and crown with warm marshmallow.
p: Egg custard is the flagship Baltimore flavor and marshmallow on top is the local signature. Shaved fine enough, the ice drinks the syrup instead of letting it run to the bottom.

m: Trim a little fat from the ham and render it in a cast-iron skillet over medium heat.
Fry the ham slices 2-3 min a side until the edges curl and brown; do not overcook or salt-cured ham turns to leather. Keep warm.
Pour the coffee into the hot skillet and scrape up every bit of browned fond.
Simmer 3-4 min until it reduces slightly and turns the color of a red eye. Add the sugar only if your ham is very salty.
Grind pepper in and pour over the ham, biscuits, or grits.
p: Two ingredients and a hot pan. The gravy is thin by design: it is a seasoned pan liquor, not a sauce, and thickening it with flour makes it something else entirely.

i: For the biscuits: 375g flour, 1 tbsp baking powder, 1 tsp salt, 1/2 tsp soda, 115g cold butter, 60g lard, 300ml cold buttermilk
m: Cut the cold fats into the dry ingredients until pea-sized, then stir in the buttermilk just until it comes together.
Pat to 2cm on a floured board, fold in thirds twice, and cut small rounds straight down without twisting.
Bake at 220C for 12-14 min until risen and gold. Cool slightly.
Split each biscuit, butter the faces, and fold in a ruffle of ham.
Add a dab of mustard or preserves and serve warm or at room temperature.
p: Small biscuits, thin ham, and something sweet or sharp to answer the salt. These are the currency of every Virginia gathering, and they are better an hour after baking than straight from the oven.

m: Simmer the chicken and pork in the water 90 min until both fall apart. Lift out, shred the meat, and keep the broth.
Return the broth to the pot with the onion, tomatoes, and potatoes and simmer 30 min until the potatoes begin to break down.
Add the limas and cook 15 min, then the corn and the shredded meat.
Season with Worcestershire, vinegar, sugar, hot sauce, salt, and pepper.
Simmer uncovered another 30-45 min, stirring often, until the stew is thick enough for a spoon to stand in it.
p: Virginia and Georgia both claim the invention and neither will yield. The finish is the test: it must be thick enough to stand a spoon, which means uncovered simmering and frequent stirring at the end.

m: Sweat the onion and celery in the butter until soft without color, 10 min.
Stir in the flour and cook 2 min.
Add the stock slowly, whisking, and simmer 15 min. Strain out the vegetables for the classic smooth texture.
Whisk the peanut butter into the hot broth until fully dissolved, then add the cream.
Season with celery salt, lemon, salt, white pepper, and a pinch of cayenne. Serve dusted with chopped peanuts.
p: Served at the King's Arms Tavern in Williamsburg since the colonial revival, and older than that in the kitchens where it started. The lemon at the end is what keeps it from tasting like a sauce.

m: Scald the milk, then rain in the cornmeal, whisking hard, and cook 5 min until very thick.
Off the heat beat in the butter, salt, and sugar, then cool 10 min.
Beat in the egg yolks one at a time, then the baking powder.
Whip the whites to soft peaks and fold them through in two additions.
Pour into a buttered dish and bake at 190C for 35-40 min until puffed and browned. Serve immediately with a spoon and plenty of butter.
p: It is closer to a savory souffle than to bread and it falls within minutes; carry it to the table straight from the oven. The name is literal: it is served with a spoon, never sliced.

m: Warm the milk and butter together until the butter melts; cool to lukewarm.
Beat the eggs into the milk, then mix into the flour, yeast, sugar, and salt to a very soft, sticky batter-dough. Beat 5 min with a mixer.
Cover and rise 90 min until doubled and bubbly.
Beat it down, turn into a buttered tube pan, and rise 45 min more.
Bake at 175C for 40-45 min until deep gold and hollow-sounding. Turn out and serve warm with butter.
p: A rich English batter bread that Virginia adopted and kept. The dough is too soft to knead by hand: beat it instead, and resist adding flour to make it behave.

m: Whisk the sugar, cornmeal, flour, and salt together in a bowl.
Beat in the eggs one at a time, then the melted butter, buttermilk, vinegar, and vanilla.
Pour into the shell and set on a low oven rack.
Bake at 175C for 45-55 min until the top is golden and cracked at the edges with a slight wobble at the center.
Cool completely, at least 3 hours, before slicing.
p: The spoon of cornmeal is the signature: it gives chess pie its faint grain and keeps the custard from being merely sweet. The vinegar does the same job from the other direction.

i: 180ml dark corn syrup or cane syrup
m: Scatter the peanuts evenly in the pie shell.
Whisk the eggs, brown sugar, syrup, melted butter, vanilla, and salt until smooth.
Pour over the peanuts; they will float to form the top layer.
Bake at 175C for 50-60 min until the center is set with only a faint tremble.
Cool completely before slicing, ideally 4 hours.
p: Virginia peanuts are large and crisp, and salted ones are correct here: the salt is what keeps a syrup pie from being unbearable. Cover the crust edge with foil if it darkens before the filling sets.

i: 1kg firm apples, cored and sliced thick, skin on
1 tbsp cider vinegar or lemon juice
m: Melt the butter in a wide cast-iron skillet over medium heat.
Lay the apples in a single layer and cook 5 min without stirring so they take color.
Turn, sprinkle with the brown sugar, cinnamon, nutmeg, and salt, and cook 8-10 min more.
Add the vinegar and let it bubble away: this keeps the dish from becoming dessert.
Serve hot alongside pork, ham, or biscuits.
p: Skin on: it holds the slices together over ten minutes of heat and carries most of the apple flavor. This is a side dish for the savory plate, which is what the splash of vinegar is defending.

i: An untreated oak or hickory plank, soaked in water 2 hours
m: Soak the plank thoroughly so it smolders rather than burns.
Season the fillets with salt, pepper, and Old Bay and set them skin-side down on the plank.
Lay bacon over the flesh and brush with the melted butter and lemon.
Cook beside a hardwood fire, or in a 200C oven with a smoking chip tray, 35-50 min, basting with butter every 15 min.
The fish is done when it flakes and the plank is charred at the edges. Serve straight from the board with lemon and parsley.
p: A Potomac spring ritual older than the Republic. The plank is the cooking vessel and the seasoning both: soak it well, and never use treated lumber or softwood.

m: Mix and knead the dough 8 min until smooth and soft; rise 1 hour until doubled.
Divide into 12 pieces and flatten each into an oval.
Lay 6-8 slices of pepperoni down the middle, with cheese if using, and roll up tightly, sealing the seam and ends.
Set seam-side down on a lined tray, cover, and rise 40 min.
Bake at 190C for 18-20 min until deep gold. Brush with melted butter as they come out: the orange grease streaks are the badge of honor.
p: Invented in Fairmont in 1927 for coal miners who needed a lunch that kept without refrigeration. The pepperoni grease soaking into the crumb is the entire point, so do not drain it or wrap it in foil.

i: For the sauce: 450g ground beef, 1 onion grated, 2 tbsp chili powder, 1 tsp cumin, 1 tsp paprika, 2 tbsp tomato paste, 250ml water, salt
For the slaw: 400g cabbage shredded fine, 4 tbsp mayonnaise, 1 tbsp vinegar, 1 tbsp sugar, 1/2 tsp celery seed, salt
m: Simmer the raw ground beef in the water with the onion, spices, and tomato paste 45 min until thick and fine-grained; never brown it first.
Chop the cabbage very fine and dress with the mayonnaise, vinegar, sugar, celery seed, and salt. Chill.
Steam or griddle the hot dogs and warm the buns.
Build in the state-mandated order: dog, mustard, sauce, onion, then slaw on top.
Serve immediately, before the slaw warms.
p: The slaw goes on top, the sauce goes underneath, and the cabbage must be chopped fine rather than shredded long. Cross the state line into Ohio and the order changes; West Virginia does not.

i: 150g salt pork or a ham hock
For the cornbread: 250g cornmeal, 60g flour, 1 tbsp baking powder, 1 tsp salt, 1 egg, 400ml buttermilk, 3 tbsp bacon fat
Chopped raw onion and chow chow to serve
m: Drain the beans, cover with fresh water by 5cm, and add the salt pork, onion, bay, and pepper.
Simmer 2-3 hours, uncovered, adding water as needed, until the beans are creamy and the liquid has turned into a thick pot liquor.
Salt only at the end: salting early keeps the skins tough.
For the cornbread, heat the bacon fat in a cast-iron skillet at 220C until smoking. Mix the batter quickly, pour it into the hot fat, and bake 20-25 min.
Serve the beans in bowls with cornbread, raw onion, and chow chow alongside.
p: The pot liquor is the dish as much as the beans: do not drain it, and cook uncovered so it reduces. Cornbread is for crumbling in, and Appalachian cornbread carries no sugar.

i: 300g ramps, cleaned, whites and greens separated
m: Render the bacon in a cast-iron skillet until crisp; lift out and keep the fat.
Add the potatoes in an even layer and cook over medium heat 12-15 min, turning occasionally, until browned and tender.
Add the chopped ramp whites and cook 3 min until softened.
Stir in the ramp greens and cook 1 min only: they wilt instantly.
Season, return the bacon, and finish with a splash of vinegar.
p: Ramp season is three weeks in April and half the state marks it with a supper. Dig responsibly: cut leaves and leave bulbs where you can, or there will be no ramps for the next generation.

i: 55g butter, melted, plus more for the griddle
Sausage, butter, and syrup to serve
m: Whisk the dry ingredients together in a wide bowl.
Beat the eggs, buttermilk, and melted butter and stir into the dry ingredients with a light hand.
Rest the batter 15 min: buckwheat needs the time to hydrate or the cakes taste raw.
Griddle in butter over medium heat until bubbles break across the surface, then flip once.
Serve stacked with butter, syrup, and sausage.
p: Preston County holds a buckwheat festival every autumn. Buckwheat is not wheat at all and brings a dark, faintly bitter earthiness. The plain flour in the mix keeps the cakes tender rather than dense.

m: Simmer the apples in the cider 45 min until completely soft, then pass through a food mill: the cores and skins give pectin and go in the mill, not the bin.
Return the puree to a heavy pot with the sugar, spices, salt, and vinegar.
Cook over the lowest heat 4-5 hours, stirring often as it thickens and darkens. A spatter screen saves your arms.
It is done when a spoonful mounded on a cold plate weeps no liquid at the edges.
Jar hot and seal, or refrigerate for a month.
p: The old way was a copper kettle over a fire and a wooden paddle worked all day by whoever was losing the argument. Low and slow is the only method: high heat scorches the sugar and the whole batch tastes burnt.

m: Brown the sausage in a cast-iron skillet over medium heat, breaking it into rough pieces and letting it stick and crust a little.
Sprinkle the flour over the meat and its fat and cook 2 min, stirring, until the raw taste goes.
Add the warm milk in a slow stream, whisking constantly to keep it smooth.
Simmer 8-10 min until it coats a spoon; it thickens further off the heat, so stop a little thin.
Season hard with black pepper, sage, cayenne, and salt. Ladle over split biscuits.
p: Pepper past the point that seems polite: this gravy is properly speckled. If it thickens too far, more warm milk fixes it; a stiff sausage gravy is a paste with meat in it.

i: 400g pawpaw pulp, seeds and skin removed
m: Press the ripe pawpaw flesh through a sieve to remove the large seeds and any skin.
Whisk the sugar, flour, baking powder, salt, and cinnamon together.
Beat the eggs with the milk, melted butter, and vanilla, then stir in the pawpaw pulp.
Combine wet and dry and pour into a buttered dish.
Bake at 175C for 50-55 min until set and browned. Serve warm with whipped cream.
p: America's largest native fruit, tasting of mango and banana, and it ripens for two weeks in September before it goes. Never cook the seeds and never eat the skin.

i: 115g bacon fat or butter for frying
m: Pat the trout dry inside and out and season lightly.
Mix the cornmeal, flour, salt, pepper, and cayenne in a wide dish.
Dip the fish in buttermilk, then dredge in the cornmeal, pressing it on well.
Fry in hot bacon fat 4-5 min a side for whole fish, 2-3 for fillets, until the crust is deep gold and the flesh flakes.
Drain briefly and serve with lemon and parsley.
p: Mountain stream trout, fried in the fat you rendered at breakfast. Cornmeal alone can go sandy: the spoonful of flour is what binds the crust to the fish.

i: For the starter: 60g cornmeal, 250ml scalded milk, 1 tbsp sugar, 1/2 tsp salt, 1/4 tsp baking soda
For the sponge: 500ml warm water, 2 tbsp sugar, 1 tsp salt, 250g flour
For the dough: about 700g flour, 3 tbsp butter softened, 2 tsp salt
m: Stir the scalded milk into the cornmeal with the sugar, salt, and soda. Keep it at 40-45C overnight, 12 hours, until it foams and smells sharp and cheesy.
Strain the starter into the warm water with the sugar, salt, and 250g flour. Keep warm 2-3 hours until bubbly and risen.
Work in the butter, salt, and enough flour to make a firm dough, and knead 10 min.
Shape into two loaves in buttered pans and rise in a warm place 3-4 hours: this bread is slow and needs steady warmth.
Bake at 190C for 35-40 min until deep brown and hollow-sounding.
p: It uses no commercial yeast at all: the rise comes from wild bacteria in the cornmeal, which is why it needs constant warmth and why it smells so strongly while it works. Appalachia has baked it for two centuries and nobody has made it faster.

i: 1 pork shoulder, about 4kg, bone in (or a whole hog if you dare)
For the mop and sauce: 500ml cider vinegar, 250ml water, 2 tbsp crushed red pepper, 1 tbsp black pepper, 1 tbsp salt, 1 tbsp sugar, 1 tsp hot sauce
m: Build a fire for indirect heat and hold the cooker at 110-120C with hickory or oak.
Season the shoulder only with salt and pepper and set it fat-side up, away from the coals.
Smoke 10-12 hours, mopping with the vinegar mixture every hour after the first three, until the meat pulls apart at 92C internal.
Rest 30 min, then chop or pull the whole thing, skin and all, working the crisp bits through.
Dress with the vinegar sauce, not too wet, and pile onto buns with slaw.
p: Eastern North Carolina uses the whole hog and a thin vinegar-pepper sauce with no tomato at all. The chopped bark worked back through the meat is the soul of it: keep the sauce sharp, and let the vinegar cut the fat.

i: For the dip: 250ml cider vinegar, 120ml ketchup, 120ml water, 2 tbsp brown sugar, 1 tbsp red pepper flakes, 1 tsp black pepper, 1 tsp salt
For red slaw: 400g cabbage, 120ml of the dip, extra sugar
m: Hold the smoker at 110C over hickory. Season the shoulder with salt and pepper.
Smoke fat-side up 8-10 hours until it pulls at 92C internal, spritzing with vinegar in the last hours.
Simmer the dip ingredients together 5 min into a thin tomato-tinged sauce.
Rest, then chop the shoulder, working through the bark, and dress lightly with the dip.
Toss the cabbage with dip and extra sugar for red slaw and serve both on a bun or a plate.
p: Lexington, in the Piedmont, uses the shoulder alone and a dip that admits a little ketchup, the great North Carolina schism. The red slaw dressed in the same dip is the tell that you are west of the coastal plain.

i: 1kg firm white fish (rockfish or catfish), in large pieces
Salt, black pepper, and hot sauce
m: Render the bacon in a heavy pot; lift out the bits.
Layer the onions and potatoes in the pot, add the tomatoes, water, and red pepper, and simmer 25 min until the potatoes soften.
Lay the fish on top, cover, and poach gently 12 min without stirring; stirring breaks the fish.
Crack the eggs onto the surface if using and poach 4 min in the steam.
Season hard, scatter the bacon over, and ladle out carefully so the fish stays whole.
p: An Eastern Carolina river-camp dish, built in layers and never stirred once the fish goes in. The eggs poached on top are the old riverbank touch, and they are better than they sound.

m: Simmer the liver and pork with the onion 1 hour until tender. Strain, keeping 1L of the broth, and grind or chop the meat fine.
Bring the broth to a simmer and whisk in the cornmeal, cooking 20 min until very thick.
Stir in the meat, salt, pepper, sage, and cayenne. Season boldly.
Pack into a loaf pan, cool, and chill overnight until firm.
Slice 1cm thick and fry in butter over medium heat 4-5 min a side until a deep crust forms. Do not flip early.
p: A Piedmont cousin of scrapple with more liver and more pepper. As with scrapple, the rule at the stove is patience: leave it alone until the crust sets or it falls to pieces in the pan.

i: For the dressing: 120ml mayonnaise, 2 tbsp cider vinegar, 1 tbsp yellow mustard, 1 tbsp sugar, 1 tsp celery seed, salt and pepper
m: Shred the cabbage as fine as you can and grate the carrot.
Salt the cabbage lightly and let it drain in a colander 20 min, then press out the water.
Whisk the dressing ingredients together.
Toss the cabbage and carrot with just enough dressing to coat; it should not be swimming.
Chill an hour before serving so the flavors marry.
p: Draining the salted cabbage first is what keeps barbecue slaw from turning to soup by the second helping. On an Eastern Carolina plate the slaw goes right on top of the pork sandwich.

m: Whisk the cornmeal, flour, baking powder, salt, and sugar.
Stir in the grated onion, egg, and buttermilk to a thick batter. Rest 10 min.
Heat the oil to 180C.
Drop the batter in by heaped spoonfuls, 5 or 6 at a time, and fry 3-4 min, turning, until deep gold and cooked through.
Drain on a rack and salt immediately.
p: The name is said to come from frying scraps to quiet the dogs. Keep the batter thick so they hold their shape, and fry a test one first: if the middle stays raw, your oil is too hot.

m: Roast the sweet potatoes whole until collapsing, then scoop and mash the flesh smooth.
Beat in the brown sugar, eggs, evaporated milk, melted butter, spices, vanilla, and salt until silky.
Pour into the shell.
Bake at 200C for 15 min, then 175C for 35-40 min until set at the edges with a slight wobble.
Cool completely before slicing.
p: North Carolina grows more sweet potatoes than any state, and roasting rather than boiling them is the difference: boiling waterlogs the flesh and dilutes the flavor you are baking the pie for.

m: Soak the shrimp in buttermilk 20 min.
Mix the flour, cornmeal, Old Bay, salt, and pepper in a wide dish.
Heat the oil to 190C.
Lift the shrimp from the buttermilk, dredge in the flour, shake off the excess, and fry in small batches 90 seconds until pale gold — they cook fast.
Drain on a rack, salt, and serve at once with lemon and cocktail sauce.
p: Named for the fishing town of Calabash, where the style is a light, thin, barely-there crust, never a heavy batter. Fry hot and fast and pull them the second they turn gold; a minute too long and shrimp go rubbery.

m: Warm the potato water and dissolve the yeast in it with a spoon of the sugar.
Beat the mashed potato with the remaining sugar, butter, and eggs, then add the yeast liquid, flour, and salt to a soft dough. Knead briefly.
Rise 90 min, then press into a buttered sheet pan and rise 45 min more.
Dimple the surface all over with a floured finger and fill the dimples with pieces of butter and brown sugar mixed with cinnamon.
Bake at 190C for 20-25 min until the dimples bubble with cinnamon butter and the cake is gold.
p: The Moravians of Winston-Salem made this for Easter and the potato in the dough is the reason it stays tender for days. Press the dimples deep: they are wells for the cinnamon butter, which is the whole reward.

m: Sweat the onions in the butter until soft.
Add the tomatoes, potatoes, and stock and simmer 30 min until the potatoes start to break down.
Add the limas and cook 15 min, then the corn, pork, and chicken.
Stir in the barbecue sauce and Worcestershire and simmer 45 min more, uncovered, stirring often.
Season with hot sauce, salt, and pepper. It should be thick, not soupy.
p: In North Carolina the stew rides shotgun to a barbecue plate and often starts with the smoked pork itself. Long uncovered simmering at the end is what turns a vegetable soup into a proper Brunswick stew.

i: 100g crab roe if you can get it
m: Sweat the shallot in the butter until soft, then stir in the flour and cook 2 min to a blond roux.
Whisk in the stock and milk and simmer 10 min until smooth and lightly thickened.
Add the cream, mace, and Worcestershire and heat through without boiling.
Fold in the crab and roe and warm 3 min.
Off the heat stir in the sherry, season with salt, white pepper, and cayenne, and serve with an extra thread of sherry in each bowl.
p: The roe is what makes it she-crab soup and gives the pale orange color; without it you have a fine crab bisque but not the Charleston classic. The sherry goes in off the heat so it does not cook away.

i: 2 tbsp parsley, hot sauce, salt, and pepper
m: Simmer the grits in the water and milk 40-50 min, stirring often, until creamy. Beat in the butter and cheddar and keep warm.
Render the bacon until crisp; lift out and reserve, leaving the fat.
Cook the onion and garlic in the bacon fat until soft, add the shrimp, and cook 2 min a side until just pink.
Add the stock and lemon and simmer 2 min into a light pan sauce.
Season, fold in the bacon and parsley, and spoon over the grits.
p: Lowcountry grits must be stone-ground and cooked slow — instant grits are a different, sadder dish. Pull the shrimp the moment they curl; carryover heat in the sauce finishes them.

m: Bring a very large pot of water to a boil with the Old Bay, onion, and lemons.
Add the potatoes and boil 10 min.
Add the sausage and corn and boil 8 min more.
Add the shrimp and cook 3 min only, until they just turn pink.
Drain the whole pot and pour it out onto a newspaper-covered table. Serve with butter and cocktail sauce.
p: Also called Lowcountry boil or Beaufort stew, and the timing is the whole recipe: everything is staged so it all finishes together and nothing overcooks. The shrimp go in last and come out fast.

i: 400g dried field peas or black-eyed peas, soaked
Salt, black pepper, and hot sauce
m: Simmer the drained peas with the ham hock, onion, celery, bay, and thyme in the water 45 min until tender.
Pull the hock, shred its meat, and return it to the pot.
Stir in the rice, adding water if needed to cover by a finger, and season.
Cover and cook 18-20 min until the rice is tender and the liquid absorbed.
Rest 10 min, fluff, and serve with scallions and hot sauce.
p: The Lowcountry's New Year's dish, eaten for luck, with the peas standing for coins. Cook the rice in the pea liquor so it takes on the smoke; plain rice stirred in afterward misses the point.

m: Render the bacon until crisp; lift out and reserve.
Sweat the onion and celery in the bacon fat until soft, 8 min.
Rinse the rice, add it to the pot, and stir 1 min to coat.
Add the stock, bay, and thyme, bring to a boil, then cover and cook on the lowest heat 18 min.
Rest 10 min off the heat, fold in the bacon and scallions with a fork, and season.
p: Pilau (say 'perlo') is the Lowcountry's one-pot rice, and Carolina Gold is the heirloom grain that built the plantation economy and nearly vanished. Do not stir it while it cooks: you want separate grains, not risotto.

i: 1kg raw green peanuts in the shell
m: Rinse the raw peanuts well to remove field dirt.
Put them in a large pot, cover with the water, and add the salt and any spice.
Weight them down with a plate so they stay submerged and bring to a boil.
Simmer 3-4 hours, tasting after two, until the peanuts are soft as a cooked bean. Add water as needed.
Turn off the heat and let them soak another hour in the brine for the salt to penetrate. Eat warm from the shell.
p: The official state snack, sold from roadside pots and gas stations all summer. Green peanuts (freshly dug, not dried) are essential; dried peanuts never soften right. They should be soft, not crunchy.

m: Grate the cheddar yourself on the large holes — pre-grated cheese will not bind properly.
Beat the cream cheese and mayonnaise smooth.
Fold in the cheddar, pimentos, Worcestershire, onion powder, and cayenne.
Season with black pepper and mash lightly so it holds together but stays coarse.
Chill an hour. Serve as a dip, a sandwich, or a burger topping.
p: The pate of the South, and hand-grated cheese is the one rule that matters — the anti-caking dust on pre-grated cheddar keeps it from coming together and makes it grainy.

m: Simmer the chicken in the stock 45 min until tender. Lift out, pull the meat, and keep the broth.
Brown the sausage in the pot, then sweat the onion and celery in the rendered fat.
Add the rice and stir 1 min, then add the measured broth, bay, and thyme.
Return the chicken meat, cover, and cook on low 20 min until the rice is tender and wet.
Rest 10 min. A bog is meant to be moist, not dry: season well and finish with scallions.
p: A chicken bog is wetter than a pilau, which is the whole distinction: the rice should be soft and loose, almost soupy. Williamsburg County holds a festival for it every autumn.

m: Toast the sesame seeds in a dry pan until golden and fragrant, then cool.
Cream the butter and brown sugar, beat in the egg and vanilla.
Fold in the flour, baking powder, salt, and toasted seeds.
Drop tiny half-teaspoons far apart on lined trays: they spread dramatically.
Bake at 175C for 8-10 min until deep gold at the edges. Cool on the tray until crisp.
p: Benne is the West African word for sesame, brought to Charleston by enslaved people, and the wafers are a Lowcountry emblem of good luck. Space them wide: they spread to twice their size and weld together if crowded.

m: Render the bacon and sausage in a heavy pot until browned; lift out and reserve.
Sweat the onion, pepper, and celery in the fat until soft, 10 min.
Stir in the tomato paste and cook 2 min, then add the crushed tomatoes and cook 5 min more.
Rinse the rice, stir it in, then add the stock, thyme, and the reserved meat.
Cover and cook on the lowest heat 25 min. Rest 10 min, then fork through gently: the grains should be separate and stained deep red.
p: A direct descendant of West African jollof, carried to the Lowcountry. The tomato paste cooked dark before the liquid goes in is what gives the color and depth; skip it and you get pink rice, not red.

i: For the batter: 115g butter, 190g flour, 200g sugar, 2 tsp baking powder, 1/4 tsp salt, 240ml milk
m: Toss the peaches with the sugar, lemon, cinnamon, and cornstarch and let them macerate 20 min.
Melt the butter in a 23x33cm baking dish in the oven as it heats to 190C.
Whisk the flour, sugar, baking powder, salt, and milk into a smooth batter and pour it over the melted butter. Do not stir.
Spoon the peaches and their juice evenly over the batter; again do not stir.
Bake 45-55 min until the batter has risen up and around the fruit and browned. The cake rises through the peaches as it bakes.
p: The magic is not stirring: the batter floats up through the fruit as it bakes, so you get cake on top and peaches suspended below. Georgia peaches in July are the reason the state is nicknamed for them.

i: 180ml dark corn syrup or cane syrup
m: Scatter the pecans in the shell.
Whisk the eggs, brown sugar, syrup, melted butter, bourbon, vanilla, and salt until smooth.
Pour over the pecans; they rise to form the top crust.
Bake at 175C for 50-60 min until the center is set with only a slight jiggle.
Cool completely, at least 4 hours, before slicing.
p: Georgia grows more pecans than any state. Toast the pecans for eight minutes first if you have the time: it deepens the flavor past what raw nuts can give, and it is the one improvement worth making.

i: Peanut oil or lard for frying
m: Brine the chicken in the buttermilk and hot sauce at least 4 hours, ideally overnight.
Mix the flour with all the seasonings in a wide dish.
Lift each piece from the buttermilk, letting the excess drip, and dredge heavily in the seasoned flour. Rest on a rack 15 min so the coating sets.
Heat the oil to 165C in a cast-iron skillet. Fry the dark meat 14-16 min, the white 12-14, turning once, to a deep gold and 74C internal.
Drain on a rack, salt at once, and rest 5 min before serving.
p: Cast-iron and a modest 165C are the Southern way; too hot and the crust burns before the inside cooks. Resting the dredged chicken before it fries is what glues the coating on.

m: Sweat the onions slowly in the butter until soft and sweet but not browned, 20 min; the sweetness of a Vidalia is the whole point.
Whisk the cream, eggs, half the Parmesan, nutmeg, salt, and pepper.
Spread the onions in a buttered dish and pour the custard over.
Top with the cracker crumbs and remaining Parmesan.
Bake at 175C for 30-35 min until set and golden.
p: Vidalias are sweet only because of the low-sulfur soil around Vidalia, Georgia; they are a legally protected crop. Cook them low and slow so their sugar comes forward without browning to bitterness.

m: Sweat the onions in the butter until soft.
Add the tomatoes, potatoes, and stock and simmer 30 min.
Add the limas and cook 15 min, then the corn, pork, and chicken.
Stir in the barbecue sauce, Worcestershire, and vinegar and simmer 60 min uncovered, stirring often, until thick.
Season with hot sauce, salt, and pepper.
p: Brunswick, Georgia, claims the invention on a plaque by an old iron pot; Virginia disagrees. Either way the Georgia version leans smoky and sweet with barbecue in the base, and it must cook down thick.

m: Dredge the chicken in seasoned flour and brown well in the oil; set aside.
Sweat the onion, pepper, and garlic in the pan, then add the curry powder and cook 1 min until fragrant.
Add the tomatoes and stock and scrape up the fond.
Return the chicken, add the currants, cover, and simmer 40 min until tender.
Scatter the toasted almonds and parsley over and serve on rice.
p: A curried chicken that came into Savannah and Charleston through the spice trade in the 1800s. Bloom the curry powder in the fat before the liquid goes in: raw curry powder tastes dusty and flat.

m: Sweat the onion and celery in the butter until soft, then stir in the flour and cook 2 min.
Whisk in the stock and milk and simmer 10 min until lightly thickened.
Add the cream and mace and heat through without boiling.
Fold in the crab and the chopped egg and warm gently 3 min.
Off the heat add the sherry, season, and finish with parsley.
p: Coastal Georgia's answer to she-crab soup, thickened a little more and enriched with chopped egg. As always with a sherry-finished stew, the sherry goes in off the heat to keep its perfume.

m: Butter a large sheet pan and warm it slightly.
Boil the sugar, corn syrup, and water to 120C, then add the butter and peanuts.
Keep cooking, stirring constantly, to 150C: the syrup will turn amber and the peanuts will smell toasted.
Off the heat quickly stir in the salt, baking soda, and vanilla; it will foam up pale.
Pour onto the pan, spread thin with a buttered spatula, and cool completely before breaking into shards.
p: The baking soda is what makes brittle brittle: it foams the hot syrup full of tiny bubbles so it shatters instead of cracking teeth. Work fast once it goes in; the candy sets in minutes.

i: 500g day-old brioche or French bread, cubed
For the sauce: 115g butter, 150g brown sugar, 60ml bourbon, 120ml cream
m: Butter a baking dish and scatter in the bread and peaches.
Whisk the eggs, milk, cream, sugar, bourbon, vanilla, and cinnamon and pour over. Press the bread down and soak 30 min.
Dot with butter and bake at 175C for 45-50 min until puffed and set.
For the sauce, simmer the butter, brown sugar, bourbon, and cream 5 min until glossy.
Pour the warm sauce over the pudding and serve.
p: Stale bread is essential — fresh bread turns to paste. Let it drink the custard for a full half hour before it bakes, and do not skimp on the bourbon sauce; it is the reason anyone remembers the dish.

i: For the crust: 200g graham crackers crushed, 100g sugar, 115g butter melted
For the filling: 4 egg yolks, 400g sweetened condensed milk, 150ml key lime juice, 1 tbsp lime zest
Whipped cream and lime zest to finish
m: Mix the crumbs, sugar, and butter and press into a 23cm pie plate. Bake at 175C for 10 min and cool.
Whisk the yolks with the lime zest until pale, then beat in the condensed milk.
Add the lime juice and whisk until the mixture thickens visibly: the acid sets it.
Pour into the crust and bake at 175C for 12-15 min, just until set with a faint wobble.
Cool, then chill 4 hours. Top with whipped cream and zest before serving.
p: Real key lime juice is tarter and more floral than regular lime, and the filling is genuinely cooked, not just chilled: the short bake sets the egg and keeps it safe. The color is pale yellow, never green; green means food coloring and a stranger's recipe.

n: Florida Stone Crab with Mustard Sauce
i: 1.5kg stone crab claws, cooked and chilled
For the sauce: 200g mayonnaise, 2 tbsp Colman's dry mustard, 1 tbsp Worcestershire, 1 tbsp cream, 1 tsp lemon juice, pinch of salt
m: Chill the claws thoroughly; stone crab is always served cold.
Whisk the dry mustard into the mayonnaise and let it sit 10 min to bloom and sharpen.
Beat in the Worcestershire, cream, lemon, and salt.
Crack the claws with a mallet, cracking each segment so the meat pulls free clean.
Serve the claws on ice with the mustard sauce and lemon.
p: Only the claws are taken; the crab is returned to the sea to regrow them, which makes stone crab one of the few truly sustainable luxuries. The mustard sauce is the traditional partner and it must be sharp: let the dry mustard bloom.

i: Butter or lard for the press
m: Split the bread lengthwise and spread mustard on both faces.
Layer in order: ham, then roast pork, then salami, then Swiss, then pickles.
Close the sandwich and butter the outside of the bread.
Press in a plancha or a heavy skillet with a weight on top, 4-5 min, until the cheese melts and the bread is flat and crisp.
Cut on a sharp diagonal and serve hot.
p: Tampa's Cuban includes Genoa salami, a mark of the Italian immigrants in Ybor City, a point of pride that starts arguments with Miami. The bread must be flattened hard in the press until it crackles.

i: 400g conch meat, ground or minced fine
m: Tenderize the conch by mincing it fine: it is naturally tough and needs it.
Whisk the flour, baking powder, egg, and milk into a thick batter.
Fold in the conch, onion, pepper, celery, hot sauce, and Old Bay.
Drop heaped spoonfuls into 180C oil and fry 3-4 min, turning, until deep gold and cooked through.
Drain, salt, and serve with key lime wedges and remoulade.
p: Key West and the Bahamas share the conch, and the trick is mincing it fine enough that it never turns rubbery. Fry a test fritter to check the seasoning and that the center cooks through before the outside burns.

i: For the sauce: 150g mayonnaise, 2 tbsp relish, 1 tbsp lemon, 1 tsp hot sauce
m: Soak the grouper in buttermilk 15 min.
Mix the flour, cornmeal, and Old Bay. Whisk the sauce ingredients and chill.
Heat the oil to 190C. Dredge the fish, shake off the excess, and fry 3-4 min until gold and flaking.
Toast the rolls and spread with the sauce.
Build with lettuce, tomato, onion, and the hot fish, and serve at once.
p: The Gulf grouper sandwich is a Florida coast institution and it can be fried, grilled, or blackened. Fried is the classic; whatever you do, do not overcook grouper: it goes from succulent to cottony fast.

m: Simmer the drained beans with the halved onion, halved pepper, and bay in fresh water 90 min until tender. Discard the halved vegetables.
Make a sofrito: cook the diced onion, diced pepper, and garlic in the olive oil until soft, then add the cumin and oregano and cook 1 min.
Stir the sofrito into the beans, add the vinegar, and simmer 30 min uncovered until thick, mashing some beans against the pot for body.
Cook the rice separately until fluffy.
Season the beans well and serve over or alongside the rice.
p: Frijoles negros are the everyday soul of Cuban Miami. Mashing a ladle of the beans against the pot thickens the pot liquor into something silky, and the splash of vinegar at the end brightens the whole thing.

i: For the glaze: 150g icing sugar, 3 tbsp orange juice, 1 tsp zest
m: Cream the butter, sugar, and orange zest until light and fragrant.
Beat in the eggs one at a time.
Alternate the dry ingredients with the orange juice and buttermilk in three additions.
Pour into a buttered bundt or loaf pan and bake at 175C for 45-55 min until a skewer comes clean.
Cool 15 min, then spoon the orange glaze over while still warm so it soaks in.
p: Rubbing the zest into the sugar first releases the oils and perfumes the whole cake: juice alone gives sweetness but not aroma. Florida's citrus peaks in winter, when this cake tastes most of the state.

m: Cook the onion, pepper, and garlic in the olive oil to a soft sofrito, 10 min.
Add the cumin and oregano and cook 1 min, then the wine and let it reduce by half.
Add the tomatoes, bay, capers, and olives and simmer 15 min into a thick sauce.
Add the shrimp and cook 3-4 min only, until they curl and turn pink.
Season with salt, pepper, and cayenne and serve over rice.
p: The Spanish-Caribbean cousin of Louisiana shrimp creole, built on a sofrito with olives and capers. Add the shrimp at the very end: they need only minutes, and a shrimp simmered too long is a small tragedy.

m: Melt the sugar in a dry pan to a deep amber caramel and pour it into a round mold, swirling to coat the base.
Whisk the eggs, yolks, condensed milk, evaporated milk, vanilla, lime zest, and salt until smooth; do not froth it.
Strain into the caramel-lined mold.
Set the mold in a roasting pan, pour hot water halfway up the sides, and bake at 160C for 55-65 min until just set with a slight wobble.
Cool, then chill overnight. Run a knife around the edge and invert onto a plate so the caramel floods over.
p: The Cuban flan of Miami is denser than a French creme caramel because of the condensed milk. The water bath is essential (it keeps the custard from splitting), and the overnight chill lets the caramel liquefy into sauce.

i: Butter and cane syrup to serve
m: Cut the cold butter and lard into the flour, sugar, and salt until the pieces are pea-sized.
Stir in the buttermilk just until it comes together into a shaggy dough.
Pat to 3cm thick, fold in thirds twice for layers, and cut straight down with a floured cutter.
Bake at 230C for 12-15 min until tall and golden, brushing with butter as they come out.
Fry the sausage patties until browned and serve tucked in the split biscuits with cane syrup.
p: Southern biscuits live and die on cold fat and a light hand: the moment the dough looks smooth you have overworked it. Cut straight down without twisting or the layers seal and the biscuit stays squat.

i: 500g firm white fish or 400g minced clams
m: Render the salt pork until crisp; lift out and reserve.
Sweat the onion, pepper, celery, and garlic in the fat until soft, 10 min.
Add the tomatoes, stock, potatoes, datil pepper, bay, and thyme and simmer 25 min.
Add the fish or clams and cook 8 min until the fish flakes.
Season and scatter the pork bits over: it should carry a real, fruity heat from the datil.
p: St. Augustine's Minorcan community built this around the datil pepper, a fiery fruit they have grown there for two centuries. The datil brings heat with a distinct sweetness; a habanero is the nearest substitute if you cannot find one.

i: For the white sauce: 300ml mayonnaise, 120ml cider vinegar, 2 tbsp lemon juice, 1 tbsp horseradish, 1 tsp black pepper, 1 tsp sugar, 1/2 tsp cayenne, 1 tsp salt
m: Season the spatchcocked chicken hard with salt and pepper and let it sit an hour.
Smoke or grill over indirect heat at 150C for about 75 min until 74C in the thigh.
Whisk all the white sauce ingredients together: it should be thin, sharp, and peppery.
When the chicken comes off the heat, dunk the whole bird in the white sauce or brush it on generously.
Rest 10 min and serve with more sauce on the side.
p: Big Bob Gibson invented this in Decatur in 1925, and northern Alabama has dunked smoked chicken in it ever since. The sauce is mayonnaise and vinegar, not tomato: keep it thin and tangy, and sauce the bird at the end, never during the smoke.

m: Salt the tomato slices and let them drain on paper 15 min.
Set up a dredge: buttermilk in one dish, and the cornmeal, flour, salt, pepper, and cayenne mixed in another.
Dip each slice in buttermilk, then cornmeal, pressing it on.
Fry in 5mm of oil over medium-high heat 2-3 min a side until deep gold and crisp.
Drain, salt, and serve hot with remoulade.
p: Under-ripe tomatoes are firm and tart enough to hold up to frying where a ripe one collapses. Cornmeal is the traditional Southern coat and it gives the crunch that plain flour cannot.

i: For the meringue: 4 egg whites, 100g sugar, 1/4 tsp cream of tartar
m: Make a custard: heat the milk and cream, whisk yolks with sugar and cornstarch, temper, return, and cook to a thick boil. Off heat beat in butter and vanilla.
Layer wafers, banana slices, and custard in a dish, repeating and ending with custard.
Whip the whites with cream of tartar, adding the sugar slowly, to stiff glossy peaks.
Spread the meringue over the pudding, sealing to the edges.
Bake at 175C for 15-20 min until the meringue is golden. Cool, then chill 2 hours.
p: The baked, meringue-topped version is the Southern church-supper standard, distinct from the icebox kind. Seal the meringue right to the edge of the dish or it will shrink and weep as it bakes.

m: Soak the catfish in buttermilk and hot sauce 30 min.
Mix the cornmeal, flour, and seasonings in a wide dish.
Heat the oil to 190C in a cast-iron skillet or deep pot.
Dredge the fillets in the cornmeal, pressing it on, and fry 4-5 min until deep gold and floating.
Drain on a rack, salt at once, and serve with lemon, hot sauce, hush puppies, and slaw.
p: All-cornmeal coating is the Deep South standard for catfish: it fries up sandy-crisp and shatters. Get the oil properly hot so the crust sets before the fish overcooks.

i: For the cake: 320g flour, 1 tbsp baking powder, 1/2 tsp salt, 225g butter, 400g sugar, 8 egg whites, 250ml milk, 1 tsp vanilla
For the filling: 8 egg yolks, 200g sugar, 115g butter, 150g raisins, 100g pecans, 100g coconut, 120ml bourbon
m: Cream the butter and sugar, alternate the dry ingredients with the milk, then fold in whipped egg whites. Bake in three 23cm pans at 175C for 22-25 min. Cool.
For the filling, cook the yolks, sugar, and butter over low heat, stirring, until thick, 8 min.
Off the heat stir in the raisins, pecans, coconut, and bourbon.
Cool the filling, then spread it thick between the cake layers.
Cover the outside with a simple white frosting and let it set.
p: Made famous by Harper Lee's Mockingbird, where it is described as loaded enough with bourbon to affect a neighbor. The boozy fruit-and-nut filling is the heart of it: the cake is just the vehicle.

i: Salt, black pepper, and hot sauce
m: Brown the sausage in a heavy pot until it renders and colors; lift out and reserve.
Sweat the onion, celery, and garlic in the fat until soft.
Add the drained beans, bay, thyme, and stock and simmer 90 min until the beans are creamy.
Return the sausage and simmer 20 min more, mashing some beans against the pot to thicken.
Season and serve with cornbread and hot sauce.
p: Conecuh County sausage is Alabama's smoky pride, and a pot of white beans is its natural home. Salt only near the end: early salt keeps the bean skins tough for hours.

i: For the topping: 190g flour, 100g sugar, 2 tsp baking powder, 1/2 tsp salt, 115g butter melted, 180ml milk
m: Toss the peaches with sugar, cornstarch, and cinnamon and spread in a buttered dish.
Whisk the topping ingredients into a batter and spoon it over the fruit in patches.
Scatter the pecans over the top.
Bake at 190C for 45-50 min until the topping is gold and the fruit bubbles.
Rest 20 min and serve with ice cream.
p: Chilton County peaches are Alabama's summer glory. The pecans on top toast as the cobbler bakes and add a crunch the fruit and cake lack on their own.

m: Sweat the onions in the butter until soft.
Add the tomatoes, potatoes, and stock and simmer 30 min.
Add the limas and cook 15 min, then the corn and the smoked meat.
Stir in the barbecue sauce, Worcestershire, and vinegar and simmer 45 min uncovered.
Season and cook down until thick enough to hold a spoon upright.
p: Served alongside barbecue across the state, and like all Brunswick stews it must be cooked down thick. The smoked meat in the base is what ties it to the pit it sits beside.

i: For the cornbread: 250g cornmeal, 60g flour, 1 tbsp baking powder, 1 tsp salt, 2 eggs, 400ml buttermilk, 3 tbsp bacon fat
m: Bake the cornbread in a hot cast-iron skillet and let it go stale overnight; crumble it with the torn white bread.
Sweat the onion and celery in the butter until soft.
Mix the crumbs, vegetables, sage, and thyme, then stir in the beaten eggs and enough stock to make it wet and loose, wetter than seems right.
Spread in a buttered dish.
Bake at 190C for 40-45 min until set and browned on top.
p: Southern dressing is baked in a pan, not stuffed in a bird, and it starts with real cornbread gone stale. Make the mixture wetter than you think: it firms as it bakes, and a dry dressing is the holiday's quiet disappointment.

m: Toss the sliced okra in the buttermilk to coat.
Mix the cornmeal, flour, salt, pepper, and cayenne in a bag.
Lift the okra out, letting the excess buttermilk drip, and toss in the cornmeal mix until coated.
Fry in 1cm of hot oil over medium-high heat, in batches, 4-5 min until deep gold and crisp, turning as it browns.
Drain on paper, salt at once, and serve immediately.
p: High heat and a cornmeal coat are what defeat okra's famous slime: the mucilage sets and crisps instead of running. Do not crowd the pan or the temperature drops and the okra steams into the very thing you were avoiding.

i: For the crust: 250g chocolate cookies crushed, 115g butter melted
For the fudge layer: 200g dark chocolate, 115g butter, 3 eggs, 150g sugar, 50g flour
For the mousse: 300g dark chocolate, 500ml cream, 2 tbsp sugar
m: Mix the cookie crumbs and butter, press into a springform, and chill.
Melt the chocolate and butter, whisk in the eggs, sugar, and flour, pour over the crust, and bake at 175C for 25 min until set with a slight wobble. Cool.
Melt the mousse chocolate and cool slightly. Whip the cream with the sugar and fold it in.
Spread the mousse thick over the cooled fudge layer.
Chill 4 hours, then top with chocolate shavings and unmould.
p: Named for the thick dark mud of the Mississippi River, and the point is the layers of increasing intensity, dense fudge under airy mousse. Let the fudge layer cool fully before the mousse goes on or it will melt into it.

m: Whisk the mayonnaise, chili sauce, and oil together until smooth.
Beat in the Worcestershire, mustard, hot sauce, and grated garlic.
Add the paprika, black pepper, and lemon juice.
Season to taste: it should be tangy, garlicky, and a little spicy.
Chill at least 2 hours so the garlic mellows and the flavors marry. Keeps a week.
p: Jackson's all-purpose sauce, born in the Greek-owned restaurants of the mid-century — good on everything from fried catfish to crackers to salad. The rest in the fridge is essential; freshly made, the raw garlic dominates everything.

i: For the filling: 700g ground beef or pork, 2 tbsp chili powder, 1 tbsp cumin, 1 tbsp paprika, 1 tsp cayenne, 3 garlic cloves minced, 1 tsp salt
For the masa: 400g masa harina, 120ml lard, 700ml warm broth, 1 tbsp chili powder, 2 tsp salt
m: Mix the raw meat with all the filling spices and garlic; it cooks inside the tamale.
Beat the lard until fluffy, then work in the masa harina, spiced broth, chili powder, and salt to a soft, spreadable dough.
Spread masa thinly on each soaked husk, add a line of filling, and roll tight, folding the bottom.
Stand the tamales upright, packed close, in a deep pot and cover with spiced broth.
Simmer covered 90 min until the masa pulls cleanly from the husk. Serve dripping in the broth.
p: The Delta tamale is simmered in broth rather than steamed, which is what makes it wetter and spicier than its Mexican cousin, a Mississippi tradition since sharecropping days. Spread the masa thin; a thick-walled tamale is stodgy.

m: Soak the catfish in the buttermilk and hot sauce 30 min.
Season the cornmeal with salt, pepper, cayenne, and garlic powder.
Heat the oil to 190C.
Dredge the fillets in seasoned cornmeal, pressing it on, and fry 4-5 min until they float and turn deep gold.
Drain, salt, and serve with lemon, hush puppies, and slaw.
p: Mississippi is the catfish-farming capital of America, and the Delta fries it in pure cornmeal, no flour. A candy thermometer earns its keep here: below 180C the crust sponges up oil, above 200C it burns before the fish is done.

i: 1 packet ranch seasoning (or 2 tbsp dried herbs, buttermilk powder, garlic)
1 packet au jus mix (or 2 tbsp beef base and cornstarch)
8 pepperoncini peppers, plus 60ml of their brine
m: Dust the roast with flour and sear all sides hard in the oil in a Dutch oven.
Scatter the ranch and au jus seasonings over the meat.
Lay the stick of butter on top and arrange the pepperoncini and their brine around.
Cover and braise at 150C for 4 hours, or in a slow cooker on low 8 hours, until it shreds.
Shred the meat, stir it through the buttery pepper juices, and serve on rolls or over mashed potatoes.
p: A viral 2010s recipe from Ripley, Mississippi, and genuinely good despite the packet mixes. The pepperoncini brine is the secret: it cuts the butter and richness with just enough tang to keep the whole thing from being heavy.

m: Grate the raw sweet potatoes on the coarse side of a box grater.
Whisk the cane syrup, brown sugar, eggs, milk, melted butter, spices, salt, and orange zest.
Stir in the grated sweet potato.
Pour into a buttered dish and bake at 175C for 55-65 min, stirring once at the halfway mark so it cooks evenly.
The finished pone is dense, dark, and set. Serve warm.
p: Older than sweet potato pie and made from raw grated potato rather than mashed cooked flesh, which gives it a chewy, pudding-dense texture. Stirring once partway through keeps the edges from setting hard before the middle cooks.

i: Lard or peanut oil for frying
m: Brine the chicken in buttermilk and hot sauce overnight.
Season the flour heavily with the salt, pepper, paprika, cayenne, and garlic powder.
Dredge each piece, rest on a rack 15 min so the crust sets, then dredge a second time for extra crunch.
Fry in 165C fat in a cast-iron skillet, dark meat 15 min and white 13, turning once, to a deep mahogany and 74C internal.
Drain on a rack and rest 5 min before serving.
p: The double dredge is the Delta trick for an armored crust. Lard fries the finest chicken there is, and a cast-iron skillet holds heat steady where a thin pan swings and burns.

m: Soak the shrimp in buttermilk 20 min.
Mix the flour, cornmeal, Cajun seasoning, and salt.
Heat the oil to 190C.
Dredge the shrimp, shake off the excess, and fry in small batches 90 seconds until gold.
Drain, salt, and serve with a bowl of comeback sauce for dipping.
p: Gulf shrimp and comeback sauce are a Mississippi marriage. Shrimp fry in barely a minute and a half: pull them the second they turn, because carryover heat finishes them on the plate.

i: For the pastry: 375g flour, 1 tsp salt, 170g cold butter or shortening, 120ml cold buttermilk
For the filling: 300g dried apricots or peaches, 250ml water, 100g sugar, 1/2 tsp cinnamon
m: Simmer the dried fruit with the water and sugar until soft and thick, 20 min, then mash and cool.
Cut the fat into the flour and salt, bind with buttermilk, and chill 30 min.
Roll the pastry thin and cut 12cm rounds. Spoon fruit onto one half, fold over, and crimp the edges hard with a fork.
Fry in 180C oil 2-3 min a side until deep gold and blistered.
Drain and dust with icing sugar while warm.
p: Dried fruit, not fresh, is traditional: it makes a thick filling that will not burst the crust in the fryer. Crimp the edges firmly and fry a test pie first to make sure the seal holds.

m: Whisk the cocoa, sugar, flour, and salt together in a saucepan while it is still off the heat.
Slowly whisk in the milk until smooth, then set over medium heat.
Cook, whisking constantly, 6-8 min until it thickens to a pourable gravy.
Off the heat beat in the butter and vanilla.
Ladle hot over split biscuits and serve immediately.
p: An Ozark breakfast tradition, poured over biscuits like sausage gravy's sweet cousin. Whisk the dry ingredients before the milk goes in: cocoa and flour added to hot liquid clump instantly and never smooth out.

i: Salt, black pepper, and hot sauce
m: Dredge the meat in seasoned flour and brown hard in the oil; set aside.
Cook the onions in the same pan until deep gold, scraping up the fond, then add the garlic.
Sprinkle in the remaining seasoned flour and cook to a brown roux.
Whisk in the stock and thyme, return the meat, cover, and simmer 45 min until tender and the gravy is rich.
Season and serve over the cooked rice.
p: Arkansas grows nearly half the nation's rice, so rice and gravy is a weeknight birthright. The browned onions and a proper brown roux are what give the gravy its color and depth: pale gravy tastes of flour.

i: For the crust: 150g flour, 115g butter, 75g chopped pecans
For the cream layer: 200g cream cheese, 100g icing sugar, 250ml whipped cream
For the chocolate layer: 500ml milk, 4 yolks, 100g sugar, 40g cornstarch, 100g dark chocolate
Whipped cream and pecans to finish
m: Rub the flour, butter, and pecans together, press into a pie plate, and bake at 175C for 20 min. Cool.
Beat the cream cheese and icing sugar smooth, fold in the whipped cream, and spread over the cooled crust.
Make a chocolate pudding: heat the milk, whisk yolks with sugar and cornstarch, temper, return, add the chocolate, and cook to a thick boil. Cool slightly.
Spread the chocolate pudding over the cream cheese layer.
Chill 3 hours, then top with whipped cream and pecans.
p: It is called possum pie because it plays possum: the plain-looking top hides the layers beneath. Let the chocolate pudding cool before it goes on the cream cheese or the two layers merge into one.

m: Melt the butter in a saucepan and cook the garlic 30 seconds.
Add the cheese and milk and melt over low heat, stirring constantly, until smooth.
Stir in the tomato, jalapenos, cumin, and chili powder.
Keep warm over the lowest heat, loosening with a splash of milk if it thickens.
Serve hot with tortilla chips.
p: Arkansas claims to have invented cheese dip in the 1930s, before Texas queso, and holds a competition over it. Low heat and constant stirring keep it silky: a boil makes the cheese seize and turn oily.

i: For the batter: 115g butter, 190g flour, 200g sugar, 2 tsp baking powder, 1/4 tsp salt, 240ml milk
m: Toss the blackberries with the sugar, cornstarch, and lemon and let them stand 15 min.
Melt the butter in a baking dish in the oven as it heats to 190C.
Whisk the flour, sugar, baking powder, salt, and milk into a batter and pour it over the melted butter: do not stir.
Spoon the berries and juice over the batter; do not stir.
Bake 45-55 min until the cake has risen around the fruit and browned deeply.
p: Wild blackberries grow thick along Ozark fencerows in July. As with all batter cobblers, the trick is not stirring: the cake floats up through the berries as it bakes, and stirring ruins the effect.

i: 2 tbsp salt, 1 tbsp pepper, 1 tsp cayenne, 1 tsp paprika
For the waffles: 250g flour, 2 tsp baking powder, 1 tbsp sugar, 1/2 tsp salt, 2 eggs, 400ml buttermilk, 85g butter melted
m: Brine the chicken in buttermilk and hot sauce 4 hours. Dredge in seasoned flour, rest, and fry at 165C for 14-16 min until deep gold and 74C internal.
Whisk the waffle dry ingredients. Separately whisk eggs, buttermilk, and melted butter, then combine lightly.
Cook the waffles in a hot iron until crisp and golden.
Set a piece of fried chicken on each waffle.
Drizzle with maple syrup and hot honey and serve at once.
p: The sweet-savory-spicy combination is the whole joy: maple for sweet, hot honey for heat, salt from the crust. Keep the fried chicken on a rack in a warm oven so it stays crisp while the waffles cook.

i: For the dumplings: 250g flour, 2 tsp baking powder, 1 tsp salt, 3 tbsp cold butter, 180ml cold buttermilk
m: Sweat the onion, celery, and carrot in the butter, then stir in the flour and cook 2 min.
Whisk in the stock and simmer 15 min, then add the cream, thyme, and shredded turkey.
Cut the cold butter into the flour, baking powder, and salt, then bind with buttermilk to a soft dough.
Drop spoonfuls of dough onto the simmering stew, cover tightly, and cook 15 min without lifting the lid.
Season, scatter with parsley, and serve.
p: Smoked turkey gives the stew a depth that plain poached bird cannot. Do not lift the lid while the dumplings cook: they steam-rise, and letting the steam out gives you dense, gummy dumplings.

i: For the Mornay: 55g butter, 55g flour, 500ml milk, 100g Pecorino or Parmesan, 60ml cream, pinch of nutmeg
m: Make the Mornay: melt the butter, cook in the flour 2 min, whisk in the milk, and simmer to a thick sauce. Off the heat stir in the cheese, cream, and nutmeg.
Set two pieces of toast in each gratin dish and pile the turkey on top.
Cover the turkey completely with the Mornay: it must be sealed or it will dry out.
Grill under a hot broiler until bubbling and browned in spots.
Top each with tomato slices, crisp bacon, paprika, and parsley and serve at once.
p: Invented at the Brown Hotel in Louisville in 1926 as a late-supper dish for dancers. The turkey must be fully blanketed in Mornay before it goes under the grill: any exposed meat dries to leather.

m: Simmer all three meats in the water 2 hours until falling apart. Lift out, shred, discarding bones, and keep the broth.
Return the broth to the pot with the onions, tomatoes, and potatoes and simmer 45 min.
Add the limas, corn, and cabbage and cook 30 min.
Return the shredded meat, add Worcestershire and vinegar, and simmer 90 min, stirring often, until thick and melded.
Season hard with cayenne, salt, and pepper. It should be almost a stew, not a soup.
p: A Bluegrass burgoo is a communal pot for festivals and derby day, traditionally with three meats and whatever the garden gives. Long, slow, uncovered cooking is what marries it: a burgoo rushed is just vegetable soup with too much meat.

m: Scatter the pecans and chocolate chips in the shell.
Whisk the eggs, both sugars, melted butter, flour, bourbon, vanilla, and salt until smooth.
Pour over the nuts and chocolate.
Bake at 175C for 45-50 min until set at the edges with a slight wobble at the center.
Cool completely before slicing so the chocolate re-sets.
p: A chocolate-walnut-bourbon pie tied to the Derby (the trademarked name belongs to one bakery, so everyone else calls it something careful). The flour in the filling keeps it sliceable rather than gooey: do not leave it out.

m: Let the cheese come to room temperature and grate it fresh.
Put the cheese, garlic, mustard, Worcestershire, cayenne, and paprika in a food processor.
With the motor running, pour in the flat beer a little at a time until it comes together into a smooth, spreadable paste.
Taste and adjust the heat and salt.
Chill at least 2 hours; it firms and the flavors meld. Serve with pretzels and vegetables.
p: A snack from the Ohio River towns near Winchester, spread on everything at a Kentucky gathering. Use flat, room-temperature beer: cold beer seizes the cheese, and the fizz makes the paste foamy.

m: Scald the milk, rain in the cornmeal whisking hard, and cook 5 min to a thick mush.
Beat in the butter, salt, and sugar, then cool 10 min.
Beat in the egg yolks one at a time, then the baking powder.
Whip the whites to soft peaks and fold through in two additions.
Pour into a buttered dish and bake at 190C for 35-40 min until puffed and golden. Serve at once with a spoon.
p: Kentucky claims spoonbread as hard as Virginia does, and Berea holds a festival for it. It is a savory cornmeal souffle and it falls fast: get it to the table straight from the oven.

i: A drop of green food coloring (traditional, optional)
m: Grate the cucumber and onion, then squeeze both hard in a cloth to remove all their water: this is the crucial step.
Beat the cream cheese smooth with the mayonnaise and lemon.
Fold in the drained cucumber and onion.
Season with salt and white pepper, and tint the palest green if you want the traditional look.
Chill an hour. Spread on crustless white bread for tea sandwiches, or serve as a dip.
p: Created by Louisville caterer Jennie Benedict around 1900. Wringing every drop of water from the cucumber is the difference between a spread and a puddle: a watery benedictine soaks the bread to mush within minutes.

i: 150g vanilla wafers or pecans, ground fine
m: Beat the butter with the icing sugar, bourbon, and corn syrup until smooth.
Work in the ground wafers and chopped pecans to a stiff, moldable paste.
Roll into small balls and chill on a tray until firm, 30 min.
Melt the chocolate and dip each ball, letting the excess drip off.
Set on parchment, press a pecan half on top, and let the chocolate firm up. They improve after a day.
p: A Derby-season confection and a bourbon-country gift. Chill the centers hard before dipping or they fall apart in the warm chocolate, and let them rest a day so the raw bourbon mellows into the pecan.

m: Brine the chicken in buttermilk overnight.
Season the flour with the salt, pepper, paprika, cayenne, and sage.
Dredge each piece and rest on a rack 15 min so the coating sets.
Melt lard in a cast-iron skillet to a depth of 2cm and heat to 165C. Fry covered for the first half so the meat steams through, then uncovered to crisp, turning once, 15-18 min total.
Drain on a rack and rest 5 min.
p: Skillet-fried and lard-cooked is the old Kentucky way, older than any bucket. Covering the pan for the first half steams the meat tender before the crust locks; uncovering finishes the crackle.

m: Salt the tomato slices and drain on paper 15 min.
Set up buttermilk in one dish and the cornmeal, flour, salt, pepper, and cayenne in another.
Dip each slice in buttermilk, then dredge in the cornmeal mix.
Fry in 5mm oil over medium-high 2-3 min a side until deep gold and crisp.
Drain, salt, and serve hot with comeback sauce.
p: Firm green tomatoes hold up to the fryer where a ripe one turns to mush. Comeback sauce is the Mississippi partner, sharp and garlicky against the tart fruit.

m: Butter a sheet of parchment on a tray.
Combine both sugars, the cream, butter, and salt and cook to 116C on a candy thermometer, stirring.
Off the heat stir in the vanilla and pecans and beat until the mixture starts to lose its shine and thicken.
Drop tablespoons quickly onto the parchment before it sets.
Cool until firm. They should be creamy, not grainy.
p: Beating the candy off the heat is what turns it from a shiny syrup into a creamy praline. Stop dropping the moment it thickens: it seizes fast, and a praline poured too late is a lump.

m: Soak the livers in buttermilk and hot sauce 30 min.
Season the flour with the salt, pepper, cayenne, and garlic powder.
Heat the oil to 180C.
Dredge the livers, shake off the excess, and fry carefully 3-4 min until deep gold and just cooked through: they spit, so use a screen.
Drain, salt, and serve with comeback sauce.
p: A Southern snack and diner staple. Do not overcook them: livers turn chalky in seconds past done, and they should stay just pink and creamy at the center.

m: Put the bacon fat in a cast-iron skillet and heat it in a 220C oven until smoking.
Whisk the cornmeal, flour, baking powder, soda, and salt.
Beat in the eggs and buttermilk quickly to a loose batter.
Pour the batter into the screaming-hot fat, it should sizzle hard, and return to the oven.
Bake 20-25 min until the top is gold and the edges are crisp. Turn out and serve hot with butter.
p: The smoking-hot skillet is the whole secret to the crackling crust. Ozark cornbread carries no sugar — sweet cornbread is a Northern habit that starts arguments below the Mason-Dixon line.

m: Whisk the sugar and melted butter together.
Beat in the eggs one at a time, then the cream, flour, vanilla, and salt.
Pour into the shell.
Bake at 175C for 40-50 min until the top is golden and just set with a slight wobble.
Cool completely; it firms as it cools into a translucent custard.
p: A Maysville specialty and cousin to chess pie, but simpler and clearer: no cornmeal, no vinegar, just a translucent butter custard. It should set to a shimmer, so pull it while the center still moves.

m: Sweat the onion, carrot, and celery in the butter until soft, 10 min.
Stir in the flour and cook 2 min to a blond roux.
Whisk in the stock and beer and simmer 10 min, then add the milk.
Off the heat, add the cheese in handfuls, stirring until each melts before adding more: never let it boil after the cheese goes in.
Season with mustard, Worcestershire, cayenne, salt, and pepper. Top each bowl with popcorn, the Kentucky touch.
p: The soup form of Kentucky's beloved beer cheese. As with any cheese soup, the pot comes off the heat before the cheese goes in: a boil turns it grainy and greasy. Popcorn on top is not a joke; it is tradition.

m: Break the raw beef into the water in a cold pot and mash it very fine: never brown it first; the boiling is what gives the smooth texture.
Add the grated onion, all the spices, cloves, bay, vinegar, and tomato paste.
Simmer uncovered 1.5-2 hours, stirring, until dark and slightly thickened but still loose.
Cook the spaghetti and lay it on plates.
Ladle the chili over for a two-way; add beans and onions for a three or four-way, and always bury it under a mound of fine-grated cheddar.
p: Greek-Macedonian immigrants built this in 1922 and it is a spiced meat sauce, not a Texas chili: the cocoa, cinnamon, and clove are the signature. Simmering raw beef in water is the trick to its fine, saucelike grind.

m: Simmer the oats in the water with the bay, onions, and seasonings 1 hour until thick and creamy.
Add the raw ground meats, breaking them up, and cook 1 more hour, stirring often, until very thick.
Season boldly: it dulls once cold. Pack into loaf pans and chill overnight until solid.
Slice 1cm thick.
Fry in butter over medium heat 5-6 min a side without moving it, until a deep crust forms.
p: Cincinnati's German answer to scrapple, bulked with oats instead of cornmeal. As with scrapple, the one rule is patience in the pan: leave the slice alone until the crust sets or it crumbles.

m: Beat the peanut butter, butter, vanilla, and salt together.
Work in the icing sugar until stiff enough to roll into balls.
Roll into balls and chill on a tray 30 min until firm.
Melt the chocolate with the shortening. Spear each ball on a toothpick and dip most of the way, leaving a circle of peanut butter showing at the top.
Set on parchment and smooth the toothpick hole. Chill to firm.
p: They are made to look like the nut of the Ohio buckeye tree, hence the ring of exposed peanut butter left at the top. Keep the centers cold before dipping or they slump in the warm chocolate.

i: 500g sauerkraut, drained and squeezed dry, chopped
For coating: 100g flour, 2 eggs beaten, 150g breadcrumbs
m: Brown the sausage with the onion, then stir in the flour and cook 2 min.
Add the chopped kraut, cream cheese, mustard, and caraway and cook until it binds into a thick paste. Cool and chill.
Roll into walnut-sized balls.
Dredge in flour, then egg, then breadcrumbs.
Fry at 180C for 3-4 min until deep gold. Drain and serve hot with mustard.
p: An Akron party staple with roots in the German communities. Squeeze the kraut bone-dry before it goes in: any water left in it makes the mixture too loose to roll and the balls burst in the oil.

m: Whisk the flour, baking powder, salt, and sugar.
Beat in the eggs and milk to a thick batter.
Fold in the corn, bacon, and scallions.
Drop heaped spoonfuls into 180C oil and fry 3-4 min, turning, until deep gold.
Drain and salt at once.
p: A late-summer supper from the corn belt. Keep the batter thick enough that a spoonful holds its shape when it hits the oil: a thin batter spreads and the fritters fry greasy and flat.

i: 6 small tart apples, peeled and cored
Pastry for a double batch, rolled thin
For the filling: 100g brown sugar, 55g butter, 1 tsp cinnamon
For the syrup: 400g sugar, 500ml water, 55g butter, 1 tsp cinnamon
m: Cut the pastry into six squares large enough to wrap an apple.
Set an apple on each square, pack the cavity with brown sugar, butter, and cinnamon, and draw the pastry up to seal at the top.
Arrange in a buttered baking dish.
Boil the syrup ingredients together 5 min and pour around the dumplings.
Bake at 190C for 40-45 min, basting once with the syrup, until the pastry is gold and the apples are tender. Serve warm with cream.
p: An Amish-country dessert where the apple bakes whole inside its pastry shell. Baste once with the syrup partway through: it glazes the pastry and keeps the tops from drying before the apples soften.

i: For the fries: 500g cut fries, fried crisp
For the slaw: 300g cabbage, 4 tbsp mayonnaise, 1 tbsp vinegar, 1 tsp sugar, salt
m: Grill or fry the kielbasa until browned and blistered.
Fry the potatoes until deeply crisp and salt them.
Dress the cabbage with mayonnaise, vinegar, sugar, and salt for a quick slaw.
Set a sausage in each bun, then pile the fries directly on top.
Douse with warm barbecue sauce and crown with slaw. Eat with many napkins.
p: A Cleveland street-food monument: sausage, fries, slaw, and barbecue sauce all in one bun. The fries go inside, on top of the sausage, and the whole thing is meant to be structurally unsound.

m: Season and brown the chicken thighs skin-side down until deeply gold; set aside.
Sweat the onion and garlic in the fat until soft.
Add the stock, cider, vinegar, brown sugar, mustard, and thyme and scrape up the fond.
Return the chicken skin-side up, cover, and simmer 30 min. Uncover and reduce the sauce 10 min more until glossy.
Season and serve with the pan sauce over mashed potatoes.
p: A cider-braised farmhouse chicken from Ohio's orchard country. Uncovering it at the end to reduce the sauce is what turns thin braising liquid into a glaze worth the potatoes underneath.

m: Butter a marble slab or sheet pan.
Boil the sugar, cream, corn syrup, butter, and salt to 114C, stirring gently.
Pour onto the slab and let it cool to lukewarm without stirring.
Work it with a spatula, folding and turning, until it turns creamy, opaque, and thick, 10-15 min.
Add the vanilla, form into small logs or squares, let them dry an hour, then dip in melted chocolate.
