p: A Cincinnati confectionery tradition, softer and creamier than fudge. The patience is in the cooling: stir it hot and it turns grainy; let it drop to lukewarm before you work it and it turns silk.

i: 4 pork loin cutlets, pounded to 5mm and wider than the bun
1 tsp salt, 1/2 tsp pepper, 1/2 tsp garlic powder
m: Pound the cutlets between plastic to a thin, wide oval — they should overhang the bun by inches.
Set up flour, the egg wash, and the seasoned crumbs.
Dredge each cutlet in flour, then egg, then crumbs, pressing them on firmly.
Fry in 5mm of 180C oil 2-3 min a side until deep gold and crisp.
Set on a bun that it dwarfs and dress lightly with mustard, pickle, and onion.
p: The tenderloin must be pounded thin and fried wide enough to embarrass the bun: the comic overhang is the whole Indiana identity. Pound it between plastic wrap so it stretches instead of tearing.

m: Whisk the brown sugar, cornstarch, and salt in a saucepan.
Slowly whisk in the cream until smooth, then set over medium heat.
Cook, whisking constantly, until it thickens and bubbles, 8-10 min. Off the heat beat in the butter and vanilla.
Pour into the baked shell and dust the top with nutmeg and cinnamon.
Bake at 220C for 10 min just to set the top, then cool and chill 3 hours.
p: The unofficial state pie, also called Hoosier pie: a custard with no eggs, thickened by cornstarch alone. Whisk without stopping while it cooks; the moment you pause, the bottom scorches and the whole pie tastes of it.

m: Push very ripe persimmons through a sieve for smooth pulp: under-ripe fruit is unbearably astringent.
Beat the pulp with the sugar and eggs, then the buttermilk and melted butter.
Whisk the flour, soda, baking powder, cinnamon, and salt and stir in, then thin with the milk to a loose batter.
Pour into a buttered dish and bake at 175C for 55-65 min until set and deeply browned, the edges pulling from the sides.
Cool and serve in squares with whipped cream.
p: Southern Indiana holds a persimmon festival in Mitchell every autumn. Only fully ripe, jelly-soft native persimmons will do; an under-ripe one turns the whole pudding mouth-puckeringly astringent.

n: Hoosier Fried Biscuits with Apple Butter
m: Mix the flour, yeast, sugar, and salt, then add the milk and melted butter and knead to a soft dough. Rise 1 hour.
Roll to 1cm thick and cut into squares or rounds.
Heat the oil to 180C.
Fry the biscuits 2-3 min, turning, until puffed and deep gold.
Drain and serve hot with apple butter.
p: A Brown County tradition, served by the basket at family-style restaurants. Fry them the moment they are cut: a fried biscuit left to over-proof deflates in the oil instead of puffing.

m: Brown the sausage in a large skillet; lift out and reserve.
Cook the diced potato in the rendered fat until tender and browned, 10 min.
Add the onion and pepper and cook 5 min, then the corn and cook 3 min over high heat.
Return the sausage, add the cream and thyme, and simmer 3 min until it thickens slightly.
Season and finish with parsley. Serve straight from the skillet.
p: A one-pan farm supper built on the corn belt's summer glut. Cook the corn hard and briefly so it keeps its snap; simmered corn goes starchy and tired.

i: For the noodles: 250g flour, 3 egg yolks, 1 egg, 1/2 tsp salt, 3 tbsp broth
m: Make the noodles: mound the flour, add the eggs and salt, and work to a stiff dough with a little broth. Rest 30 min, roll very thin, cut into ribbons, and dry 20 min.
Brown the chicken in the oil, then set aside and sweat the vegetables in the fat.
Add the stock, return the chicken, and simmer 30 min. Pull the chicken, shred it, and return the meat.
Drop the noodles into the simmering broth and cook 12-15 min until tender and the broth thickens.
Season and serve: traditionally ladled over mashed potatoes.
p: Chicken and noodles over mashed potatoes is a Hoosier comfort classic, carbohydrate on carbohydrate without apology. Homemade egg noodles thicken the broth as they cook — that starch is the point.

m: Rub the flour, sugar, and butter to crumbs, press into a lined pan, and bake at 175C for 18 min until pale gold.
Whisk the brown sugar and cornstarch in a pan, slowly add the cream, and cook stirring until thick.
Off the heat beat in the butter and vanilla and pour over the crust.
Dust with nutmeg and chill until set.
Cut into bars.
p: Sugar cream pie in a hand-held form. As with the pie, whisk the filling without stopping: the cornstarch catches and scorches the instant you turn your back.

i: For the dough: 400g flour, 60g cornmeal, 7g yeast, 1 tsp salt, 240ml warm water, 60ml oil, 3 tbsp melted butter
400g crushed San Marzano tomatoes, seasoned with garlic, oregano, salt
m: Mix the dough with the cornmeal and butter, knead briefly, and rise 1 hour.
Press the dough up the sides of an oiled deep 23cm cake pan to form a tall crust.
Lay the mozzarella slices directly on the dough first: this protects it from the sauce.
Add any fillings, then top with the crushed tomatoes and a blanket of Parmesan.
Bake at 220C for 30-35 min until the crust is deep gold and the sauce bubbles. Rest 10 min before cutting.
p: The order is upside down for a reason: cheese on the bottom keeps the long bake from turning the crust soggy, and the chunky tomato on top does not overcook. Rest it before cutting or the whole thing lands in your lap.

i: 2kg beef top round or sirloin roast
For giardiniera: pickled peppers, celery, carrot, chopped
m: Rub the roast with the seasonings and roast at 160C to 55C internal for rare, about 90 min. Chill completely: this is essential for thin slicing.
Slice the cold beef as thin as humanly possible on a slicer or with a very sharp knife.
Heat the stock with the roasting juices and any leftover seasoning to make the jus.
Warm the beef slices in the jus just until heated through: never simmer them.
Pile into rolls and top with giardiniera or sweet peppers. For 'wet', dip the whole roll in jus.
p: Chilling the roast before slicing is non-negotiable: warm beef tears instead of shaving thin. Order it dipped, wet, or dry, hot with giardiniera or sweet with peppers, but the beef only warms in the jus; boiling it makes it grey and tough.

m: Steam or simmer the hot dogs until plump and hot, never grilled, by tradition.
Steam the poppy seed buns until soft.
Lay the dog in the bun and add, in order: mustard, relish, onion, tomato wedges along one side.
Tuck in a pickle spear and two sport peppers.
Finish with a dash of celery salt. And never, under any circumstances, ketchup.
p: Dragged through the garden, as they say: the whole point is the parade of toppings. The one iron law of Chicago is no ketchup on a hot dog; the celery salt at the end is what ties the garden together.

i: 4 hamburger patties or fried pork cutlets
For the cheese sauce: 55g butter, 55g flour, 500ml milk, 300g sharp cheddar, 1 tsp mustard, 1 tsp Worcestershire, dash of beer, cayenne
m: Make the cheese sauce: cook a roux with the butter and flour, whisk in the milk, and simmer to a thick sauce. Off the heat stir in the cheddar, mustard, Worcestershire, beer, and cayenne.
Toast the bread and lay it in a shallow dish or plate.
Set the cooked meat patties on the toast.
Pile the crisp fries on top of the meat.
Smother the whole thing in the hot cheese sauce and dust with paprika. Eat with a fork.
p: A Springfield open-faced monster: the name comes from the U-shape the meat once made on the plate. The cheese sauce must be smooth and pourable; keep it off a hard boil once the cheese goes in or it turns grainy.

i: 6 ears corn, kernels and scraped milk
m: Cut the kernels from the cobs, then scrape the cobs hard for the starchy milk.
Whisk the eggs, milk, cream, melted butter, flour, sugar, salt, and pepper.
Stir in the corn and scrapings and pour into a buttered dish.
Grate nutmeg over the top.
Bake at 175C for 45-55 min until set at the edges with a slight wobble at the center.
p: Prairie-state corn at its most comforting. Scraping the cobs for their milk is what sets the pudding: that starchy liquid is nature's cornstarch, and skipping it leaves you with corn soup.

i: 2 garlic cloves, mashed with 2 tbsp oil and salt (mojo)
m: Peel the plantains and cut each lengthwise into two flat slabs.
Fry the slabs in 170C oil 3 min until soft but pale; flatten each between two boards, then fry again until crisp and golden. These are the 'bread'.
Season and quickly sear the skirt steak with the garlic oil until browned.
Brush one plantain slab with the garlic mojo, then layer steak, cheese, lettuce, tomato, and mayonnaise.
Top with a second plantain slab, press, and cut in half.
p: A Puerto Rican Chicago invention using fried flattened plantains in place of bread. Fry the plantains twice (once to soften, once to crisp) and brush the mojo on while they are hot so it soaks in.

m: Whisk the flour, baking powder, cinnamon, ginger, and salt.
Beat the eggs, sugar, oil, and pumpkin until smooth, then fold in the dry ingredients.
Spread in a lined sheet pan and bake at 175C for 25-30 min until a skewer comes clean. Cool completely.
Beat the cream cheese, butter, icing sugar, and vanilla into a smooth frosting.
Spread over the cooled bars and cut into squares.
p: Illinois grows more pumpkins than any state, nearly all of it for canning near Morton. These sheet-pan bars are the church-supper staple. Cool them completely before frosting or the cream cheese slides right off.

i: For the dough: 400g bread flour, 300ml warm water, 7g yeast, 1 tsp salt, 2 tbsp oil
300g brick cheese or Monterey Jack, cubed, spread to the edges
m: Mix the wet dough, knead briefly, and rise 1 hour. Press it into a well-oiled rectangular steel pan and rise 1 hour more until it fills the pan.
Lay the pepperoni on the dough if using.
Scatter the cheese cubes right to the edges of the pan: the cheese caramelizing against the metal is the whole point.
Spoon the sauce over in three racing stripes.
Bake at 260C for 15 min until the cheese edges are deep brown and lacy. Run a knife around and lift out.
p: Born in Detroit auto-parts pans in the 1940s. The cheese must reach the pan wall to form the crunchy caramelized 'frico' edge, and the sauce goes on top in stripes, added last so it stays bright.

i: For the pastry: 375g flour, 1 tsp salt, 170g lard or suet, 120ml cold water
300g beef skirt or chuck, diced small
Salt and plenty of black pepper
m: Cut the fat into the flour and salt, bind with cold water, and rest 30 min.
Mix the raw beef, potato, rutabaga, and onion with lots of salt and pepper: the filling cooks inside the pastry, so season it hard.
Roll the pastry into rounds, mound filling on one half, dot with butter, fold over, and crimp the edge into a rope seal.
Cut a vent, brush with egg, and set on a tray.
Bake at 200C for 20 min, then 175C for 40 min until deep gold. Cool 10 min: the filling is molten.
p: Cornish miners brought the pasty to the Upper Peninsula's copper mines and it became Yooper soul food. Everything goes in raw, so dice it small and season it hard; the crimped rope seal was once the miner's handle, held and discarded.

m: Toss the cherries with the sugar, cornstarch, lemon, almond extract, and salt and let stand 15 min.
Line the pie plate with pastry and fill with the cherries. Dot with butter.
Lay a lattice top, brush with egg, and dust with sugar.
Bake at 220C for 20 min, then 190C for 35-40 min until the juices bubble thickly through the lattice.
Cool at least 4 hours so the filling sets.
p: Michigan grows most of America's tart cherries around Traverse City. Tart Montmorencies, not sweet, make a real cherry pie, and the drop of almond extract amplifies the cherry flavor, a trick worth knowing.

i: For the sauce: 450g ground beef, 1 onion grated, 2 tbsp chili powder, 1 tbsp cumin, 1 tbsp paprika, 1 tbsp Worcestershire, 2 tbsp tomato paste, 250ml beef stock, salt
m: Simmer the raw ground beef in the stock with the grated onion, spices, Worcestershire, and tomato paste 45 min until fine-grained and loose: never brown it first.
Grill or steam the hot dogs and warm the buns.
Set a dog in each bun and stripe with mustard.
Ladle the coney sauce over.
Top with diced raw onion and serve at once.
p: Detroit and Flint argue endlessly over whose coney is right, but both agree the sauce is a loose, fine-ground meat sauce simmered from raw, not a chunky chili. The onion and mustard go on last.

m: Simmer the chicken, beef, and pork in the water with the bay 2.5 hours until all fall apart. Lift out, shred, discard bones, and keep the broth.
Return the broth to the pot with the onions, carrots, celery, and potatoes and simmer 45 min.
Add the tomatoes, peas, corn, and green beans and cook 30 min.
Return the shredded meat and simmer 1 hour more until everything melds.
Season well. It should be a thick, rich meal in a bowl.
p: A Belgian-American three-meat stew of the Upper Midwest, cooked in vast kettles for church and firehouse fundraisers. The name is thought to come from 'bouillon'. It is meant to cook all day: the long simmer is the flavor.

m: Butter a marble slab or a shallow pan.
Boil the sugar, cream, milk, corn syrup, and butter to 114C, stirring gently.
Off the heat add the chocolate, vanilla, and salt but do not stir: let it cool to lukewarm.
Beat hard with a wooden spoon until it thickens, loses its shine, and holds its shape.
Pour onto the slab, spread, and score into squares before it sets fully.
p: Mackinac Island shops still pour and paddle fudge on marble slabs in the window. The rule is the same as any fudge: cool it undisturbed to lukewarm before beating, or you fold in sugar crystals and it turns grainy.

i: For the crumb: 100g sugar, 75g flour, 1 tsp cinnamon, 55g cold butter
m: Cream the butter and sugar, beat in the egg, then alternate the dry ingredients with the milk.
Fold in the blueberries and spread in a buttered 23cm pan.
Rub the crumb ingredients to pebbles and scatter over the top.
Bake at 180C for 45-50 min until a skewer comes clean.
Cool 20 min and cut in the pan.
p: Michigan grows more blueberries than any state. Wild or small berries beat the big cultivated ones here (less water, more flavor), and tossing them in a spoonful of the flour keeps them from sinking.

i: 4 Great Lakes whitefish fillets, about 180g each
m: Pat the fillets dry, season, and lay skin-side down in a buttered dish.
Toss the cracker crumbs with the melted butter, parsley, and paprika.
Squeeze lemon over the fish and pack the crumb topping on.
Bake at 200C for 12-15 min until the crumbs are gold and the fish flakes.
Serve at once with lemon.
p: Lake whitefish is the sweet, delicate signature of the Great Lakes. Buttered cracker crumbs are the traditional coat and they beat breadcrumbs. Do not overcook the fish, which flakes and dries within a minute of doneness.

i: 600g pork shoulder and 300g veal, in 3cm cubes
m: Thread the pork and veal cubes onto short skewers to resemble a small drumstick.
Dredge each skewer in flour, then egg, then breadcrumbs.
Brown all sides in the oil in an ovenproof skillet.
Add the stock, cover, and braise at 175C for 30 min until tender.
Uncover for the last 10 min to re-crisp the coating. Serve with the pan juices.
p: A Depression-era dish from when chicken cost more than pork — the skewers were shaped to mimic drumsticks. There is no chicken in it at all, which is the whole charming joke.

i: 1 tbsp salt, 1 tsp pepper, 1 tsp cayenne
For cornbread: 250g cornmeal, 60g flour, 1 tbsp baking powder, 1 tsp salt, 2 eggs, 400ml buttermilk, 3 tbsp bacon fat
m: Heat the bacon fat in a cast-iron skillet at 220C, mix the cornbread batter, pour it in, and bake 20-25 min.
Soak the catfish in buttermilk 20 min.
Season the cornmeal and flour with salt, pepper, and cayenne.
Dredge the fillets and fry in 190C oil 4-5 min until deep gold and floating.
Drain, salt, and serve with the cornbread and hot sauce.
p: River catfish and skillet cornbread are Ohio Valley staples. Pure cornmeal on the fish fries up sandiest and crispest; the spoon of flour just helps it cling.

i: For topping: 2 onions sliced thin, 60g flour, oil for frying
m: Fry the thin-sliced onions in flour until crisp and gold for the topping; drain and salt.
Blanch the beans 4 min and drain.
Sweat the mushrooms and diced onion in the butter, stir in the flour, and cook 2 min. Whisk in the milk and cream and simmer to a sauce. Add soy sauce, salt, and pepper.
Fold in the beans and turn into a baking dish.
Bake at 190C for 20 min, top with the crisp onions, and bake 5 min more.
p: The from-scratch version of the mid-century casserole, invented for a 1955 recipe booklet in the Midwest. Fresh mushroom sauce and hand-fried onions turn a joke into a genuinely good dish.

m: Whisk the flour, baking powder, soda, and salt.
Cream the butter and sugar, beat in the egg, sour cream, and vanilla.
Fold in the dry ingredients to a soft dough and chill 1 hour.
Roll walnut-sized balls in sugar and set well apart on lined trays.
Bake at 175C for 10-12 min until set but pale: they should stay soft and cakey.
p: A soft, cakey sugar cookie leavened partly by sour cream, a Hoosier bakery tradition. Pull them while still pale; a browned sugar cookie has crossed from soft into crisp and lost the point.

i: For the applesauce: 4 apples peeled and chopped, 60ml water, 2 tbsp sugar, 1/2 tsp cinnamon, squeeze of lemon
m: Simmer the apples with the water, sugar, cinnamon, and lemon until soft, then mash to a chunky sauce.
Season the chops and brown hard in the oil and butter, 3 min a side; set aside.
Soften the onion in the pan, add the cider and thyme, and scrape up the fond.
Return the chops, cover, and simmer 15 min until cooked through.
Rest the chops, reduce the pan sauce, and serve with the warm applesauce.
p: Corn-belt pork is Illinois's pride, and pork with apples is a marriage older than the state. Make the applesauce chunky and fresh: jarred sauce is sweeter and thinner and misses the tart contrast.

i: 4 ears sweet corn, kernels and cobs
m: Simmer the corn kernels and broken cobs in the milk and cream 20 min, then discard the cobs.
Blend the mixture and strain, pressing hard to extract the corn flavor.
Whisk the yolks with the sugar and salt, temper in the hot corn cream, and cook to 82C.
Strain, add the vanilla, and chill thoroughly.
Churn and freeze until firm.
p: A prairie-state celebration of August corn in dessert form. Steeping the cobs as well as the kernels is what gives it real corn flavor rather than just sweetness — the cob holds as much as the kernel.

m: Soften each ice cream slightly so it can be layered without melting.
Press a layer of chocolate into the bottom of the cone.
Add strawberry, then Palmer House, then pistachio.
Top with a cap of orange sherbet.
Serve immediately: the layers are meant to show in a rainbow slice.
p: A South Side Chicago institution since 1926, served as flat slabs of five flavors, not scoops. The order of the layers is fixed by tradition, and the orange sherbet on top is the tangy finish that keeps it from being cloying.

i: For the cake: 250g flour, 60g cocoa, 1 tsp soda, 1/2 tsp salt, 115g butter, 300g sugar, 2 eggs, 240ml buttermilk, 1 tsp vanilla
For the bumps: 115g butter, 300g icing sugar, 60ml cream, 1 tsp vanilla
For the ganache: 200g dark chocolate, 200ml cream
m: Make a chocolate cake: cream butter and sugar, add eggs, alternate the dry ingredients with buttermilk. Bake in a rectangular pan at 175C for 30 min. Cool.
Beat the buttercream ingredients stiff and pipe it in thick parallel ridges across the cake: these are the bumps.
Chill until the buttercream is firm.
Warm the cream, pour over the chocolate, and stir to a glossy ganache. Cool slightly.
Pour the ganache over the whole cake so it flows around the buttercream ridges, showing the bumps beneath.
p: A Detroit bakery classic from Sanders, defined by its ridges of buttercream under a chocolate glaze. Chill the buttercream bumps hard before glazing or they collapse under the warm ganache.

i: 100g blue cheese or goat cheese, crumbled
For the dressing: 3 tbsp cider vinegar, 6 tbsp oil, 1 tbsp maple syrup, 1 tsp Dijon, salt and pepper
m: Toast the walnuts until fragrant and cool them.
Whisk the dressing ingredients into an emulsion.
Toss the greens with just enough dressing to coat.
Scatter the dried cherries, walnuts, cheese, and apple over.
Serve at once, with extra dressing on the side.
p: Traverse City's dried cherries are a year-round crop from the summer glut. The sweet-tart cherry against blue cheese and toasted walnut is a study in balance: dress the greens lightly so the toppings stay the stars.

m: Sweat the onion, carrot, and celery in the butter until soft, 10 min.
Stir in the flour and cook 2 min to a blond roux.
Whisk in the stock and beer and simmer 10 min, then add the milk.
Off the heat, add the cheese in handfuls, stirring until each melts before adding more; never boil after the cheese goes in.
Season with mustard, Worcestershire, cayenne, salt, and pepper. Top with popcorn.
p: Dairy state pride in a bowl. The pot comes off the heat before the cheese to keep it silky: a boil breaks it into grease and strings. Popcorn on top is a beloved Wisconsin garnish, not a gimmick.

m: Pat the curds dry and freeze them 15 min so they hold their shape in the oil.
Whisk the flour, egg, cold beer, salt, and baking powder into a batter.
Heat the oil to 190C.
Dip the curds in batter a few at a time and fry 1-2 min until gold and puffed.
Drain, salt, and serve immediately while the inside is molten and squeaky.
p: Fresh, squeaky curds are essential: day-old curds lose the squeak that makes them worth frying. Chill them first and keep the oil hot so the batter sets before the cheese leaks out. Eat them at once; they wait for no one.

m: Simmer the brats gently in the beer with the sliced onions, butter, and caraway 20 min: do not boil, which splits the casings.
Lift the brats out and grill them over medium coals until browned and blistered, 10 min, turning.
Keep the beer and onions simmering to reduce into a soft, sweet topping.
Set each brat in a roll.
Top with the beer onions, mustard, and kraut.
p: The Sheboygan method: poach in beer first, then grill for color. Poaching cooks them through gently so the grill only has to brown: grilling raw brats chars the outside while the middle stays raw and splits the casing.

m: Simmer the chicken, beef, and pork in the water with bay 3 hours until all fall off the bone. Lift out, shred, discard bones, keep the broth.
Add the onions, carrots, celery, and potatoes to the broth and simmer 45 min.
Add the tomatoes, peas, corn, and green beans and cook 30 min.
Return the shredded meat and simmer 90 min more until thick and melded.
Season generously. It should be a spoon-standing stew.
p: Northeastern Wisconsin's Belgian church-and-tavern stew, cooked in enormous kettles overnight for fundraisers. The name comes from 'bouillon', and the all-day simmer is not optional: it is what marries three meats and a garden into one pot.

i: For the pastry: 500g flour, 7g yeast, 50g sugar, 1 tsp salt, 240ml warm milk, 3 eggs, 225g cold butter for laminating
For the filling: 200g pecans, 150g brown sugar, 55g butter, 1 tsp cinnamon
For the icing: 200g icing sugar, 3 tbsp milk
m: Make an enriched dough, chill it, then laminate with the cold butter through three fold-and-roll turns like a rough puff. Chill between turns.
Roll the dough into a long strip, fill with the pecan-sugar-butter mixture, and fold over lengthwise.
Shape into a large oval ring and set on a tray. Rise 45 min.
Bake at 190C for 25-30 min until deep gold and flaky.
Cool and drizzle with the icing.
p: Racine's Danish bakers made the flat oval kringle the official state pastry. The lamination is the work: keep the butter cold through every fold, or it melts into the dough and you lose the flake.

m: Form the beef into four patties and season well.
Griddle them in a generous knob of butter over medium-high heat, 3 min a side, basting with the melting butter.
Lay cheese on to melt in the last minute.
Toast the cut buns in more butter until gold.
Butter the toasted buns again, add the patty, onion, and pickles, and serve: butter at every stage is the point.
p: A Wisconsin obsession where butter appears at every step, including a pat inside the finished bun at some stands. Baste the patty with the browning butter as it cooks; that is where the flavor comes from.

i: For sides: rye bread, coleslaw, potato pancakes, tartar sauce, lemon
m: Pat the fish dry and dust with plain flour.
Whisk the flour, baking powder, salt, and cold beer into a batter: lumps are fine.
Heat the oil to 190C.
Dip the fish in batter, let the excess drip, and fry 3-4 min until deep gold and crisp.
Drain and serve the Wisconsin way: with rye bread, slaw, potato pancakes, tartar, and lemon.
p: The Friday fish fry is a statewide institution born of Catholic and Lutheran fasting custom. Cold beer batter is the classic coat: the carbonation lifts it crisp, so mix it at the last minute before the fizz dies.

m: Cook the cranberries with the sugar, orange zest and juice, and cornstarch until they burst and thicken, 10 min. Cool.
Mix the flour, sugar, oats, salt, and melted butter to crumbs.
Press two-thirds into a lined pan and bake at 175C for 12 min.
Spread the cranberry filling over and scatter the remaining crumb on top.
Bake 25-30 min more until golden. Cool completely before cutting.
p: Wisconsin grows more cranberries than any state, in the central marshes. Cook the berries until they truly burst and the cornstarch thickens, or the filling stays runny and the bars will not hold their cut.

i: For the dough: 400g flour, 1 egg, 1 tsp salt, 250ml warm water, 2 tbsp sour cream
For the filling: 500g mashed potato, 200g sharp cheddar grated, 1 onion sauteed, salt and pepper
Butter and more onions to finish
m: Knead the dough ingredients smooth, cover, and rest 30 min.
Mix the mashed potato, cheddar, sauteed onion, salt, and pepper for the filling.
Roll the dough thin and cut rounds. Spoon filling onto each, fold, and crimp the edges tightly.
Boil in batches 3-4 min until they float, then lift out.
Fry the boiled pierogi in butter with more onions until golden. Serve with sour cream.
p: Wisconsin's Polish communities brought pierogi and the cheese state made them cheesier. Boil first, then fry: boiling cooks the dough through, and the butter-fry gives the color and crisp that boiling alone cannot.

m: Brown the beef with the onion, celery, and mushrooms; drain and season.
In the same pan make a roux with the butter and flour, whisk in the milk and stock, and simmer to a sauce with the Worcestershire: this is the from-scratch soup base.
Stir the beef and vegetables into the sauce with the peas and corn and spread in a baking dish.
Arrange the tater tots in neat rows over the top and scatter with cheese.
Bake at 200C for 35-40 min until the tots are crisp and gold and the filling bubbles.
p: The signature hotdish of church basements and family suppers. Making the sauce from a roux instead of canned soup is the upgrade that turns it from convenience food into something genuinely good, and the tots must go on in tidy rows.

i: 150g American cheese, cut in thick squares
m: Divide the beef into 8 thin patties. Season them.
Place a folded square of cheese in the center of four patties, leaving a border.
Top each with a second patty and pinch the edges tightly all around to seal the cheese inside.
Griddle over medium heat 4-5 min a side: medium, not high, so the cheese melts before the outside burns. Pierce is forbidden.
Set on buttered buns with onion, pickle, and mustard. Warn everyone to wait: the cheese is molten.
p: Two Minneapolis bars claim the invention and spell it differently. Seal the edges completely or the cheese escapes, and cook it over medium heat: the whole point is molten cheese inside, which needs time, not a hard sear.

m: Simmer the wild rice in the water 45 min until the grains split open. Drain any excess.
Sweat the onion, carrot, celery, and mushrooms in the butter until soft, 10 min.
Stir in the flour and cook 2 min, then whisk in the stock and simmer 10 min.
Add the cooked rice, chicken, and cream and heat through without boiling.
Finish with the sherry, season, and scatter with chives.
p: True wild rice is a Minnesota native grain, hand-harvested from lakes by the Ojibwe. Cook it until the grains burst open and curl: that is doneness, and undercooked wild rice stays tough and grassy no matter how long the soup sits.

m: Pat the fillets dry.
Set up flour, beaten egg, and the crushed saltines seasoned with salt, pepper, and paprika.
Dredge each fillet in flour, then egg, then the cracker crumbs, pressing them on.
Fry in a mix of butter and oil over medium-high heat 3-4 min a side until the crust is deep gold and the fish flakes.
Serve immediately with lemon. Traditionally cooked on the lakeshore right after the catch.
p: Walleye is the prized freshwater fish of the northern lakes, and the shore lunch is a ritual of frying the morning's catch on the spot. Saltine crumbs make the classic crust; do not overcook walleye, which is lean and flakes dry fast.

m: Boil, rice, and cool the potatoes completely: warm potato makes a gluey dough.
Mix the riced potato with the melted butter, cream, salt, and sugar, then chill overnight.
Work in the flour just until it comes together; the less flour, the more tender the lefse.
Roll each portion paper-thin on a floured board.
Cook on a dry hot griddle 30 seconds a side until spotted with brown. Fold with butter and sugar.
p: A Norwegian potato flatbread and a Minnesota Christmas tradition. Chilling the potato before adding flour, and using as little flour as possible, is what keeps lefse tender: too much flour and it turns to cardboard.

i: For the gravy: 55g butter, 55g flour, 750ml beef stock, 120ml cream, 1 tsp soy sauce
m: Mix the meats, grated onion, soaked breadcrumbs, egg, allspice, nutmeg, salt, and pepper. Roll into small balls.
Brown the meatballs all over in butter and set aside.
Make a roux in the pan with butter and flour, whisk in the stock, and simmer to a gravy. Add the cream and soy sauce.
Return the meatballs and simmer 15 min until cooked through and the gravy is silky.
Serve over mashed potatoes with lingonberry jam.
p: Minnesota's Scandinavian heritage runs deep. Allspice and nutmeg are the spices that make them Swedish rather than Italian, and soaking the breadcrumbs in milk first (a panade) is what keeps the meatballs tender.

i: Mustard, pickle, and onion to serve
m: Brown the beef in a dry pan, breaking it into fine crumbles, the finer the better.
Add the onion and cook until soft.
Add the stock, mustard, vinegar, sugar, salt, and pepper and simmer 20 min until most of the liquid cooks away but the meat stays moist and loose.
Spoon the loose meat onto buns: it will not hold together like a burger, and that is correct.
Top with mustard, pickle, and onion and eat with a spoon nearby for the fallout.
p: Also called a tavern or a Maid-Rite, this is a sloppy joe without the tomato: just seasoned loose ground beef. Keep it loose and moist, never a formed patty; the crumble spilling out is the whole character.

i: 4 pork loin cutlets, pounded to 5mm and very wide
1 tsp salt, 1/2 tsp pepper, 1/2 tsp garlic powder
m: Pound the cutlets between plastic until thin and wide: they should be twice the width of the bun.
Set up flour, egg wash, and seasoned cracker crumbs.
Dredge in flour, egg, then crumbs, pressing them on firmly.
Fry in 5mm of 180C oil 2-3 min a side until deep gold and crisp.
Set on the small bun it overwhelms, with mustard, pickle, and onion.
p: Iowa rivals Indiana for the tenderloin crown and both insist theirs is the original. Pound it thin between plastic wrap so it spreads wide without tearing; the comic overhang past the bun is mandatory.

i: 6 ears corn, kernels and scraped milk
m: Cut the kernels from the cobs and scrape the cobs for their milk.
Whisk the eggs, cream, melted butter, cornmeal, flour, sugar, salt, and pepper.
Stir in the corn and half the cheddar.
Pour into a buttered dish and top with the remaining cheese.
Bake at 175C for 40-50 min until set and golden.
p: Iowa grows more corn than any state, and this custardy casserole is a potluck fixture. Scrape the cobs for their starchy milk: it is what sets the custard and carries the concentrated corn flavor.

i: Yellow mustard, chopped onion, dill pickles
m: Brown and crumble the beef very fine in a dry skillet.
Add the minced onion and cook until soft.
Add the broth, mustard, Worcestershire, sugar, salt, and pepper and simmer gently until the liquid is nearly gone but the meat is still moist.
Hold it warm and loose, never pressed together.
Spoon onto buns and top with mustard, onion, and pickle.
p: The Maid-Rite chain, founded 1926 in Muscatine, made the loose-meat sandwich an Iowa institution. The steamed, never-pressed meat is the trademark; the moment you form it into a patty it becomes something else entirely.

m: Butter a 23x33cm pan.
Heat the sugar and corn syrup until it just boils, then remove from the heat.
Stir in the peanut butter until smooth, then fold in the crisped rice cereal.
Press into the pan.
Melt the chocolate and butterscotch chips together, spread over the top, and let set before cutting.
p: A church-cookbook staple across Iowa, richer and chewier than a plain rice cereal bar. Do not overboil the syrup: take it off the heat the moment it bubbles, or the bars set rock-hard instead of chewy.

i: 24 meat or cheese ravioli, fresh or thawed
Marinara and grated Parmesan to serve
m: Set up flour, egg wash, and the breadcrumbs mixed with Parmesan and oregano.
Dredge each ravioli in flour, then egg, then the breadcrumb mixture, pressing it on.
Heat the oil to 180C.
Fry the ravioli in batches 2-3 min until deep gold and crisp.
Drain, dust with more Parmesan, and serve hot with warm marinara for dipping.
p: A St. Louis Hill neighborhood accident, said to be born when a cook dropped ravioli in oil instead of water. Toasted here means fried: pat the ravioli dry first so the coating grips, and serve them the instant they drain.

i: For the base: 250g flour, 7g yeast, 50g sugar, 1/2 tsp salt, 120ml warm milk, 1 egg, 85g butter
For the gooey top: 115g butter, 300g sugar, 1 egg, 60ml corn syrup, 1 tsp vanilla, 190g flour, 60ml water
m: Make the yeasted base: mix the ingredients to a soft dough and press into the bottom of a lined pan. Rise 30 min.
Cream the butter and sugar for the topping, beat in the egg, corn syrup, and vanilla, then alternate the flour with the water to a thick batter.
Spread the topping over the base.
Bake at 175C for 30-35 min until the edges are set and golden but the center still jiggles: underbaking is essential to the gooey middle.
Cool and dust heavily with icing sugar.
p: A St. Louis bakery accident from the 1930s, when a baker reversed the proportions of butter and flour. The center must stay gooey: pull it while the middle still wobbles, because a fully set gooey butter cake has missed its own name.

i: For the egg foo young patty: 3 eggs, 100g bean sprouts, 1 scallion sliced, 50g minced onion, 100g diced cooked pork or shrimp, 1 tsp soy sauce
m: Beat the eggs and mix with the sprouts, scallion, onion, meat, and soy sauce.
Fry as a thick patty in hot oil, 2-3 min a side, until set and golden.
Spread mayonnaise on both slices of plain white bread.
Set the hot egg foo young patty on the bread with lettuce, tomato, and pickle.
Close, cut in half, and serve.
p: A Chinese-American St. Louis invention found only in the city's takeout shops: an egg foo young patty on white bread with mayonnaise and pickle. The contrast of the hot savory patty against cold mayonnaise and crisp lettuce is the whole strange charm.

m: Beat the egg and sugar until pale and thick.
Fold in the flour, baking powder, and salt.
Stir in the diced apple, pecans, and vanilla.
Spread in a buttered dish; it will be a thin layer.
Bake at 175C for 30-35 min until set and crisp on top but soft beneath. Serve warm with whipped cream.
p: A homely Ozark dessert that Bess Truman reportedly served at the White House. It bakes into a crisp meringue-like top over a soft, chewy apple-nut base: do not overbake, or you lose the pudding-soft middle.

n: Missouri Fried Chicken with Cream Gravy
i: 2 tbsp salt, 1 tbsp pepper, 1 tbsp paprika, 1 tsp cayenne
For the gravy: 4 tbsp pan drippings, 4 tbsp flour, 750ml milk, salt and lots of black pepper
m: Brine the chicken in buttermilk overnight, then dredge in the seasoned flour and rest 15 min.
Fry in 165C lard in a cast-iron skillet, dark meat 15 min and white 13, turning once, until deep gold and 74C internal. Drain.
Pour off all but 4 tablespoons of the drippings, keeping the browned bits.
Whisk in the flour and cook 2 min, then add the milk gradually, whisking, and simmer to a thick gravy.
Season hard with salt and pepper and serve the chicken smothered or with gravy alongside.
p: Cream gravy from the frying drippings is the Missouri and wider Ozark way. Keep the browned bits in the pan when you pour off the fat: those cracklings are the flavor of the gravy, and a clean pan makes a bland one.

m: Sieve the very ripe persimmons for smooth pulp.
Beat the pulp with the sugar, eggs, and oil.
Whisk the flour, soda, cinnamon, nutmeg, and salt and fold in, then the pecans and raisins.
Pour into a buttered bundt or loaf pan.
Bake at 175C for 55-65 min until a skewer comes clean. Cool before slicing.
p: Wild persimmons drop across the Missouri Ozarks in autumn after the first frost softens them. Only fully ripe, jelly-soft fruit will do: an under-ripe persimmon is so astringent it will pucker the whole cake.

i: 2 oz brandy (Wisconsin uses brandy, not whiskey)
Splash of lemon-lime soda or sour mix
m: Muddle the sugar cube with the bitters, orange slice, and one cherry in the bottom of a glass.
Add ice and the brandy.
Top with a splash of lemon-lime soda for a 'sweet' or sour mix for a 'sour'.
Stir well.
Garnish with the second cherry and an orange slice.
p: Wisconsin drinks its old fashioned with brandy, a quirk dating to the 1893 World's Fair, and orders it sweet or sour by the mixer on top. It is the unofficial state cocktail, poured in every supper club before the Friday fish fry.

n: Minnesota Hot Dish Wild Rice and Beef
m: Simmer the wild rice in salted water 45 min until the grains split; drain.
Brown the beef with the onion and mushrooms; drain and season.
Make a roux with the butter and flour, whisk in the stock and milk, and simmer to a sauce with the Worcestershire.
Fold the cooked rice and beef into the sauce and turn into a baking dish. Top with cheddar.
Bake at 190C for 30 min until bubbling and golden.
p: A heartier cousin of the tater tot hotdish, built on Minnesota's native wild rice. Cook the rice until the grains burst; undercooked wild rice stays tough and no amount of baking will soften it.

i: For the crumb: 100g sugar, 75g flour, 1 tsp cinnamon, 55g cold butter
m: Cream the butter and sugar, beat in the egg, then alternate the dry ingredients with the milk.
Fold in the blueberries and spread in a buttered pan.
Rub the crumb ingredients to pebbles and scatter over.
Bake at 180C for 45-50 min until a skewer comes clean.
Cool 20 min and cut in the pan.
p: The northern lakes country fills with wild blueberries in late summer. Small wild berries beat the big cultivated ones (less water and more flavor), and a toss in the flour keeps them from sinking to the bottom.

m: Whisk the flour, sugar, baking powder, and salt.
Beat the eggs, buttermilk, and melted butter, then combine with the dry ingredients.
Fold in the cooked wild rice.
Griddle in butter over medium heat until bubbles break, then flip once.
Serve stacked with butter and maple syrup.
p: Cooked wild rice folded into the batter gives the pancakes a nutty chew and a northwoods character. Make sure the rice is fully cooked and split before it goes in: a hard grain in a soft pancake is an unwelcome surprise.

m: Simmer the chicken, beef, and pork in the water with bay 3 hours until falling apart. Lift out, shred, discard bones, keep the broth.
Add the onions, carrots, celery, potatoes, and rutabaga and simmer 45 min.
Add the tomatoes, peas, and corn and cook 30 min.
Return the meat and simmer 90 min more until thick.
Season generously.
p: Minnesota spells it booya and makes it a communal event, cooked in huge kettles overnight for church fundraisers, especially in the St. Paul area. The rutabaga is the northern touch, and the all-day cook is the tradition and the flavor both.

i: 8 ears fresh sweet corn, kernels cut off
m: Cut the kernels from the cobs and scrape the cobs for their milk.
Melt the butter in a skillet and add the corn, kernels and scrapings.
Cook over medium-high heat 5 min, stirring, until it takes a little color.
Sprinkle the flour over, then add the cream and sugar and simmer 3 min until it thickens.
Season with salt and pepper and finish with chives.
p: Iowa sweet corn in August needs almost nothing done to it. Cook it briefly and hot so it keeps its snap and its sugar — corn simmered soft turns starchy and loses the very freshness that makes Iowa corn famous.

i: For the glaze: 200g brown sugar, 120ml cider vinegar, 120ml water, 1 tbsp dry mustard
m: Mix the ground ham, pork, breadcrumbs, eggs, and milk and roll into balls.
Arrange in a baking dish.
Whisk the brown sugar, vinegar, water, and mustard into a glaze and pour over the balls.
Bake at 175C for 45-55 min, basting twice with the glaze, until browned and cooked through.
Serve with the thickened glaze spooned over.
p: A Midwestern potluck fixture built on the ham-and-pork farm economy. The sweet-and-sour mustard glaze is what makes them; baste as they bake so the sauce lacquers the balls instead of pooling in the pan.

m: Dice the apples and chop the Snickers bars into bite-sized pieces.
Fold the prepared vanilla pudding into the whipped cream.
Gently fold in the apples and chopped candy bars.
Drizzle with caramel and fold once.
Chill 30 min and serve: assemble close to serving so the apples stay crisp and the candy does not dissolve.
p: A tongue-in-cheek Midwestern 'salad' that appears at every Iowa gathering. Assemble it near serving time; make it too early and the apples weep and the candy bars go soft, turning a crisp dish into pudding.

m: Crumble the blue cheese, leaving some larger pieces for texture.
Whisk the sour cream, mayonnaise, lemon, and grated garlic.
Fold in the blue cheese and chives, leaving it chunky.
Season with black pepper: the cheese brings the salt.
Chill 1 hour and serve with vegetables and crackers.
p: Maytag Dairy Farms in Newton has made its famous blue cheese since 1941, from the family that also made washing machines. Fold it in rather than beating it smooth: the crumbles of sharp blue are the whole reason to make the dip.

m: Toss the rhubarb with half the sugar and let it stand 15 min.
Whisk the eggs, remaining sugar, flour, cream, vanilla, and salt.
Spread the rhubarb in the shell and pour the custard over. Dot with butter.
Bake at 200C for 15 min, then 175C for 35-40 min until the custard is set and the rhubarb tender.
Cool completely before slicing.
p: Rhubarb grows in every Iowa backyard and returns every spring without asking. The custard tames rhubarb's sourness into something mellow — pull the pie while the center holds a faint wobble, as it firms as it cools.

m: Rub the brisket point all over with the mixed sugar and spices.
Smoke at 110C over hickory 6-7 hours until the internal temperature reaches 90C and the bark is dark.
Cut the point into 3cm cubes.
Toss the cubes with the barbecue sauce and honey and return them to the smoker in a pan.
Smoke 1-2 hours more until the sauce caramelizes and the cubes turn sticky and tender.
p: Kansas City made burnt ends famous: the fatty point of the brisket, cubed and re-smoked in sauce until candied. The second smoke is what separates true burnt ends from merely sauced brisket; do not skip it.

i: For the rub: 4 tbsp brown sugar, 2 tbsp paprika, 1 tbsp salt, 1 tbsp pepper, 1 tbsp garlic powder, 1 tsp cayenne
For the sauce: 250ml ketchup, 120ml molasses, 60ml cider vinegar, 2 tbsp brown sugar, 1 tbsp mustard, 1 tsp smoked paprika
m: Peel the membrane from the back of the ribs and coat both racks in the rub. Rest 1 hour.
Smoke at 110C over hickory 5-6 hours until the meat pulls back from the bones and bends easily.
Simmer the sauce ingredients together 15 min into the thick, sweet, tomato-based Kansas City style.
Brush the ribs with sauce in the last 30 min and let it set into a glaze.
Rest 10 min and cut between the bones.
p: Kansas City barbecue means a thick, sweet, molasses-and-tomato sauce, and pork ribs are its showcase. Sauce only at the very end: brush it on too early over the long smoke and the sugar burns black and bitter.

i: 6 ears corn, kernels and scraped cobs
m: Simmer the stripped cobs in the milk 20 min to draw out their sweetness, then discard them.
Render the bacon; lift out the bits and sweat the onion in the fat.
Sprinkle in the flour, cook 1 min, add the potatoes and the corn milk, and simmer 15 min.
Add the corn kernels and cream and cook 5 min more.
Season, finish with butter, and scatter bacon and chives over each bowl.
p: A farm-country chowder that puts the state's corn front and center. Steeping the cobs in the milk first is the free step that doubles the corn flavor: the cob holds as much sweetness as the kernel.

i: For the batter: 115g butter, 190g flour, 200g sugar, 2 tsp baking powder, 1/4 tsp salt, 240ml milk
m: Toss the blackberries with the sugar, cornstarch, and lemon and let stand 15 min.
Melt the butter in a baking dish in the oven as it heats to 190C.
Whisk the flour, sugar, baking powder, salt, and milk into a batter and pour over the melted butter. Do not stir.
Spoon the berries and juice over the batter; do not stir.
Bake 45-55 min until the cake rises around the fruit and browns.
p: Wild blackberries grow thick along Ozark fencerows and roadsides in July. The magic is not stirring: the batter floats up through the berries as it bakes, giving cake on top and fruit suspended below.

i: For the knoephla: 300g flour, 1 egg, 1/2 tsp salt, 120ml milk
m: Make a stiff dough from the flour, egg, salt, and milk. Rest 20 min, then roll into ropes and snip small pea-sized dumplings.
Sweat the onion and celery in the butter until soft.
Add the potatoes and stock and simmer 15 min until nearly tender.
Drop the knoephla into the simmering soup and cook 12-15 min until they float and are cooked through.
Add the cream and thyme, season, and finish with parsley.
p: A German-Russian dumpling soup that defines North Dakota comfort food, brought by settlers from the Ukrainian steppe. Keep the knoephla small, pea-sized, so they cook through; large ones stay doughy at the center.

i: For the dough: 400g flour, 1 egg, 1 tsp salt, 250ml warm water
For the filling: 500g ground beef, 1 onion grated, 1 tsp salt, 1/2 tsp pepper, 1/2 tsp allspice, 60ml water
m: Knead the dough smooth and rest it 30 min.
Mix the raw ground beef with the grated onion, seasonings, and water so it stays moist.
Roll the dough thin and cut large rounds. Spread raw filling over half, fold into a half-moon, and seal the edge firmly.
Heat the oil to 180C.
Fry the pockets 4-5 min a side until deep gold and the meat inside is cooked through.
p: A German-Russian fried meat pocket, a fair and church-supper staple across the state. The filling goes in raw and cooks inside the dough, so keep the meat moist with a little water or it dries out during the fry.

i: For the dough: 400g flour, 7g yeast, 50g sugar, 1/2 tsp salt, 180ml warm milk, 1 egg, 55g butter
For the custard: 4 eggs, 250ml cream, 100g sugar, 1 tsp vanilla
Fruit: sliced apples, prunes, or peaches
m: Make a soft yeasted dough and rise 1 hour. Press into round pans, building up a rim.
Arrange the fruit over the dough.
Whisk the custard ingredients and pour over the fruit.
Dust with cinnamon sugar.
Bake at 175C for 30-35 min until the custard is set and the crust golden.
p: The official state dessert, a German-Russian custard cake with fruit. The trick is a dough rim high enough to hold the custard: too shallow and it runs over the edge and burns onto the pan.

m: Boil, rice, and cool the potatoes completely.
Mix the riced potato with the melted butter, cream, salt, and sugar, then chill overnight.
Work in the flour just until it comes together.
Roll each portion paper-thin on a floured board.
Cook on a dry hot griddle 30 seconds a side until spotted. Fold with butter and sugar.
p: Norwegian settlers made lefse a Dakota Christmas tradition too. Chill the potato before adding flour and use as little flour as possible: the less flour, the more tender the lefse; too much and it turns to cardboard.

m: Season the bison well and brown all sides hard in the oil: bison is lean and needs a good crust.
Sweat the onions, add tomato paste and cook until brick red, then deglaze with the wine.
Return the roast with stock, bay, and thyme. Cover and braise at 150C for 2.5 hours.
Add the carrots and potatoes and cook 1 hour more.
Rest the meat, skim the fat, and reduce the sauce if needed. Slice against the grain.
p: Bison is North Dakota's native meat and far leaner than beef, so it wants low, slow, moist heat: a hot fast cook turns it to leather. Do not overcook it past fork-tender or the lack of fat shows immediately.

i: For the dough: 500g flour, 7g yeast, 50g sugar, 1 tsp salt, 240ml warm milk, 2 eggs, 85g butter
For the caramel: 170g butter, 220g brown sugar, 120ml cream
For filling: 85g butter, 150g brown sugar, 2 tbsp cinnamon
m: Knead the dough and rise 90 min until doubled.
Melt the caramel ingredients together and pour into a baking pan.
Roll the dough into a rectangle, spread with the filling, roll up, and cut into 12.
Set cut-side up on the caramel and rise 45 min.
Bake at 180C for 30 min until golden. Invert onto a tray immediately so the caramel flows down over the rolls.
p: Caramel rolls are a Dakota cafe institution, served warm and gooey. Invert the pan within a couple of minutes of baking: wait too long and the caramel welds to the pan instead of flooding the rolls.

m: Simmer the wild rice 45 min until the grains split; drain.
Brown the beef with the onion and mushrooms; drain and season.
Make a roux, whisk in the stock and milk, and simmer to a sauce with the Worcestershire.
Fold in the rice and beef, turn into a dish, and top with cheddar.
Bake at 190C for 30 min until bubbling.
p: Wild rice grows in the northern lakes and rivers and gives the hotdish a nutty backbone. Cook the rice until the grains truly burst; undercooked wild rice stays tough no matter how long it bakes.

n: North Dakota Sour Cream Raisin Pie
m: Simmer the raisins in the water 10 min until plump; drain.
Whisk the sour cream, sugar, yolks, cornstarch, and spices in a pan and cook over medium heat, stirring, until thick.
Fold in the raisins and pour into the baked shell.
Whip the whites with the sugar to stiff peaks and spread over, sealing to the crust.
Bake at 175C for 15 min until the meringue is golden. Cool and chill.
p: A Great Plains diner classic beloved across the Dakotas. Cook the custard until it truly thickens before the raisins go in, and seal the meringue right to the crust edge or it shrinks and weeps.

m: Simmer the beef in the water 90 min until tender. Lift out, dice the meat, and keep the broth.
Add the beets, onion, and carrots to the broth and simmer 20 min.
Add the cabbage, potatoes, and tomatoes and cook 25 min until everything is tender.
Return the meat, add vinegar, sugar, and dill, and simmer 10 min. Balance the sweet and sour to taste.
Serve topped with sour cream and fresh dill.
p: The German-Russian settlers of the Dakotas brought their own borscht, heartier and beefier than the Ukrainian original. Balance the vinegar and sugar at the end: that sweet-sour tension is what makes a borscht sing.

m: Cream the butter and sugar, beat in the yolks and vanilla.
Fold in the flour and salt to a soft dough.
Roll into balls and press a deep well into each with your thumb.
Fill each well with chokecherry jelly.
Bake at 175C for 12-15 min until set but pale. Cool on the tray.
p: The chokecherry is North Dakota's state fruit, tart and wild along the prairie draws. Its jelly is the traditional filling: press the wells deep so they hold enough jelly, and refill any that puff closed as they bake.

i: 800g lamb or beef sirloin, in 2cm cubes
Saltine crackers and hot sauce to serve
m: Toss the cubed meat with the garlic, oil, Worcestershire, and seasonings and marinate 30 min.
Heat oil in a deep skillet to 190C, or heat a grill very hot.
Fry or grill the cubes in batches 2-3 min, turning, until browned outside and still pink within.
Drain briefly and dust with more garlic salt.
Serve on toothpicks with saltine crackers and hot sauce.
p: The official state nosh, brought by German-Russian immigrants from the Crimea and traditionally made with mutton. Cook it hot and fast so the outside sears while the inside stays pink; overcooked chislic is chewy and dull. Saltines are the mandatory partner.

i: For fry bread: 400g flour, 2 tbsp baking powder, 1 tsp salt, 300ml warm milk, oil for frying
Lettuce, tomato, cheese, salsa, sour cream
m: Mix the flour, baking powder, salt, and milk into a soft dough. Rest 30 min.
Divide, pat into rounds, and fry in 180C oil until puffed and golden, about 1 min a side.
Brown the beef with the onion and spices, then stir in the beans and simmer 10 min.
Spoon the meat and beans onto each fry bread round.
Top with lettuce, tomato, cheese, salsa, and sour cream.
p: Fry bread carries a complicated history as a food of survival on the reservations, and the Indian taco built on it is now a powwow and state fair staple. Fry the bread the moment it is shaped so it puffs; over-rested dough fries flat and dense.

i: For the dough: 400g flour, 7g yeast, 50g sugar, 1/2 tsp salt, 180ml warm milk, 1 egg, 55g butter
For the custard: 4 eggs, 250ml cream, 100g sugar, 1 tsp vanilla
m: Make a soft yeasted dough and rise 1 hour. Press into round pans with a raised rim.
Arrange the fruit over the dough.
Whisk the custard and pour over the fruit.
Dust with cinnamon sugar.
Bake at 175C for 30-35 min until the custard sets and the crust is golden.
p: South Dakota named kuchen its official state dessert, a legacy of German-Russian settlement. Build the dough rim high enough to hold the custard: the whole dish fails if the custard escapes over a shallow edge.

n: South Dakota Pheasant with Cream Gravy
i: 2 pheasants, cut in pieces (or 8 pheasant breasts)
2 tsp salt, 1 tsp pepper, 1 tsp paprika
For the gravy: 4 tbsp drippings, 4 tbsp flour, 750ml milk, salt and pepper
m: Soak the pheasant in buttermilk 1 hour: it is lean and dries easily, so the brine matters.
Dredge in seasoned flour.
Brown in oil and butter, then cover and cook gently 25-30 min until just done; do not overcook lean pheasant.
Pour off all but 4 tbsp drippings, whisk in the flour, cook 2 min, and add the milk to make a gravy.
Season the gravy hard and serve the pheasant smothered.
p: South Dakota is the pheasant-hunting capital of America, and this is how the birds are cooked come autumn. Pheasant is far leaner than chicken; the buttermilk soak and gentle cooking are what keep it from turning dry and stringy.

i: 500g very fresh lean beef, ground twice
Raw onion and more pepper to serve
m: Use only the freshest lean beef, ground twice by a trusted butcher.
Mix the beef with the grated onion, salt, and plenty of pepper, and the yolk if using.
Chill thoroughly and keep cold until the moment of serving.
Spread on slices of cocktail rye bread.
Top with raw onion and a crack of pepper and serve at once, cold.
p: A German-Russian raw beef spread, a holiday-table tradition in the Dakotas akin to steak tartare. Absolute freshness and constant cold are non-negotiable with raw beef: buy from a butcher you trust and serve it straight from the fridge.

m: Brown the bison hard, then add the onion, pepper, and garlic and cook until soft.
Add the chili powder, cumin, and oregano and cook 1 min.
Add the tomatoes, beans, stock, and cocoa and simmer 90 min, stirring, until thick.
Season with salt and pepper.
Serve with cornbread, cheese, and onions.
p: Bison is South Dakota's native meat and leaner than beef, so it takes well to the long moist cooking of a chili. The spoon of cocoa deepens the color and roundness without reading as chocolate.

n: South Dakota Corn and Wild Rice Casserole
m: Simmer the wild rice 45 min until the grains split; drain.
Sweat the onion and mushrooms in the butter, stir in the flour, and cook 2 min.
Whisk in the stock and cream and simmer to a sauce.
Fold in the wild rice, corn, and half the cheese, then turn into a dish and top with the rest.
Bake at 190C for 30 min until bubbling and golden.
p: Wild rice and prairie corn together in one dish. Cook the wild rice fully, until the grains burst and curl, before it goes in, because it will not soften further inside the creamy casserole.

n: South Dakota Sour Cream Kuchen Bars
i: For the crust: 250g flour, 100g sugar, 170g butter
For the topping: 300ml sour cream, 2 eggs, 150g sugar, 1 tsp vanilla, 3 tbsp flour
m: Rub the flour, sugar, and butter to crumbs and press into a lined pan. Bake at 175C for 15 min.
Whisk the sour cream, eggs, sugar, vanilla, and flour into a custard.
Pour over the warm crust and add fruit if using.
Dust with cinnamon sugar.
Bake 25-30 min until the custard is just set. Cool and cut into bars.
p: A hand-held take on the state dessert. Do not overbake the custard: pull it while the center holds the faintest wobble, as it firms as it cools into the silky kuchen texture.

m: Fry the chipped potatoes at 150C until soft, rest, then fry again at 190C until crisp; salt at once.
Pat the walleye dry and dust with flour.
Whisk the flour, baking powder, salt, and cold beer into a batter.
Dip the fish and fry at 190C for 3-4 min until deep gold and the fish flakes.
Serve with the chips, tartar, and lemon.
p: Walleye from the Missouri River reservoirs is South Dakota's prize fish. Mix the beer batter at the last moment so the carbonation lifts it crisp, and do not overcook the lean walleye: it flakes dry in seconds past done.

i: For the dough: 500g flour, 7g yeast, 60g sugar, 1 tsp salt, 240ml warm milk, 2 egg yolks, 85g butter
For filling: poppy seed paste, prune butter, or sweetened cream cheese
For posypka topping: 50g flour, 50g sugar, 25g butter
m: Make a rich yeasted dough and rise 1 hour until doubled.
Divide into balls, set on trays, and rise 30 min. Press a deep well into each.
Fill the wells with poppy seed, prune, or cheese filling.
Rub the posypka ingredients to crumbs and sprinkle over the filling.
Rise 20 min, then bake at 190C for 12-15 min until golden.
p: Czech immigrants brought kolaches to the eastern Dakotas and Nebraska. Press the wells deep and re-press them after the second rise: the dough wants to close over the filling, and a shallow kolache spills as it bakes.

i: For the dough: 500g flour, 7g yeast, 50g sugar, 1 tsp salt, 240ml warm milk, 1 egg, 55g butter
For the filling: 500g ground beef, 1 onion diced, 400g cabbage shredded, 1 tsp salt, 1 tsp pepper
m: Make a soft yeasted dough and rise 1 hour until doubled.
Brown the beef with the onion, add the cabbage, and cook until wilted and the liquid has gone. Season well and cool.
Roll the dough into rectangles, spoon filling into the center, and fold into sealed rectangular pockets, seam-side down.
Rise 30 min, then brush with egg.
Bake at 190C for 20-25 min until deep gold.
p: A German-Russian stuffed bread that became a Nebraska icon, sold at its own fast-food chain. Cook the cabbage filling until dry: any liquid left in it steams inside the dough and makes the bottom soggy and the seal burst.

i: For the dough: 500g flour, 7g yeast, 50g sugar, 1 tsp salt, 240ml warm milk, 1 egg, 55g butter
For the filling: 500g ground beef, 1 onion, 400g cabbage, 2 tbsp mustard, 1 tsp caraway, salt and pepper
m: Make a soft yeasted dough and rise 1 hour.
Brown the beef with the onion, add the cabbage, mustard, and caraway, and cook until wilted and dry. Season and cool.
Roll the dough into squares, fill, and pinch closed into round buns.
Set seam-down, rise 30 min, and brush with egg.
Bake at 190C for 20-25 min until golden.
p: Bierocks and runzas are close cousins from the same German-Russian roots: bierocks tend to be round with caraway and mustard. As with runzas, cook the filling dry, or the moisture ruins the seal and the crumb.

i: For Russian dressing: 150g mayonnaise, 3 tbsp ketchup, 2 tbsp minced pickle, 1 tsp horseradish
m: Whisk the dressing ingredients.
Butter one side of each bread slice. On the unbuttered sides, spread dressing.
Build: Swiss, corned beef, drained kraut, more Swiss, and close with butter-side out.
Griddle over medium heat 4-5 min a side, pressing gently, until the bread is deep gold and the cheese melts.
Cut on the diagonal and serve hot.
p: Omaha claims the Reuben was invented at the Blackstone Hotel in the 1920s. Drain the sauerkraut hard: wet kraut steams the bread limp and floods the griddle, and a soggy Reuben is a fallen one.

m: Whisk the flour, baking powder, salt, and sugar.
Beat in the eggs and milk to a thick batter.
Fold in the corn kernels.
Drop heaped spoonfuls into 180C oil and fry 3-4 min, turning, until deep gold.
Drain, salt, and serve hot drizzled with honey.
p: Nebraska is corn country to its core. Keep the batter thick so the fritters hold their shape, and fry a test one to check the center cooks before the outside burns: a runny batter fries flat and greasy.

i: 2 tsp salt, 1 tsp pepper, 1 tsp paprika, 1/2 tsp cayenne
For the gravy: 4 tbsp drippings, 4 tbsp flour, 750ml milk, lots of black pepper
m: Set up buttermilk beaten with eggs, and seasoned flour.
Dredge each steak in flour, then the egg wash, then flour again, pressing it on.
Fry in 5mm of 180C oil 3-4 min a side until deep gold and crisp. Keep warm.
Pour off all but 4 tbsp drippings, whisk in the flour, cook 2 min, and add the milk to make a peppery cream gravy.
Serve the steak smothered in gravy with mashed potatoes.
p: Beef country makes chicken fried steak a birthright: breaded and fried like chicken, hence the name. The double flour dredge builds the crust; keep the browned bits in the pan for the gravy, as they are its whole flavor.

m: Whisk the Kool-Aid powder into the sweetened condensed milk until the color is even.
Add the lemon juice and stir: the acid thickens the filling.
Fold in the whipped topping until smooth.
Spread into the graham crust.
Chill at least 3 hours until set. Top with more whipped topping.
p: Kool-Aid was invented in Hastings, Nebraska, in 1927, and this no-bake pie is a nostalgic tribute. The acid in the drink powder and lemon juice sets the condensed milk: no baking needed, just time in the fridge.

i: For Dorothy Lynch-style dressing: 120ml tomato soup, 120ml oil, 80ml vinegar, 100g sugar, 1 tbsp grated onion, 1 tsp celery seed, 1 tsp paprika, salt
m: Blend all the dressing ingredients until smooth and emulsified; it should be sweet, tangy, and tomato-red.
Chill the dressing at least an hour.
Chop the greens and vegetables and combine in a bowl.
Toss with the dressing just before serving.
Serve cold.
p: Dorothy Lynch is a sweet-and-sour tomato dressing invented in Nebraska in the 1940s and treated as a state condiment. It is good on far more than salad: Nebraskans put it on everything from fries to sandwiches.

m: Keep the popped corn warm in a large bowl, picking out unpopped kernels.
Boil the sugar, corn syrup, butter, and salt to 115C.
Off the heat stir in the vanilla, then pour over the popcorn and fold quickly to coat.
With buttered hands, press handfuls into firm balls while still warm.
Set on parchment to cool and firm.
p: Nebraska is a top popcorn-producing state. Work fast with buttered hands while the syrup is still hot and pliable; let it cool too far and it sets before you can shape the balls, and burnt fingers help no one.

m: Render the bacon until crisp; lift out and reserve, keeping the drippings hot.
Put the torn lettuce and scallions in a bowl.
Add the sugar, vinegar, salt, and pepper to the hot drippings and swirl.
Pour the hot dressing over the lettuce and toss immediately: it wilts the greens just so.
Top with the bacon and chopped egg and serve at once.
p: A prairie farmhouse salad that turns spring lettuce into something warm and savory. The dressing must be poured boiling hot and tossed instantly: that flash of heat wilts the greens without cooking them, and it must be eaten right away.

i: For the chili: 500g ground beef, 1 onion, 400g crushed tomatoes, 400g kidney beans, 2 tbsp chili powder, 1 tsp cumin, 500ml stock
m: Brown the beef with the onion, add the chili powder and cumin, and cook 1 min.
Add the tomatoes, beans, and stock and simmer 40 min until thick.
Warm the cinnamon rolls.
Serve a bowl of chili with a cinnamon roll alongside, the traditional Nebraska school-lunch pairing.
Eat by alternating bites, or dunk the roll in the chili.
p: Chili and a cinnamon roll is a genuine Nebraska (and Iowa) school-lunch tradition that locals defend fiercely. The sweet roll against the savory, slightly sweet chili is the whole point: dunking is encouraged and not the least bit strange to a Nebraskan.

m: Heat the bacon fat in a cast-iron skillet at 220C until smoking.
Whisk the cornmeal, flour, baking powder, salt, and sugar.
Beat in the eggs and buttermilk to a loose batter, then fold in the cracklings.
Pour the batter into the screaming-hot fat and return to the oven.
Bake 22-25 min until the top is gold and the edges crisp. Turn out and serve hot.
p: Cracklin cornbread studs a plain skillet cornbread with crisp bits of rendered pork, a thrifty way to use every scrap of the hog. The smoking-hot skillet gives the shattering crust, and Kansas cornbread stays unsweet.

i: For the dough: 500g flour, 7g yeast, 50g sugar, 1 tsp salt, 240ml warm milk, 1 egg, 55g butter
For the filling: 500g ground beef, 1 onion, 400g cabbage, 1 tsp salt, 1 tsp pepper
m: Make a soft yeasted dough and rise 1 hour.
Brown the beef with the onion, add the cabbage, and cook until wilted and dry. Season and cool.
Roll the dough into squares, fill, and pinch into sealed buns.
Set seam-down, rise 30 min, and brush with egg.
Bake at 190C for 20-25 min until golden.
p: Volga German immigrants brought bierocks to the Kansas wheat plains, where they remain a Friday and church-supper staple. Cook the cabbage filling dry; leftover moisture bursts the seal and sogs the bottom.

i: 2 tbsp salt, 1 tbsp pepper, 1 tbsp paprika, 1 tsp cayenne
m: Brine the chicken in buttermilk overnight.
Season the flour heavily and dredge each piece; rest on a rack 15 min so the crust sets.
Melt lard in a cast-iron skillet to 2cm depth and heat to 165C.
Fry covered for the first half to steam the meat through, then uncovered to crisp, turning once, 15-18 min total.
Drain on a rack and rest 5 min.
p: The Brookville Hotel and Stroud's built Kansas fried-chicken fame on cast-iron, pan-fried birds. Covering the pan for the first half steams the meat tender before the crust locks in; uncovering finishes the crackle.

m: Mix the flours, yeast, and salt. Add the honey, oil, and water and knead 10 min to a smooth, elastic dough.
Rise, covered, 1 hour until doubled.
Knock back, shape into a loaf, and set in a buttered tin.
Rise 45 min until it crowns the tin.
Bake at 200C for 30-35 min until deep brown and hollow-sounding. Cool before slicing.
p: Kansas is the wheat state, growing more than any other, and a good loaf honors the harvest. Knead until the dough is truly smooth and elastic: that gluten development is what gives wheat bread its rise and chew.

m: Soak the bran in the buttermilk 15 min until softened.
Beat in the egg, brown sugar, oil, and molasses.
Whisk the flour, soda, and salt and fold in, then the raisins.
Spoon into muffin cups.
Bake at 190C for 18-20 min until risen and set.
p: A wheat-country breakfast that puts the bran to use. Soaking the bran in buttermilk first is essential: it softens the coarse flakes so the muffins are moist rather than gritty.

i: For the noodles: 250g flour, 3 egg yolks, 1 egg, 1/2 tsp salt, 3 tbsp broth
m: Brown the beef hard in the oil, then add the onion and cook until soft.
Add the stock and bay and simmer 90 min until the beef is tender.
Make the noodles: work the flour, eggs, and salt to a stiff dough, rest, roll thin, cut into ribbons, and dry 20 min.
Drop the noodles into the simmering broth and cook 12-15 min until tender and the broth thickens.
Season and serve over mashed potatoes.
p: Beef and noodles over mashed potatoes is a Kansas plains comfort staple. Homemade egg noodles thicken the broth as they cook — that released starch is what turns thin stock into a rich gravy.

m: Butter a large sheet pan.
Boil the sugar, corn syrup, and water to 120C, then add the butter and sunflower seeds.
Cook, stirring, to 150C until amber and the seeds smell toasted.
Off the heat quickly stir in the salt, baking soda, and vanilla; it foams pale.
Pour onto the pan, spread thin, and cool before breaking into shards.
p: The sunflower is the state flower and Kansas grows them by the field. Sunflower seeds stand in for peanuts here; the baking soda foams the syrup so the brittle shatters crisp rather than cracking teeth.

m: Season and brown the chicken thighs skin-side down; set aside.
Sweat the onion, celery, and mushrooms in the fat until soft.
Stir in the rice to coat, then add the stock and thyme.
Nestle the chicken back in skin-side up, cover, and bake at 180C for 35 min until the rice is tender and the chicken cooked.
Rest 10 min, season, and finish with parsley.
p: A one-pan farmhouse supper. Brown the chicken skin well first: it renders fat to cook the rice in and gives the crisp skin that a covered bake alone cannot, so the browning is worth the extra pan.

m: Cream the butter and sugar, beat in the egg and molasses.
Whisk the flour, soda, and all the spices and work into a stiff dough.
Roll into thin ropes and chill until firm.
Cut the ropes into tiny pea-sized pieces and spread on trays.
Bake at 175C for 10-12 min until firm. They harden as they cool and keep for weeks.
p: Pfeffernusse, or peppernuts, are a Mennonite Christmas tradition in Kansas, baked by the bowlful. Cut them tiny, the size of a hazelnut at most, and expect them to harden into a crunchy, spiced keeping-cookie as they cool.

i: For the pastry: 375g flour, 1 tsp salt, 170g shortening, 120ml cold buttermilk
For the filling: 300g dried apricots or peaches, 250ml water, 100g sugar, 1/2 tsp cinnamon
m: Simmer the dried fruit with the water and sugar 20 min until soft and thick; mash and cool.
Cut the fat into the flour and salt, bind with buttermilk, and chill 30 min.
Roll thin, cut rounds, fill one half, fold, and crimp hard with a fork.
Fry in 180C oil 2-3 min a side until deep gold and blistered.
Drain and dust with icing sugar while warm.
p: Hand pies fried rather than baked, a Plains and border-state tradition. Dried fruit makes a thick filling that will not burst the crust in the fryer — crimp the edges firmly and fry a test pie to be sure the seal holds.

m: Divide the beef into 4 loose balls.
On a hot griddle, place each ball and pile a mound of thin-sliced onion on top. Smash the ball down hard through the onions into a thin patty.
Cook 3-4 min until the underside is crusted, salt, then flip so the onions hit the griddle and caramelize.
Lay cheese on to melt, cook 2 min more.
Set on buttered buns with mustard and pickles.
p: Born in El Reno during the Depression, when onions stretched scarce beef. Smashing the onions into the patty is the whole technique: they steam the meat, then caramelize when flipped, becoming half the burger.

i: 2 tsp salt, 1 tsp pepper, 1 tsp paprika, 1/2 tsp cayenne
For the gravy: 4 tbsp drippings, 4 tbsp flour, 750ml milk, black pepper
m: Set up buttermilk beaten with eggs and seasoned flour.
Dredge each steak in flour, then egg, then flour again, pressing it on.
Fry in 5mm of 180C oil 3-4 min a side until deep gold and crisp. Keep warm.
Pour off all but 4 tbsp drippings, whisk in the flour, cook 2 min, and add the milk for a peppery cream gravy.
Serve the steak smothered with mashed potatoes.
p: Oklahoma named chicken fried steak part of its official state meal. The double flour dredge armors the crust; keep the browned cracklings in the pan for the gravy, since a clean pan makes bland gravy.

m: Toss the sliced okra in buttermilk.
Mix the cornmeal, flour, salt, pepper, and cayenne in a bag.
Lift the okra out and toss in the cornmeal mix to coat.
Fry in 1cm of hot oil over medium-high 4-5 min until deep gold and crisp, turning.
Drain, salt, and serve at once.
p: Part of the official state meal. High heat and a cornmeal coat defeat okra's slime — the mucilage sets and crisps instead of running. Do not crowd the pan, or the temperature drops and the okra steams gummy.

i: For fry bread: 400g flour, 2 tbsp baking powder, 1 tsp salt, 300ml warm milk, oil for frying
m: Mix the fry bread dough and rest 30 min. Pat into rounds and fry in 180C oil until puffed and golden.
Brown the beef with the onion and spices, stir in the beans, and simmer 10 min.
Spoon the meat and beans onto each fry bread.
Top with lettuce, tomato, cheese, and salsa.
Serve open-faced and eat with a fork.
p: Oklahoma is home to 39 tribal nations, and the Indian taco on fry bread is a powwow and state fair icon. Fry the bread the instant it is shaped so it puffs; over-rested dough fries flat.

i: 1 tbsp salt, 1 tsp pepper, 1 tsp cayenne, 1 tsp garlic powder
m: Soak the catfish in buttermilk and hot sauce 30 min.
Season the cornmeal with the salt, pepper, cayenne, and garlic powder.
Heat the oil to 190C.
Dredge the fillets in cornmeal and fry 4-5 min until they float and turn deep gold.
Drain, salt, and serve with lemon, hush puppies, and slaw.
p: Catfish from Oklahoma's lakes and rivers, fried in pure cornmeal for the sandiest crust. Get the oil properly hot so the crust sets before the lean fish overcooks and dries.

i: For the pastry: 375g flour, 1 tsp salt, 170g shortening, 120ml cold buttermilk
For the filling: 300g dried apricots or peaches, 250ml water, 100g sugar, 1/2 tsp cinnamon
m: Simmer the dried fruit with the water and sugar 20 min until thick; mash and cool.
Cut the fat into the flour and salt, bind with buttermilk, and chill 30 min.
Roll thin, cut rounds, fill one half, fold, and crimp hard.
Fry in 180C oil 2-3 min a side until deep gold.
Drain and dust with icing sugar.
p: Oklahoma has a whole town, Davis, known for its roadside fried pies. Dried fruit makes the thick filling that will not burst the crust in the fryer: crimp firmly and test one first to be sure the seal holds.

i: For the dumplings: 250g flour, 2 tsp baking powder, 1/2 tsp salt, 2 tbsp sugar, 3 tbsp oil, 120ml grape juice
m: Bring the grape juice and sugar to a simmer in a wide pot.
Mix the flour, baking powder, salt, sugar, oil, and grape juice into a soft dough.
Roll the dough thin and cut into strips.
Drop the strips into the simmering grape juice and cook 12-15 min until the dumplings are tender and the juice thickens.
Serve warm in bowls with the purple syrup.
p: A traditional dish of the Cherokee and other Oklahoma tribes, made from wild possum grapes. The dumplings thicken the juice into a purple sauce as they cook. Keep the simmer gentle so they cook through without falling apart.

i: For cornbread: 250g cornmeal, 60g flour, 1 tbsp baking powder, 1 tsp salt, 2 eggs, 400ml buttermilk, 3 tbsp bacon fat
m: Simmer the drained beans with the ham hock, onion, bay, and pepper 2-3 hours until creamy and the liquor is thick. Salt at the end.
Pull the hock, shred the meat, and return it.
Heat the bacon fat in a cast-iron skillet at 220C, mix the cornbread batter, pour it in, and bake 20-25 min.
Serve the beans in bowls with cornbread and raw onion.
Crumble the cornbread into the pot liquor to eat.
p: Beans and cornbread fed the Dust Bowl and never left the Oklahoma table. Salt the beans only at the end, early salt keeps the skins tough, and cook uncovered enough that the pot liquor thickens.

m: Scatter the pecans in the shell.
Whisk the eggs, brown sugar, corn syrup, melted butter, vanilla, and salt until smooth.
Pour over the pecans; they rise to form the top.
Bake at 175C for 50-60 min until set with a slight jiggle.
Cool completely before slicing.
p: The pecan is Oklahoma's state tree and the pie a Thanksgiving fixture. Toast the pecans for eight minutes first if you have time — it deepens the flavor beyond what raw nuts give, the one improvement worth making.

n: Oklahoma Sausage and Biscuits with Gravy
i: For biscuits: 375g self-rising flour, 1 tsp sugar, 85g cold butter, 55g lard, 300ml cold buttermilk
1 tsp black pepper, 1/4 tsp sage, pinch cayenne
m: Cut the cold fats into the flour and sugar, bind with buttermilk, pat out, fold, and cut. Bake at 230C for 12-15 min.
Brown the sausage in a cast-iron skillet, letting it crust.
Sprinkle the flour over the meat and fat and cook 2 min.
Add the warm milk in a stream, whisking, and simmer 8-10 min to a thick gravy.
Season hard with pepper, sage, cayenne, and salt. Ladle over split biscuits.
p: A cornerstone of the Oklahoma breakfast. Season the gravy with more pepper than seems polite (it should be visibly speckled), and if it thickens too far, more warm milk brings it back.

m: Toast the dried chiles in a dry pan, soak in hot water 20 min, then blend with the chipotle and a little soaking water into a smooth paste.
Brown the beef cubes hard in the lard in batches; set aside.
Sweat the onion and garlic, add the cumin and oregano, then the chile paste and cook 5 min.
Return the beef with the stock and simmer 2 hours until the meat is tender and the sauce is deep.
Whisk the masa harina with water and stir in to thicken; add vinegar and salt. Simmer 15 min more.
p: A true Texas bowl of red has no beans and no tomatoes: just beef, chiles, and time. Cube the chuck by hand rather than grinding, and toast and soak whole dried chiles rather than reaching for powder; that is the difference between chili and stew.

i: 2 potatoes, diced small and fried crisp
Salsa roja and pico de gallo to serve
m: Fry the diced potato until crisp and golden; drain.
Brown the chorizo or bacon in the same pan.
Beat the eggs, pour into the pan, and scramble softly with the meat until just set.
Warm the tortillas on a dry comal until pliable and slightly charred.
Fill each with egg, potato, and cheese and serve with salsa and pico.
p: The breakfast taco is San Antonio and Austin's morning fuel, and the tortilla must be warmed on a hot comal, never microwaved. Keep the eggs soft: pull them while still glossy, because they carry cooking on the warm tortilla.

i: For the chili: 500g ground beef, 1 onion, 2 tbsp chili powder, 1 tbsp cumin, 400g crushed tomatoes, 400g pinto beans, 500ml stock
Diced onion, jalapenos, and sour cream
m: Brown the beef with the onion, add the chili powder and cumin, and cook 1 min.
Add the tomatoes, beans, and stock and simmer 40 min until thick.
Split a bag of corn chips down the side, or pile them in a bowl.
Ladle the hot chili over the chips.
Top with cheddar, onion, jalapenos, and sour cream and eat straight from the bag.
p: A Texas and New Mexico ballpark and gas-station classic, often served right in the split chip bag. Add the chili just before eating so the chips keep some crunch: a Frito pie built too early is a bag of mush.
