i: For the marinade: 120ml lime juice, 60ml oil, 4 garlic cloves, 1 tsp cumin, 1 tsp chili powder, 1 tsp salt
Guacamole, pico de gallo, sour cream
m: Marinate the skirt steak in the lime, oil, garlic, and spices 2-4 hours.
Grill the steak over very high heat 3-4 min a side for medium-rare, then rest it.
Grill or sear the onions and peppers until charred and soft.
Slice the steak thin against the grain: this is essential for tender fajitas.
Pile onto warm tortillas with the vegetables and toppings.
p: Fajita means little belt, after the skirt steak cut ranch hands were given. High heat and slicing against the grain are the two rules: skirt steak is stringy along the grain and must be cut across it, or every bite is chewy.

i: For the dough: 500g flour, 7g yeast, 60g sugar, 1 tsp salt, 240ml warm milk, 2 egg yolks, 85g butter
For klobasniky: sausage links wrapped in dough
For kolaches: fruit or cream cheese filling
m: Make a rich yeasted dough and rise 1 hour until doubled.
For klobasniky, wrap a sausage link in a piece of dough and seal.
For kolaches, shape balls, press wells, and fill with fruit or cheese; top with posypka crumb.
Set on trays and rise 30 min.
Bake at 190C for 12-15 min until golden.
p: Czech immigrants settled central Texas and made West, Texas the kolache capital; the savory sausage-filled version is a klobasnik, not a kolache, a distinction Texans enforce. Seal the sausage dough well or it splits open in the oven.

i: 180ml dark corn syrup or cane syrup
m: Scatter the pecans in the shell.
Whisk the eggs, brown sugar, syrup, melted butter, bourbon, vanilla, and salt until smooth.
Pour over the pecans; they rise to form the top.
Bake at 175C for 50-60 min until set with a slight jiggle.
Cool completely before slicing.
p: The pecan is the Texas state tree and the pie a point of pride. Toast the pecans eight minutes first for deeper flavor, and cover the crust edge with foil if it browns before the filling sets.

i: White bread, pickles, onion, and mustard to serve
m: Mix the coarse-ground meat with all the seasonings and the cold water until it just binds.
Stuff into the soaked hog casings and twist into links; do not pack too tight.
Rest in the fridge overnight to develop flavor and dry the casing.
Smoke at 110C over post oak 3-4 hours until the internal temperature reaches 68C.
Serve Central Texas meat-market style: on butcher paper with white bread, pickles, onion, and mustard.
p: The German and Czech meat markets of Central Texas built the barbecue tradition, and sausage was their signature. Coarse grind and post oak are the Texas markers, and the overnight rest is what lets the casing dry so it snaps.

m: Whisk the flour, sugar, soda, and salt.
Boil the butter, cocoa, and water, then pour over the dry ingredients and mix. Beat in the eggs, buttermilk, and vanilla.
Pour into a large sheet pan and bake at 175C for 20 min.
For the icing, boil the butter, cocoa, and milk, then beat in the icing sugar, vanilla, and pecans.
Pour the warm icing over the warm cake and let it set.
p: A thin, fast chocolate cake made in a big sheet pan for a crowd, church suppers and funerals alike. The icing goes on while both cake and icing are warm, so it soaks in and sets to a fudgy glaze rather than a frosting.

i: Warm tortillas, salsa, and refried beans to serve
m: Fry the tortilla strips in the oil until crisp and golden; leave them in the pan.
Add the onion and jalapeno and cook until soft.
Add the tomato, then pour in the beaten eggs and scramble softly with the crisp tortilla strips.
Fold in the cheese as the eggs set.
Serve with warm tortillas, salsa, and refried beans.
p: Migas means crumbs, and the dish rescues day-old tortillas by frying them crisp and folding them into eggs. Fry the strips until genuinely crisp before the eggs go in: they soften in the eggs but should keep some chew.

m: Whisk the sugar and flour together.
Beat in the eggs, then the buttermilk, melted butter, lemon, vanilla, and salt.
Pour into the shell and dust with nutmeg.
Bake at 175C for 45-55 min until the top is golden and just set with a slight wobble.
Cool completely before slicing.
p: A thrifty custard pie made from pantry staples, a fixture of the Texas and Southern table. The lemon juice cuts the richness and keeps it from being merely sweet; pull it while the center still moves, as it sets on cooling.

i: 6-8 roasted Hatch green chiles, peeled and chopped
m: Brown the pork cubes hard in the oil; set aside.
Sweat the onion and garlic, add the cumin and oregano.
Return the pork with the stock, chile, and potatoes and simmer 90 min until the pork is tender and the potatoes soft.
Mash a few potatoes against the pot to thicken the stew.
Season and serve with warm flour tortillas.
p: Hatch green chile is New Mexico's obsession and its official state question is red or green. Roasted, peeled Hatch chile is non-negotiable: its smoky heat is the soul of the stew, and no other pepper substitutes for it.

i: 10 dried New Mexico red chiles, stemmed and seeded
m: Toast the dried chiles briefly, soak in hot water 20 min, then blend with the garlic, cumin, oregano, salt, and some soaking water into a smooth red sauce.
Toss the pork cubes in the red chile sauce and marinate at least 4 hours, ideally overnight.
Turn everything into a Dutch oven with the stock.
Braise at 160C for 2.5-3 hours until the pork is falling apart and the sauce is deep and thick.
Stir in the vinegar and season. Serve with rice, beans, or tortillas.
p: Pork marinated and braised in pure red chile: no tomatoes, just chile, garlic, and time. Use whole dried New Mexico chiles, not powder; the long marinade lets the chile penetrate the meat, which is the whole point of adovada.

i: 4 dried red chiles, or 6 green chiles for green posole
Garnishes: shredded cabbage, radish, lime, oregano
m: If using dried posole, simmer it 2-3 hours until the kernels burst open like flowers; canned needs only warming.
Brown the pork, then add the onion and garlic and cook until soft.
Blend the soaked red chiles into a paste (or chop the green chiles) and add with the oregano and bay.
Add the posole and stock and simmer 90 min until the pork is tender and the broth rich.
Serve with cabbage, radish, lime, and oregano to add at the table.
p: Posole is the New Mexican celebration stew, made for Christmas and feast days. The dried hominy must simmer until each kernel bursts open: that blooming is doneness, and canned hominy, while faster, never quite matches the texture.

m: Mix the flour, baking powder, and salt, cut in the lard, then add the water to make a soft dough. Rest 30 min.
Roll the dough thin, 5mm, and cut into squares or triangles.
Heat the oil to 190C.
Fry the pieces one or two at a time, spooning hot oil over so they puff into hollow pillows, 1-2 min a side.
Drain and serve hot with honey to pour into the hollow center.
p: The hollow puff is the whole magic: roll the dough thin and keep the oil hot so each piece balloons in seconds. In New Mexico they arrive with every meal, drizzled with honey to cool the chile heat.

i: For the red sauce: 10 dried New Mexico red chiles, 4 garlic cloves, 1 tsp cumin, 1 tsp oregano, 500ml stock, salt
m: Toast and soak the dried chiles, then blend with the garlic, cumin, oregano, stock, and salt into a smooth sauce. Simmer 15 min.
Warm each tortilla in oil until pliable, then dip in the red sauce.
New Mexico serves them stacked, not rolled: layer tortilla, cheese, onion, sauce, and repeat into a stack.
Top the stack with more sauce and cheese and bake at 190C for 10 min until bubbling.
Crown each stack with a fried egg and shredded lettuce.
p: New Mexico stacks its enchiladas flat rather than rolling them, and crowns them with a fried egg. The red sauce is pure chile, no tomato, so toast and soak whole dried pods, and let the sauce simmer to lose its raw edge.

i: 225g lard (or shortening for a vegetarian version)
m: Cream the lard and sugar until fluffy, beat in the egg, anise seed, and brandy.
Fold in the flour, baking powder, and salt to a firm dough.
Roll out and cut into shapes, traditionally fleur-de-lis.
Bake at 175C for 10-12 min until set but pale.
Toss the warm cookies in cinnamon sugar.
p: The official state cookie of New Mexico, a lard-shortbread scented with anise. Lard is traditional and gives the flaky, tender crumb butter cannot; the anise and brandy are the flavors that mark it as New Mexican.

i: 8 roasted Hatch green chiles, peeled, slit, seeds removed
300g Monterey Jack or asadero cheese, in batons
3 tbsp flour, plus more for dusting
For the sauce: red or green chile sauce, warmed
m: Stuff each roasted chile with a baton of cheese and pinch the slit closed.
Dust the stuffed chiles lightly with flour.
Whip the egg whites to stiff peaks, then fold in the yolks and 3 tbsp flour for a light batter.
Dip each chile in the batter and fry in 180C oil, spooning oil over, until golden and puffed.
Drain and serve smothered in warm chile sauce.
p: The whipped-egg batter is what makes a relleno light rather than heavy. Fold the yolks in gently to keep the air. Roast and peel real Hatch chiles; the smoky flesh is the whole reason to make the dish.

m: Sweat the onion and garlic in the oil until soft.
Add the diced squash and cook 8 min until it begins to soften.
Add the corn and green chile and cook 5 min more.
Stir in the cream and cheese and cook until melted and bound.
Season and serve as a side or a vegetarian main.
p: A squash, corn, and green chile side that turns up on every New Mexican plate in late summer. Do not overcook the squash: it should keep some bite, and green chile plus corn is the flavor that makes it local.

m: Form the beef into four patties and season well.
Griddle over medium-high heat 3-4 min a side.
Pile chopped roasted green chile on each patty and lay cheese over to melt it into the chile.
Toast the buns.
Build with the chile-cheese patty, onion, mustard, and pickles.
p: New Mexico claims the green chile cheeseburger as its own and holds a trail of shrines to it. The chile must be roasted Hatch, chopped and piled on hot so the cheese melts down into it: a raw pepper misses the smoky point entirely.

m: Whisk a little of the milk with the yolks, sugar, cornstarch, and salt into a smooth slurry.
Heat the rest of the milk, then temper in the slurry and cook, stirring, until thickened.
Off the heat add the vanilla.
Whip the egg whites to soft peaks and fold them through the warm custard for lightness.
Chill and serve dusted with cinnamon.
p: A soft stirred custard of Spanish New Mexico, lightened with folded egg white. Fold the whites in while the custard is still warm so they lighten it without cooking to lumps: the texture should be loose, almost pourable.

i: For the crema: mayonnaise, mustard, and jalapeno salsa
Grilled scallions and jalapenos to serve
m: Wrap each hot dog spirally in bacon and secure the ends.
Griddle over medium heat, turning, until the bacon is crisp all around and the dog is hot.
Warm the split-top bolillo buns.
Set the bacon dog in the bun and top with pinto beans, tomato, and onion.
Drizzle with mayonnaise, mustard, and salsa and serve with a grilled scallion and jalapeno.
p: A Tucson and Sonora border creation: the bacon-wrapped dog in a fluffy bolillo, loaded like a taco. Wrap the bacon spirally and crisp it fully; a limp bacon wrap slides off and misses the smoky point of the whole thing.

i: 600g shredded beef or chicken, cooked in red chile
For topping: red or green chile sauce, sour cream, guacamole, lettuce
m: Warm the tortillas so they fold without cracking.
Spread refried beans, then pile shredded chile meat and cheese in the center of each.
Fold into tight sealed burritos, tucking the ends in.
Fry seam-side down in 180C oil, turning, until deep gold and crisp all over.
Drain and smother with chile sauce, sour cream, guacamole, and lettuce.
p: Tucson claims the chimichanga was born when a burrito was dropped in the fryer. Seal the ends tightly and fry seam-side down first so it holds together: an unsealed chimichanga bursts and spills its filling into the oil.

i: 300g Monterey Jack or longhorn cheddar, grated
m: Brush a large flour tortilla lightly with melted butter.
Lay it flat on a hot comal or in the oven and scatter cheese right to the edges.
Add green chile if using.
Cook until the tortilla is crisp and browned and the cheese is bubbling and lacy at the edge.
Cut into wedges and serve flat with salsa.
p: An Arizona invention: a flat, open-faced crisped tortilla under bubbling cheese, distinct from a quesadilla, which is folded. Take the cheese right to the edge so it caramelizes against the pan, and serve it crisp before it softens.

i: 1kg beef flank or round, sliced thin
For cooking: 3 tbsp oil, 1 onion sliced, 2 tomatoes, 3 green chiles, chopped
m: Marinate the thin beef slices in lime, garlic, and salt, then dry them, traditionally in the desert sun, or in a low oven or dehydrator until leathery.
Shred or chop the dried beef finely.
Saute the onion, tomato, and green chile in the oil until soft.
Add the shredded carne seca and cook until it absorbs the flavors and heats through.
Serve piled in warm flour tortillas.
p: Tucson's carne seca is beef dried in the Sonoran sun, then rehydrated by cooking with chile and tomato. El Charro Cafe still dries it in a cage on the roof. The drying concentrates the beef flavor into something jerky-deep.

m: Cut the kernels from the corn and grind or blend them coarse; reserve the fresh husks.
Beat the lard, then work in the ground fresh corn, masa harina, salt, and sugar into a soft dough.
Spread the corn masa on each husk, add a strip of cheese and green chile, and fold.
Stand the tamales upright, packed close, in a steamer.
Steam 60-75 min until the masa sets and pulls cleanly from the husk.
p: Made only in high summer when fresh sweet corn is in, these Sonoran-style tamales use ground fresh corn rather than dried masa alone, giving a sweeter, softer texture. The cheese and green chile inside are the Arizona signature.

i: 60ml prickly pear syrup (from the fruit of the nopal cactus)
Lime and salt for the rim
m: Rub a lime around the glass rim and dip in salt.
Combine the tequila, lime juice, orange liqueur, and prickly pear syrup in a shaker with ice.
Shake hard until cold.
Strain over fresh ice in the salted glass.
Garnish with a lime wheel; the drink glows a deep magenta from the cactus fruit.
p: Prickly pear fruit, the tuna of the nopal cactus, grows across the Arizona desert and turns the margarita a vivid magenta. The fruit is more floral than sweet. Balance it with enough lime so the drink stays tart, not candied.

i: Honey, powdered sugar, or savory toppings
m: Mix the flour, baking powder, and salt, then add the liquid to make a soft dough. Rest 30 min.
Divide and pat each piece into a thin round, pressing a hole in the center to help it cook evenly.
Heat the oil to 180C.
Fry each round 1-2 min a side until puffed and golden.
Serve hot with honey and powdered sugar, or as the base for a Navajo taco.
p: Fry bread carries a difficult history as a food of survival on the Navajo reservation, born of government commodity rations. It is now central to gatherings across Arizona: fry it the moment it is shaped so it puffs.

i: 2 tbsp dried chiltepin peppers (the wild desert chile)
m: Char the tomatoes, garlic, and onion on a comal until blackened in spots.
Toast the tiny chiltepin peppers briefly — they are fierce, so use fewer if unsure.
Blend or crush everything in a molcajete with the lime and salt.
Stir in chopped cilantro.
Rest 20 min for the flavors to meld before serving.
p: The chiltepin is the wild mother of all chiles, growing on the Arizona-Sonora border and packing serious heat in a tiny package. Use them sparingly, they are far hotter than they look, and char the tomatoes for smoky depth.

i: 4 nopal cactus pads, spines removed, diced
m: Boil the diced nopales in salted water 10-15 min until tender; they release a sticky liquid, so rinse well after draining.
Combine the cooled nopales with the tomato, onion, and jalapeno.
Dress with olive oil, lime, salt, and pepper.
Fold in the cilantro.
Top with crumbled queso fresco and serve cool.
p: Nopales, the pads of the prickly pear cactus, taste like a tart green bean and are a desert staple. Rinse them well after boiling to wash away the mucilage they release, just as you would defeat okra's slime.

i: For the masa cakes: 300g masa harina, 250ml warm water, 1 tsp salt
For the red sauce: 8 dried red chiles, 3 garlic cloves, 1 tsp cumin, 500ml stock
m: Mix the masa harina, water, and salt into a dough and pat into thick round cakes.
Fry the masa cakes on a comal or in oil until set and lightly crisp.
Toast and soak the dried chiles, then blend with the garlic, cumin, and stock into a red sauce; simmer 15 min.
Dip the masa cakes in the sauce and layer with cheese and onion.
Bake at 190C for 10 min until bubbling.
p: Sonoran-style enchiladas use thick fresh masa cakes rather than tortillas, a distinctive Arizona border form. Fry the masa cakes until they hold together before saucing, or they fall apart under the red chile.

m: Season the lamb well and brown all sides hard in the oil in a Dutch oven.
Sweat the onions, garlic, and pepper in the fat until soft.
Add the wine and reduce, then the tomatoes, stock, bay, and thyme.
Return the lamb, cover, and braise at 150C for 3 hours until falling off the bone.
Rest, skim the fat, and reduce the sauce. Serve family style with beans and bread.
p: Basque sheepherders settled northern Nevada, and their boarding-house hotels still serve family-style feasts. Lamb is the centerpiece: brown it hard for the crust, then braise it slow, and serve it the Basque way: family style, passed around a long table.

i: 500g small bay shrimp, cooked and chilled
For the cocktail sauce: 200ml ketchup, 3 tbsp horseradish, 1 tbsp lemon juice, 1 tsp Worcestershire, dash hot sauce
m: Chill the cooked bay shrimp thoroughly.
Whisk the ketchup, horseradish, lemon, Worcestershire, and hot sauce into a sharp cocktail sauce.
Spoon a little sauce into the bottom of each tall glass.
Pile the shrimp in and top with more sauce.
Serve ice-cold with a lemon wedge and a long spoon.
p: The Las Vegas shrimp cocktail, served in a sundae glass, was a casino loss-leader for decades, famously fifty cents at the Golden Gate. Use small sweet bay shrimp and keep everything ice cold: it is a dish about chill and sharpness, nothing more.

i: 500g dried pinto or red beans, soaked
m: Brown the chorizo in a heavy pot until it renders; lift out and reserve.
Sweat the onion, garlic, and pepper in the fat until soft.
Add the paprika, tomatoes, drained beans, and stock.
Simmer 90 min until the beans are creamy, then return the chorizo and cook 20 min more.
Mash a few beans to thicken and season well.
p: Beans and chorizo are the everyday side of the Basque boarding-house table in Nevada. Salt the beans only near the end, as early salt keeps the skins tough, and let the chorizo fat flavor the whole pot from the start.

m: Fill a stemmed glass with ice.
Add the grenadine and Amer Picon.
Top with soda water and stir gently.
Float the brandy on top.
Garnish with a lemon twist and serve.
p: The unofficial cocktail of Basque Nevada, served in every sheepherder hotel bar before dinner. The bitter Amer Picon is the backbone; the brandy float on top is traditionally sipped through first, before the drink is stirred.

i: Special sauce: mayonnaise, ketchup, relish, mustard
m: Form the beef into large patties and season.
Griddle over medium-high heat 4 min a side, melting cheese in the last minute.
Toast the buns and spread with special sauce.
Build with the patty, lettuce, tomato, onion, and pickle.
Serve with a pile of fries; the Reno diner tradition calls it awful big, awful good.
p: The Awful Awful is a Reno casino-coffee-shop legend from the Nugget, named for being awful big and awful good. It is a diner burger writ large: pile it high and serve it with a mountain of fries, the way the graveyard-shift crowd expects.

m: Break up the almond paste and beat with the sugar until crumbly.
Beat in the egg whites and salt to a sticky dough.
Roll spoonfuls into balls and press each into a bowl of pine nuts to coat all over.
Set on lined trays and flatten slightly.
Bake at 165C for 15-18 min until golden. Dust with icing sugar when cool.
p: Pinyon pine nuts are a native Nevada harvest, gathered by the Great Basin tribes for millennia. Their rich, resinous flavor coats these soft almond cookies: press them on generously, as the nuts are the whole character.

m: Pat the trout dry and dredge lightly in seasoned flour.
Fry in half the butter over medium-high heat 3-4 min a side until golden and the fish flakes. Keep warm.
Wipe the pan, add the rest of the butter, and toast the almonds until golden.
Add the lemon and parsley and swirl into a pan sauce.
Pour the almond butter over the trout and serve with lemon.
p: Trout from the Sierra Nevada streams and Lake Tahoe, dressed in the classic almondine style. Toast the almonds until genuinely golden and watch the butter: brown butter is the goal, but a second too long turns it black and bitter.

m: Brown the linguica in a pot; lift out and reserve.
Sweat the onion, garlic, and carrot in the fat.
Add the beans, potato, paprika, and stock and simmer 90 min until the beans are tender.
Add the kale and the linguica and cook 15 min more.
Mash a few beans to thicken, and season.
p: Portuguese and Basque immigrants both shaped Nevada's ranch tables, and this hearty bean and sausage soup reflects it. The smoky linguica flavors the whole pot — brown it first to render its paprika-rich fat into the base.

m: Brown the pork cubes hard in the oil; set aside.
Char the tomatillos and blend with the roasted green chiles, garlic, and cumin into a green sauce.
Sweat the onion, add the green sauce, and cook 10 min until it darkens.
Return the pork with the stock and simmer 90 min until tender and the sauce thick.
Finish with cilantro and lime and serve with tortillas.
p: Green chile pork is a staple across the mining and ranching towns of Nevada. Char the tomatillos before blending: that roasting is what gives the sauce its depth instead of a raw, sour edge.

m: Soak the dates in a little of the milk 10 min to soften.
Blend the dates with the milk until smooth, scraping down.
Add the ice cream, vanilla, and salt.
Blend just until thick and creamy.
Pour into a tall glass and serve at once.
p: Dates thrive in the desert oases of the Southwest, and the date shake is a roadside institution across the Mojave into Nevada. Soak the dates first so they blend smooth: un-soaked dates leave chewy bits that clog the straw.

i: For topping: 100g crushed cornflakes, 3 tbsp melted butter
m: Sweat the onion in the butter, stir in the flour, and cook 2 min. Whisk in the milk and simmer to a sauce.
Off the heat stir in the sour cream and two-thirds of the cheese, then season.
Fold in the hash browns and turn into a buttered dish. Top with the rest of the cheese.
Toss the crushed cornflakes with melted butter and scatter over.
Bake at 180C for 40-45 min until bubbling and the cornflake top is golden.
p: A cornerstone of the Latter-day Saint potluck, so named because they appear at every funeral luncheon. The buttered cornflake topping is the signature crunch: do not skip it, and use real shredded cheese, not pre-grated, so the sauce stays smooth.

i: For the fry sauce: 150g mayonnaise, 100g ketchup, 1 tbsp pickle brine, 1/2 tsp paprika, pinch of garlic powder
m: Whisk the mayonnaise, ketchup, pickle brine, paprika, and garlic powder into fry sauce.
Form the beef into patties, season, and griddle 3-4 min a side, melting cheese in the last minute.
Toast the buns and spread generously with fry sauce.
Build with the patty, lettuce, tomato, onion, and pickle.
Serve with fries and extra fry sauce for dipping.
p: Fry sauce is a Utah institution, popularized by the Arctic Circle chain in the 1950s and beloved across the state. The exact ratio is argued endlessly: the pickle brine and paprika are what lift it above plain mayo-ketchup.

i: For honey butter: 115g butter softened, 60ml honey, pinch of salt
m: Mix the flour, yeast, sugar, and salt, then add the milk and melted butter to a soft dough. Rise 1 hour.
Roll to 1cm thick and cut into squares.
Heat the oil to 180C.
Fry the squares 1-2 min a side until puffed and golden.
Whip the honey butter and serve slathered on the hot scones.
p: A Utah scone is not a British scone — it is fried yeast dough, closer to a sopaipilla or fry bread, served with honey butter. Fry them the moment they are cut so they puff into hollow pillows before the dough over-proofs.

m: Dissolve the Jell-O in the boiling water, then stir in the cold water. Chill until syrupy but not set.
Fold in the drained pineapple and cottage cheese.
Fold in the whipped topping for a creamy set.
Add grated carrot or walnuts if you like.
Pour into a mold and chill until firm, at least 4 hours.
p: Utah is the unofficial Jell-O capital of America, and lime green is the state's signature. Chill the Jell-O until syrupy before folding in the add-ins, or they sink to the bottom instead of suspending through the mold.

i: For fry sauce: mayonnaise, ketchup, pickle brine
m: Form and season the beef patties and griddle 3-4 min a side.
Warm the pastrami on the griddle until the edges crisp.
Melt cheese over the patty in the last minute.
Pile the warm pastrami on the cheeseburger.
Set on a fry-sauced bun with lettuce, tomato, onion, and pickle.
p: A Greek-American Utah creation: a cheeseburger crowned with a pile of hot pastrami, found at Crown Burgers and its many imitators across Salt Lake. Warm the pastrami until the edges crisp; cold deli pastrami just sits there limp.

m: Blend the raspberries with the milk and sugar until smooth.
Strain out the seeds if you prefer, or leave them for texture.
Add the ice cream and salt.
Blend just until thick.
Pour into a tall glass and serve at once.
p: Bear Lake on the Utah-Idaho border is famous for its raspberries, and the raspberry shake is the summer tradition there. Use ripe berries and a touch of sugar to balance their tartness: great raspberries need very little help.

m: Season and brown the chicken in a cast-iron Dutch oven over campfire coals or in the oven.
Add the potatoes, carrots, and onions around the chicken.
Pour in the stock and Worcestershire and season with paprika and thyme.
Cover and set coals on the lid, or bake at 190C, for 60-75 min until the chicken and vegetables are tender.
Rest and serve straight from the pot.
p: Dutch-oven cooking is a Utah pioneer tradition, and the cast-iron pot is the official state cooking pot. For the authentic method, set coals on the lid as well as underneath so the heat surrounds the pot and browns the top.

i: For fry bread: 400g flour, 2 tbsp baking powder, 1 tsp salt, 300ml warm milk, oil for frying
1 onion, 2 tbsp chili powder, 1 tsp cumin
m: Mix and rest the fry bread dough, then pat into rounds and fry until puffed and golden.
Brown the beef with the onion and spices, then add the beans and simmer.
Spoon the beef and beans onto each fry bread.
Top with lettuce, tomato, cheese, and salsa.
Serve open-faced.
p: Southern Utah is Navajo country, and the Navajo taco on fry bread is a fixture from Bluff to Monument Valley. Fry the bread the moment it is shaped so it puffs, and build the taco just before eating so the bread stays crisp underneath.

i: Melted butter and honey for brushing
m: Mix the flours, yeast, and salt. Add the honey, butter, milk, and egg and knead 10 min to a smooth dough.
Rise, covered, 1 hour until doubled.
Divide into rolls, shape, and set in a buttered pan. Rise 45 min.
Bake at 190C for 18-20 min until golden.
Brush with melted butter and a little honey as they come out.
p: Utah's honey and wheat both feature in this soft dinner roll, a Sunday-table staple. Local honey in the dough and brushed on top after baking gives a floral sweetness: do not rush the second rise, or the rolls bake dense.

i: For the batter: 115g butter, 190g flour, 200g sugar, 2 tsp baking powder, 240ml milk
m: Toss the peaches with sugar, cornstarch, and cinnamon.
Melt the butter in a Dutch oven, then whisk the flour, sugar, baking powder, and milk into a batter and pour it over the butter. Do not stir.
Spoon the peaches over the batter; do not stir.
Cover and bake with coals above and below, or at 190C, for 45-55 min until the cake rises around the fruit and browns.
Serve warm from the pot with ice cream.
p: Utah's Dixie region in the south grows fine peaches, and cobbler in the Dutch oven is a camp and reunion tradition. As with any batter cobbler, the trick is not stirring: the cake floats up through the fruit as it bakes.

i: 8 roasted Pueblo or Hatch green chiles, chopped
m: Brown the pork cubes hard in the oil; set aside.
Sweat the onion and garlic, sprinkle in the flour, and cook 2 min to a light roux.
Add the green chile, tomatoes, cumin, and oregano and cook 5 min.
Return the pork with the stock and simmer 90 min until the pork is tender and the chili thickened.
Season and serve as a stew or smothered over burritos and eggs.
p: Colorado green chili is thicker and often pork-and-tomato based, distinct from New Mexico's version; a roux gives it body. Pueblo chiles are the Colorado pride; the chili is poured over everything from breakfast burritos to fries across the Front Range.

m: Render the bacon in a cast-iron skillet until crisp; lift out and reserve the fat.
Dredge the trout in the cornmeal, flour, salt, and pepper.
Fry in the bacon fat and half the butter 3-4 min a side until the crust is gold and the fish flakes.
Add the rest of the butter, lemon, and parsley to make a pan sauce.
Serve the trout with the crumbled bacon and lemon.
p: Rainbow trout from the cold Rocky Mountain streams is Colorado's classic catch, often cooked streamside. Cornmeal gives the crisp crust and bacon fat the flavor. Do not overcook trout, which is lean and flakes dry within a minute of done.

m: Saute the ham, green pepper, and onion in a little butter until softened and lightly browned.
Beat the eggs with salt and pepper.
Melt butter in an omelette pan, pour in the eggs, and let them set at the edges.
Add the ham and vegetable mixture and the cheese to one half.
Fold over, slide onto a plate, and serve with toast.
p: The Denver omelette (or Western omelette) has roots in the chuck-wagon and railroad cooks of the frontier, some say as a way to freshen aging eggs with ham and onion. Cook the filling first so it is soft and browned before it meets the delicate eggs.

m: Blanch and peel the peaches, then toss with sugar, cornstarch, lemon, cinnamon, almond extract, and salt.
Fill the lined pie plate and dot with butter.
Lay a lattice top, brush with egg, and dust with sugar.
Bake at 220C for 20 min, then 190C for 40 min until the juices bubble thickly.
Cool 4 hours before slicing.
p: Palisade, on Colorado's Western Slope, grows some of the country's finest peaches in its high desert orchards. A drop of almond extract amplifies the peach flavor, but no more than a quarter teaspoon, or it tips into marzipan.

m: Form the bison into patties and season: handle it gently, as lean bison toughens if overworked.
Griddle over medium-high heat 3 min a side, no more; bison is lean and dries out past medium.
Melt cheese over the patty and add green chile if using.
Toast the buns.
Build with the patty, onion, lettuce, tomato, and pickle.
p: Bison ranching is big across Colorado's plains, and the leaner, sweeter meat makes a fine burger. The key is not to overcook it — bison has far less fat than beef, so pull it at medium or it turns dry and livery.

i: 500ml Colorado green chili (see separate recipe), warmed
m: Fry the diced potatoes until crisp; brown the chorizo separately.
Scramble the eggs softly.
Fill each warm tortilla with eggs, potato, chorizo, and cheese and roll into a burrito.
Set on a plate and ladle warm green chili over the top to smother it completely.
Add more cheese, sour cream, and onion and serve with a fork.
p: The smothered breakfast burrito, drowned in green chili, is a Colorado morning institution. The whole point is the green chili poured over the top; a burrito served dry on the side is not smothered, and a Coloradan will notice.

m: Rub the chops with the garlic, rosemary, olive oil, and mustard and marinate 1 hour.
Season well with salt and pepper.
Sear over high heat or on a hot grill 3-4 min a side for medium-rare.
Rest the chops 5 min.
Serve with lemon and a simple potato or green side.
p: Colorado lamb is prized for its mild flavor, raised on the high mountain pastures. Chops want high heat and a short cook: sear them hard for the crust and pull at medium-rare, as lamb past that loses its delicacy.

i: For the dough: 500g flour, 7g yeast, 50g sugar, 1 tsp salt, 240ml warm milk, 2 eggs, 85g butter
For filling: 115g butter, 200g brown sugar, 3 tbsp cinnamon
For icing: 200g cream cheese, 55g butter, 200g icing sugar, 1 tsp vanilla
m: Knead the dough and rise 90 min until doubled.
Roll into a rectangle, spread with the butter, brown sugar, and cinnamon, and roll up tightly.
Cut into 12 and set in a buttered pan. Rise 45 min.
Bake at 180C for 25-30 min until golden.
Beat the cream cheese icing and spread over the warm rolls.
p: Colorado's Johnson's Corner truck stop made its cinnamon rolls famous to generations of I-25 travelers. Roll the dough tight so the spiral holds, and ice them while still warm so the cream cheese frosting melts into the crevices.

m: Brown the elk hard, then add the onion, pepper, and garlic and cook until soft.
Add the chili powder and cumin and cook 1 min.
Add the tomatoes, beans, stock, and cocoa and simmer 90 min, stirring, until thick.
Season with salt and pepper.
Serve with cornbread, cheese, and onions.
p: Elk is a Colorado hunting-season staple, leaner and gamier than beef. The long moist simmer of a chili suits it well, and the cocoa deepens the color and rounds the gaminess without reading as chocolate.

m: Melt the white chocolate gently and spread on a lined tray.
Melt the dark chocolate and drizzle over, swirling with a skewer for a marbled effect.
While still wet, scatter the pretzels, almonds, and cranberries over.
Sprinkle with flaky salt.
Chill until firm, then break into shards.
p: A mountain-lodge treat that captures the sweet, salty, crunchy appeal of trail mix in bark form. Scatter the toppings while the chocolate is still wet so they set in, and the flaky salt is what keeps it from being merely sweet.

i: For the pastry: 375g flour, 1 tsp salt, 170g lard, 120ml cold water
350g beef skirt or sirloin, diced small
Salt and plenty of black pepper
m: Cut the lard into the flour and salt, bind with cold water, and rest 30 min.
Mix the raw beef, potato, onion, and rutabaga and season hard: everything cooks inside the crust.
Roll rounds, mound filling on one half, dot with butter, fold, and crimp a rope seal.
Vent, brush with egg, and bake at 200C for 20 min, then 175C for 40 min until deep gold.
Rest 10 min and serve with brown gravy poured over, the Butte way.
p: Cornish miners carried pasties into the copper mines of Butte, where they are still sold by the dozen. Butte serves them under brown gravy, which distinguishes them from the dry Michigan version. Season the raw filling boldly.

i: 4 boneless pork loin chops, pounded thin
Yellow mustard, pickle, and raw onion
m: Pound the chops between plastic to 5mm thick.
Dredge in flour, then egg, then cracker crumbs, pressing them on.
Fry in 5mm of 180C oil 3 min a side until deep gold and crisp.
Set on a plain soft bun.
Dress simply with mustard, pickle, and onion, nothing more.
p: A Butte institution since 1924, sold from a walk-up window on Mercury Street. The dressing is deliberately spare (mustard, pickle, onion) because the crisp pork is the whole sandwich and anything else muddies it.

m: Toss the huckleberries with the sugar, cornstarch, lemon, cinnamon, and salt and let stand 15 min.
Fill the lined pie plate and dot with butter.
Lay a lattice, brush with egg, and dust with sugar.
Bake at 220C for 20 min, then 190C for 35-40 min until the juices bubble thickly through the lattice.
Cool at least 4 hours: huckleberry juice runs freely when warm.
p: Huckleberries cannot be farmed; they are picked wild in the mountains, which is why a jar costs what it does. Their flavor is tarter and wilder than a blueberry, so do not over-sugar them: the point is that wild tartness.

m: Blend the huckleberries with the milk and sugar until smooth.
Add the ice cream and salt.
Blend briefly, just until thick: over-blending melts it.
Pour into a chilled tall glass.
Serve at once with a fat straw.
p: Every roadside stand and lodge from Glacier to Yellowstone sells one all summer. Blend it short: a milkshake worked too long warms and thins, and the whole appeal is thick, cold, and vividly purple.

i: 1kg Flathead or other sweet cherries, pitted
For the topping: 150g oats, 150g flour, 165g brown sugar, 1/2 tsp salt, 1 tsp cinnamon, 170g cold butter
m: Toss the pitted cherries with the sugar, cornstarch, lemon, and almond extract and turn into a buttered dish.
Rub the topping ingredients together with your fingers into rough clumps, leaving some butter in pieces.
Scatter over the cherries without pressing down.
Bake at 190C for 40-45 min until the topping is deep gold and the juices bubble at the edges.
Rest 20 min and serve with cream or ice cream.
p: Flathead Lake's cherry orchards ripen in late July, warmed by the lake and cooled by the mountains. Sweet cherries need the lemon and a whisper of almond extract to keep them from tasting flat — almond amplifies cherry like nothing else.

n: Montana Bison Ribeye with Wild Mushrooms
m: Bring the steaks to room temperature and season hard with salt and pepper.
Sear in a screaming-hot skillet 2-3 min a side for rare to medium-rare: bison is lean and must not go past medium.
Rest the steaks on a warm plate.
Cook the mushrooms in butter until browned, add the garlic and thyme, then deglaze with the wine.
Spoon the mushrooms and pan juices over the rested steaks.
p: Bison has perhaps a third the fat of beef, which means it cooks faster and turns to leather past medium-rare. Sear it hard and pull it early: the lean sweetness is the reward for watching the pan closely.

n: Montana Elk Backstrap with Huckleberry Sauce
i: For the sauce: 200g huckleberries, 120ml red wine, 120ml stock, 2 tbsp sugar, 1 tbsp balsamic, 1 tbsp butter
m: Season the elk medallions well and let them come to room temperature.
Sear in the hot oil 2 min a side for rare, basting with butter and thyme. Rest: elk is very lean and must stay pink.
Simmer the huckleberries with the wine, stock, sugar, and balsamic 10 min until syrupy.
Whisk the butter into the sauce off the heat for gloss.
Slice the rested backstrap and spoon the huckleberry sauce over.
p: Backstrap is the prize cut of the elk and the leanest thing in the freezer: treat it like a fine steak and never cook it past rare. Huckleberry and game is a Montana marriage: the tart wild fruit answers the mineral depth of the meat.

m: Brown the beef hard in the oil in batches; set aside.
Sweat the onion, carrot, and celery until soft, then add the mushrooms and cook until their water goes.
Return the beef with the stock, bay, and thyme and simmer 90 min until tender.
Add the barley and cook 40 min more until plump and the soup has thickened.
Season well and finish with parsley.
p: Montana grows a great deal of the nation's barley, much of it for beer, and the rest goes into pots like this on a cold ranch night. Add the barley late: it drinks liquid greedily, and a soup left standing overnight will need thinning.

m: Whisk the flour, baking powder, salt, soda, and sugar.
Cut in the cold butter until the pieces are pea-sized.
Stir in the sourdough starter and buttermilk just until it comes together, shaggy.
Pat to 3cm, fold in thirds twice, and cut straight down without twisting.
Bake at 220C for 15-18 min until risen and gold. Brush with melted butter.
p: Sourdough came west with prospectors who kept their starter warm inside their coats: the old-timers were called sourdoughs for it. The starter adds tang and tenderness; the baking powder still does the lifting.

n: Montana Lentil and Wheat Berry Salad
i: For the dressing: 4 tbsp olive oil, 2 tbsp red wine vinegar, 1 tsp Dijon, 1 garlic clove, salt and pepper
m: Simmer the wheat berries in salted water 45 min until tender but chewy; drain.
Simmer the lentils separately 20 min until tender but holding shape; drain.
Whisk the dressing and toss it through the warm grains and lentils: warm absorbs better than cold.
Fold in the onion, carrot, and herbs.
Top with feta and serve at room temperature.
p: Montana's northern plains grow lentils, peas, and wheat in rotation, and this salad puts all of them on one plate. Dress the grains while warm: cold grains repel dressing, and the difference in flavor is considerable.

m: Render the salt pork in a Dutch oven until crisp, then sweat the onion and garlic in the fat.
Add the tomato paste and cook 2 min, then the molasses, sugar, mustard, and chili powder.
Add the drained beans and water, cover, and simmer 2-3 hours until creamy, adding water as needed.
Uncover for the last 30 min so the liquid reduces to a thick sauce.
Salt only at the end and season with pepper.
p: The chuckwagon fed cattle drives out of Cheyenne and Casper, and beans were the daily bread of the trail. Salt them at the end, early salt keeps the skins tough, and finish uncovered so the pot liquor thickens to a glaze.

i: 700g calf fries (bull testicles), membrane peeled, sliced 1cm
m: Peel the tough outer membrane away and slice the meat into rounds.
Soak in buttermilk at least 1 hour to mellow the flavor.
Mix the flour, cornmeal, salt, pepper, cayenne, and garlic powder.
Dredge the slices and fry at 190C for 2-3 min until deep gold and crisp.
Drain, salt at once, and serve with cocktail sauce and lemon.
p: A ranch-country delicacy born of branding season, when nothing on the animal was wasted. Peeling the membrane is the essential prep — leave it on and the pieces curl and toughen. Fried hot and fast, they eat like tender fried mushrooms.

i: For the jus: pan drippings, 250ml red wine, 500ml beef stock
m: Rub the roast all over with salt, pepper, garlic, herbs, and oil and rest it uncovered in the fridge overnight.
Bring to room temperature, then roast at 230C for 20 min to build a crust.
Drop to 120C and roast slowly to an internal 52C for medium-rare, about 2.5 hours. Use a thermometer, not a clock.
Rest 30 min under foil: this is not optional on a roast this size.
Deglaze the pan with wine, add stock, reduce, and serve the jus with horseradish cream.
p: Cattle country eats beef at its plainest and best. The overnight uncovered salting dries the surface for a better crust and seasons deep; the long rest lets the juices redistribute, and carving early costs you the whole roast.

i: A splash of cold water for settling
An enamel pot, ideally over a fire
m: Bring the water to a boil in the pot, then pull it off the heat for 30 seconds.
Stir in the coarse grounds and return to a bare simmer for 4 minutes.
Take the pot off the heat and let it stand 2 minutes.
Sprinkle a splash of cold water over the surface: this drops the grounds to the bottom.
Pour slowly and steadily, leaving the last inch in the pot.
p: No filter, no press, just a pot and patience. The splash of cold water at the end is the trail trick that settles the grounds, and pouring slowly without jostling the pot is what keeps them there.

i: 200g ground pork (elk is too lean alone)
For the glaze: 120ml ketchup, 2 tbsp brown sugar, 1 tbsp cider vinegar
m: Mix the elk and pork with the grated onion, soaked breadcrumbs, eggs, Worcestershire, thyme, salt, and pepper; handle it lightly.
Shape into a loaf on a lined tray rather than packing it into a tin, so the sides brown.
Whisk the glaze and brush half over the loaf.
Bake at 175C for 60-70 min, brushing with the rest of the glaze twice, until 70C internal.
Rest 15 min before slicing.
p: Elk is so lean it needs pork fat to make a meatloaf that is not dry and crumbly. Free-forming the loaf on a tray rather than pressing it into a tin gives you browned sides instead of steamed ones.

i: 1kg beef eye of round, trimmed and sliced 5mm with the grain
m: Freeze the beef 1 hour to firm it, then slice thin with the grain for a chewy jerky (across the grain gives a tender one).
Marinate the slices in all the remaining ingredients 6-24 hours in the fridge.
Pat the strips dry and lay them on racks without overlapping.
Dry at 70C in an oven with the door cracked, or in a dehydrator, 4-6 hours.
It is done when a strip cracks but does not snap when bent. Cool fully before storing.
p: Drying meat is older than the state and still how ranch families handle a full freezer. The bend test is the only reliable doneness check: a strip should crack and show white fibers but not break clean, which means it has gone too far.

m: Brown the beef hard in the oil in batches; set aside.
Sweat the onions and garlic, sprinkle in the flour, and cook 2 min.
Add the stock, tomatoes, Worcestershire, and bay and return the beef. Simmer 90 min.
Add the potatoes and carrots and cook 30 min until tender.
Stir in the corn, cook 5 min more, and season well.
p: A Dutch-oven stew built from whatever the chuckwagon carried. Brown the beef in batches without crowding: a pan packed too full steams the meat grey, and that first hard crust is most of the flavor in the finished pot.

m: Simmer the chokecherries in the water 20 min until soft, mashing as they cook.
Strain through a jelly bag overnight without squeezing: squeezing clouds the jelly.
Measure 1L of the clear juice into a pot with the lemon juice and pectin and bring to a hard boil.
Add the sugar all at once and boil hard 1 minute, stirring.
Skim the foam and jar immediately, sealing while hot.
p: Chokecherries grow wild along every draw and creek bed in Wyoming and are far too astringent to eat raw: jelly is their destiny. Do not squeeze the bag: patience overnight buys a jewel-clear jelly instead of a cloudy one.

m: Cream the butter with both sugars until light, then beat in the eggs and vanilla.
Whisk the flour, soda, baking powder, and salt and fold in.
Stir through the oats, chocolate chips, pecans, and coconut: the dough will be very full.
Drop large mounds well apart on lined trays.
Bake at 175C for 12-14 min until set at the edges and still soft in the middle.
p: A cookie with everything in the pantry thrown in, meant to travel and keep. Make them large and pull them while the centers still look underdone: they finish setting on the hot tray and stay chewy for days.

m: Brown the lamb hard in the oil in batches; set aside.
Sweat the onions and garlic, sprinkle in the flour, and cook 2 min.
Deglaze with the wine, scraping the fond, then add the stock, rosemary, and bay.
Return the lamb, cover, and simmer 90 min until tender.
Add the potatoes and carrots and cook 30 min more. Season and serve.
p: Wyoming ran vast sheep bands before and alongside the cattle, and lamb remains a ranch staple. Rosemary and lamb is a fixed pairing for good reason: the resinous herb answers the fat, so be generous with it.

m: Scrub the potatoes and dry them completely, then prick each several times with a fork.
Rub all over with oil and roll in coarse salt.
Bake directly on the oven rack at 200C for 60-70 min until the skin is crisp and a skewer slides through with no resistance. Never wrap in foil, which steams the skin soft.
Split the top with a cross, squeeze the ends to fluff the interior, and season inside.
Load with butter, sour cream, cheddar, scallion, and bacon.
p: Idaho's volcanic soil and cool nights grow the russet Burbank, the definitive baking potato. Foil is the enemy: it traps steam and gives you a boiled potato in a crisp-looking jacket. Bake it naked on the rack and salt the skin.

i: 700g sirloin or tri-tip, cut in finger-sized strips
1 tsp salt, 1 tsp pepper, 1 tsp garlic powder, 1/2 tsp paprika
m: Soak the beef strips in buttermilk 30 min.
Whisk the flour with the seasonings, then beat in the egg and beer to make a loose batter.
Heat the oil to 190C.
Dip each strip in the batter, let the excess drip, and fry 2-3 min until deep gold and crisp.
Drain on a rack, salt at once, and serve with fry sauce.
p: Invented in Boise in the 1950s and found on nearly every Idaho menu since. Cut the strips no thicker than a finger so they cook through before the batter darkens, and serve immediately: a finger steak waiting on the pass goes soft.

m: Shape each scoop of ice cream into an oval and freeze hard, at least 2 hours.
Roll each frozen oval in cocoa powder until completely coated so it looks like a dirt-dusted potato.
Set on a plate and cut a slit down the middle.
Pipe whipped cream into the slit so it looks like sour cream on a baked potato.
Finish with a drizzle of chocolate sauce for gravy and nuts for chives. Serve immediately.
p: A Boise dessert joke played entirely straight: it looks exactly like a loaded baked potato. Freeze the ovals rock-hard before rolling in cocoa, or they slump and the illusion collapses on the plate.

i: 150g jamon or cured ham, minced fine
For coating: 100g flour, 2 eggs beaten, 200g fine breadcrumbs
m: Melt the butter, stir in the flour, and cook 3 min without coloring.
Add the warm milk slowly, whisking hard, and cook 10-15 min until the bechamel is very thick and pulls from the pan.
Stir in the minced ham, nutmeg, salt, and pepper. Spread in a tray, cover, and chill overnight until firm.
Shape into small cylinders, then coat in flour, egg, and breadcrumbs.
Fry at 190C for 2 min until deep gold. They should be crisp outside and molten within.
p: Boise holds one of the largest Basque communities outside Spain, and its restaurants keep croquetas on every menu. The overnight chill is not optional: a warm bechamel will burst in the fryer and leave you with breadcrumbs in oil.

m: Sweat the onion, carrot, and celery in the oil until soft, 10 min, then add the garlic.
Stir in the tomato paste, cumin, and paprika and cook 2 min.
Add the lentils and stock and simmer 35-40 min until the lentils are tender but still holding shape.
Mash a ladleful against the pot to thicken the broth.
Finish with the vinegar (this is what wakes the whole pot up) and season.
p: The Palouse region straddling Idaho and Washington grows most of America's lentils. The splash of vinegar at the end is the step people skip and the one that matters most; lentils are earthy and flat without acid to lift them.

m: Cook half the huckleberries with 2 tbsp of the sugar and the lemon juice 5 min into a loose jam; cool.
Heat the milk and cream until steaming.
Whisk the yolks with the remaining sugar and salt, temper in the hot dairy, and cook to 82C until it coats a spoon.
Strain, add the vanilla and the huckleberry jam, and chill thoroughly.
Churn, folding in the remaining whole berries in the last minute, and freeze until firm.
p: Northern Idaho's huckleberry country runs from Coeur d'Alene into the panhandle. Cooking half the berries into jam gives the base its color and depth, while folding whole berries in at the end keeps bursts of fresh tartness.

m: Render the bacon in a large skillet until crisp; lift out and keep the fat.
Dredge the trout in the cornmeal, flour, salt, and pepper.
Fry in the bacon fat 3-4 min a side until the crust is gold and the flesh flakes at the thickest point.
Add the butter and lemon juice at the end and spoon over.
Serve each trout with crumbled bacon and parsley.
p: Idaho raises more farmed rainbow trout than any state, in the cold springs of the Snake River canyon. Cornmeal and bacon fat are the traditional treatment. And pull the fish the moment it flakes, since trout is lean and dries in seconds.

m: Sweat the onion and garlic in the butter, stir in the flour, and cook 2 min.
Whisk in the milk and cream and simmer to a smooth sauce. Season with nutmeg, salt, and pepper.
Layer the thin-sliced potatoes in a buttered dish, pouring sauce over every layer and scattering cheese between.
Cover with foil and bake at 180C for 45 min, then uncover and bake 25 min more until browned and bubbling.
Rest 15 min before serving so the layers set.
p: Slice the potatoes on a mandoline if you have one: uneven slices cook unevenly and leave you with crunchy pockets. Resting the dish before serving lets the starch set the layers so it cuts into squares instead of sliding apart.

i: For the glaze: 300g icing sugar, 60ml milk, 1 tsp vanilla
m: Beat the cooled mashed potato with the milk, eggs, sugar, and melted butter.
Add the flour, yeast, and salt and knead to a soft, tacky dough. Rise 90 min until doubled.
Roll to 1cm and cut rings. Rise 30 min on floured trays until puffy.
Fry at 175C for 60-90 seconds a side until deep gold.
Dip in the glaze while still warm and set on a rack.
p: Potato doughnuts are lighter and stay softer than plain flour ones because the potato starch holds moisture. Idaho, unsurprisingly, adopted them wholesale. Do not skip the second rise: an under-proofed spudnut fries dense.

i: 300g fresh morels, halved and rinsed carefully
500g asparagus, trimmed and cut in lengths
m: Rinse the morels quickly in cold water to flush the honeycomb, then drain and dry: never soak them.
Cook the morels in butter over medium-high heat 5 min until they release their water and it cooks away.
Add the shallots and garlic and cook 2 min, then the asparagus and cook 4 min until bright and just tender.
Add the cream and thyme and simmer 2 min to bind.
Finish with lemon and season.
p: Morels flush across Idaho's burned mountain slopes each spring and must always be cooked, never eaten raw. Rinse rather than soak: the honeycomb drinks water like a sponge and a soaked morel steams instead of browning.

i: 2kg beef top round or sirloin roast
Hot mustard and horseradish to serve
m: Season the roast hard and brown all over in the oil, then roast at 160C to 52C internal for rare, about 90 min. Rest, then chill for slicing.
Simmer the pan drippings with the stock, onions, and bay 30 min to make a rich jus, then strain.
Slice the cold beef as thin as you possibly can.
Warm the slices briefly in the hot jus. Never boil them.
Pile into split rolls and either dip the whole sandwich in jus or serve the jus alongside.
p: Two Los Angeles restaurants, Philippe's and Cole's, have argued over the invention since 1908. Chill the roast before slicing — warm beef tears rather than shaving thin — and only warm the meat in the jus, since boiling turns it grey.

i: 1 head romaine and 1 bunch watercress, chopped fine
For the vinaigrette: 6 tbsp olive oil, 2 tbsp red wine vinegar, 1 tsp Dijon, 1 garlic clove, salt and pepper
m: Chop all the greens very fine and spread across a wide platter.
Arrange the chicken, bacon, egg, avocado, tomato, and Roquefort in neat parallel rows over the greens.
Whisk the vinaigrette until emulsified.
Present the salad in its rows at the table first.
Dress and toss thoroughly just before serving so every forkful carries everything.
p: Bob Cobb built it at the Hollywood Brown Derby in 1937 from leftovers found in the icebox. The rows are for presentation, but the salad is meant to be tossed, and everything must be chopped fine enough to eat with a spoon.

i: 1.5kg tri-tip roast, fat cap trimmed to 5mm
Red oak wood for the fire
To serve: pinquito beans, salsa, and grilled garlic bread
m: Rub the tri-tip with only salt, pepper, and garlic (the Santa Maria seasoning is that spare), and rest 1 hour.
Build a red oak fire and let it burn to hot coals.
Sear the roast over direct heat 5 min a side, then move it higher or to indirect heat.
Cook to 52C internal for medium-rare, about 30-40 min, turning occasionally.
Rest 15 min, then slice thin against the grain: the grain changes direction mid-roast, so watch for the turn.
p: Santa Maria barbecue is a Central Coast ranching tradition, cooked over red oak with a three-ingredient rub. The tri-tip's grain shifts direction partway along the roast; find the turn and adjust your knife, or half the slices will be tough.

i: 60ml rice vinegar, 2 tbsp sugar, 1 tsp salt
2 tbsp toasted sesame seeds or tobiko
m: Rinse the rice until the water runs clear, cook it, then fold through the warmed vinegar, sugar, and salt. Cool to body temperature.
Lay a nori sheet on a rolling mat covered in cling film and spread rice over it, then flip so the nori faces up: this is the inside-out roll.
Lay the crab, avocado, and cucumber along the center.
Roll tightly with the mat, pressing to compact.
Roll the outside in sesame seeds and cut with a wet knife into eight pieces.
p: Created in Los Angeles in the 1960s to introduce American diners to sushi by hiding the nori inside and swapping raw fish for crab and avocado. Wet the knife between every cut, or the rice drags and the roll loses its shape.

m: Steam each tortilla until soft and pliable: it must stretch without tearing.
Lay a line of rice, then beans, then meat, then cheese, salsa, guacamole, and sour cream down the center. Do not overfill, however tempting.
Fold in the sides, then roll tightly from the bottom, tucking as you go.
Wrap tightly in foil.
Griddle the wrapped burrito briefly, or unwrap and sear the seam, to seal it.
p: San Francisco's Mission District built the oversized foil-wrapped burrito in the 1960s, rice and all. Steaming the tortilla is the technique that makes it possible: a cold tortilla splits the moment you roll it this full.

m: Fry the bacon until crisp; set aside, leaving the fat in the pan.
Dredge the oysters in flour, then beaten egg, then cracker crumbs.
Fry the oysters in the bacon fat 1 min a side until golden; do not overcook them.
Beat the remaining eggs, pour into the pan with butter, and scramble softly around the oysters.
Fold in the bacon, season, finish with parsley, and serve as a loose open omelette.
p: A Gold Rush dish from Placerville, once called Hangtown, said to be ordered by a miner who wanted the three most expensive things in the house: eggs, bacon, and oysters. Keep the eggs soft and the oysters barely cooked.

m: Blend the anchovies, garlic, lemon juice, and vinegar into a paste.
Add the herbs and blend until the mixture turns bright green.
Fold in the mayonnaise and sour cream: blending them fully can loosen the emulsion.
Season with salt and pepper.
Chill at least an hour so the herbs perfume the base. Use within three days while the color holds.
p: Created at the Palace Hotel in San Francisco in 1923 for an actor starring in a play called The Green Goddess. The anchovies are not optional: they provide the savory depth beneath the herbs, and nobody will identify them.

m: Cook the noodles until just al dente and reserve a cup of the water.
Melt the butter over low heat and cook the minced garlic very gently 3-4 min until fragrant and pale gold, never browned, which turns it bitter.
Add the oyster sauce, fish sauce, soy, and sugar and swirl.
Toss the drained noodles through the garlic butter with a splash of pasta water.
Off the heat fold in the Parmesan and finish with scallions and pepper.
p: A Vietnamese-American San Francisco invention from the Crustacean kitchen, now on menus all over the Bay. Cook the garlic gently and never let it brown: bitter garlic ruins the dish, and there is a great deal of it in here.

i: For the aioli: 4 garlic cloves, 2 egg yolks, 1 tsp Dijon, 250ml olive oil, 1 tbsp lemon juice, salt
m: Trim the artichoke stems and snip the thorny leaf tips. Rub the cut surfaces with lemon.
Simmer in salted water with the lemon halves, garlic, and bay 35-45 min until an outer leaf pulls away easily.
Pound the garlic to a paste, whisk in the yolks and mustard, then add the oil drop by drop at first, then in a thin stream, until thick.
Finish the aioli with lemon and salt.
Drain the artichokes upside down and serve warm with the aioli for dipping leaf by leaf.
p: Castroville calls itself the artichoke capital of the world and once crowned Marilyn Monroe its queen. The leaf test is the only reliable doneness check, and add the oil to the aioli slowly at the start or the emulsion will break.

i: For the crust: 250g flour, 75g icing sugar, 1/4 tsp salt, 225g cold butter
For the filling: 6 eggs, 400g sugar, 180ml Meyer lemon juice, 2 tbsp zest, 60g flour, 1/4 tsp salt
m: Rub the crust ingredients to crumbs, press firmly into a lined pan, and bake at 175C for 20-25 min until pale gold.
Whisk the eggs and sugar, then the lemon juice, zest, flour, and salt until smooth.
Pour the filling over the hot crust: this is what fuses the two layers together.
Bake 25-30 min more until the center is just set and no longer wobbles when nudged.
Cool completely, chill, then cut and dust with icing sugar.
p: The Meyer lemon, a lemon-mandarin cross, grows in backyards all over California and is sweeter and more floral than a Eureka. Pour the filling onto the crust while the crust is still hot: that is the trick that stops the layers separating.

m: Toss the marionberries with the sugar, cornstarch, lemon, and salt and let stand 15 min.
Fill the lined pie plate and dot with butter.
Lay a lattice top, brush with egg, and dust heavily with sugar.
Bake at 220C for 20 min, then 190C for 40-45 min until the juices bubble thickly through the lattice.
Cool at least 4 hours: marionberry juice is copious and needs time to set.
p: The marionberry was bred at Oregon State in 1956 and is the state's own blackberry: darker, tarter, and more complex than any other. Use the full measure of cornstarch: these berries run more juice than you expect.

n: Cracked Dungeness Crab with Drawn Butter
i: 2 whole Dungeness crabs, about 1kg each, live
Sourdough bread and a green salad to serve
m: Bring a very large pot of heavily salted water to a rolling boil with the lemon and bay.
Cook the crabs 12-15 min until the shells turn bright orange-red; lift out and cool briefly.
Clean the crabs: lift the top shell, remove the gills and viscera, and rinse.
Crack the legs and body with a mallet or the back of a heavy knife.
Melt the butter gently with the garlic, skim it clear, and serve alongside with bread.
p: Dungeness season opens in December and the Oregon coast marks it like a holiday. Do not over-boil: fifteen minutes is plenty, and crab held longer goes stringy. Crack it before serving so the meat pulls free clean.

i: For the cream: 300ml cream, 2 tbsp sugar, 1 tsp vanilla
m: Toast the hazelnuts, rub off the skins in a towel, and grind to a fine meal.
Beat the yolks with three-quarters of the sugar until pale and thick, then fold in the ground nuts, flour, baking powder, vanilla, and salt.
Whip the whites with the remaining sugar to soft peaks and fold through in three additions.
Bake in two lined 23cm pans at 175C for 22-25 min until springy. Cool completely.
Whip the cream and sandwich the layers, then top with more cream and chopped hazelnuts.
p: Oregon grows nearly all of America's hazelnuts in the Willamette Valley. Toast and skin them yourself: the papery skins are bitter, and the toasting is what brings out the deep nuttiness the torte is built on.

i: For the top: 100g breadcrumbs, 3 tbsp melted butter, 50g cheddar
m: Cook the macaroni two minutes shy of al dente and drain.
Melt the butter, whisk in the flour, and cook 2 min. Add the warm milk gradually, whisking, and simmer to a smooth sauce.
Off the heat, add the cheddar in handfuls, stirring until each melts before the next. Season with mustard, nutmeg, hot sauce, salt, and pepper.
Fold the pasta through the sauce and turn into a buttered dish.
Toss the breadcrumbs with melted butter and cheese, scatter over, and bake at 190C for 25 min until bubbling and gold.
p: Tillamook's coastal creamery has made cheddar since 1909. The pot must come off the heat before the cheese goes in: a sauce that boils after cheddar is added turns grainy and weeps oil, and no amount of stirring brings it back.

n: Oregon Pinot Noir Braised Short Ribs
m: Season the short ribs hard and brown all sides in the oil; set aside.
Sweat the onion, carrot, and celery until soft, add the garlic and tomato paste, and cook until brick red.
Add the wine and reduce by half: this cooks off the raw alcohol and concentrates the fruit.
Return the ribs with the stock, bay, and thyme. Cover and braise at 150C for 3 hours until the meat pulls from the bone.
Rest, skim the fat, and reduce the sauce until it coats a spoon.
p: The Willamette Valley makes some of the world's finest Pinot Noir, and braising in it is a local pleasure. Reduce the wine hard before the stock goes in: an under-reduced braise tastes sharp and boozy rather than deep.

i: For the dough: 500g flour, 7g yeast, 60g sugar, 1 tsp salt, 240ml warm milk, 2 eggs, 85g butter
For the glaze: 300g icing sugar, 60ml maple syrup, 3 tbsp milk
8 rashers bacon, cooked crisp and broken
m: Knead the dough until smooth and rise 90 min until doubled.
Roll to 1cm, cut into bars or rings, and rise 30 min until puffy.
Fry at 175C for 60-90 seconds a side until deep gold.
Whisk the maple glaze and dip each warm doughnut.
Lay strips of crisp bacon across the wet glaze so they set in place.
p: Portland's Voodoo Doughnut made the maple bar with bacon a national curiosity in the 2000s. Lay the bacon on while the glaze is still tacky — set glaze will not hold it, and the salt against the maple is the entire argument for the thing.

m: Brush the chanterelles clean rather than washing them: they absorb water readily.
Cook them in the butter over medium-high heat 8 min until they release their liquid and it cooks away and they begin to brown.
Add the shallots and garlic, then the flour, and cook 2 min.
Whisk in the stock and simmer 20 min, then add the cream and thyme.
Finish with the sherry off the heat, season, and scatter with chives.
p: Chanterelles flush through Oregon's coastal forests each autumn and are the state mushroom. Brush rather than wash them, and cook them hard enough that their water evaporates and they brown: a wet chanterelle just steams and tastes of nothing.

i: 1 side of Chinook salmon, about 1kg, skin on
An untreated cedar plank, soaked 2 hours
m: Soak the cedar plank thoroughly so it smolders rather than catches.
Rub the salmon with the brown sugar, salt, and pepper and rest 20 min.
Set the salmon skin-side down on the plank, brush with oil, and lay lemon slices and herbs over.
Cook on a covered grill over medium heat, or at 200C in the oven, 20-30 min until the flesh flakes at the thickest point and reads 52C for medium.
Serve straight from the plank.
p: Planking salmon on cedar comes from the Pacific Northwest tribes, who cooked it on stakes beside alder and cedar fires. Soak the plank well, use untreated wood only, and pull the fish at medium: Chinook is rich and dries fast past that.

m: Fold the flaked tuna with the mayonnaise, celery, onion, lemon, and capers and season well.
Butter one side of each bread slice.
Build with cheese, the tuna salad, and more cheese: cheese on both sides glues the sandwich shut.
Griddle over medium heat 4 min a side, pressing gently, until deep gold and the cheese has melted through.
Cut on the diagonal and serve hot.
p: Oregon's troll-caught albacore is line-caught young and far richer than canned skipjack. Cheese on both sides of the filling is the structural trick: it seals the tuna in so the sandwich holds together when cut.

n: Hood River Pear and Blue Cheese Salad
i: 3 ripe Hood River pears, sliced thin
For the dressing: 3 tbsp hazelnut or olive oil, 2 tbsp cider vinegar, 1 tsp honey, 1 tsp Dijon, salt and pepper
m: Toast the hazelnuts and rub off their skins.
Whisk the dressing until emulsified and taste for balance: it should be sharp enough to answer the pear.
Toss the greens lightly with just enough dressing to coat.
Arrange the pear slices over and scatter the blue cheese and hazelnuts.
Grind pepper over and serve at once, before the pears brown.
p: The Hood River Valley grows pears in the shadow of Mount Hood, and Rogue Creamery makes the blue. Slice the pears at the last moment; they oxidize within minutes, and a browned pear looks tired next to the greens.

i: For the sauce: 250ml soy sauce, 120ml mirin, 100g brown sugar, 60ml sake, 4 garlic cloves grated, 2 tbsp ginger grated, 1 tbsp cornstarch
Iceberg lettuce, shredded, with a light vinegar dressing
m: Simmer the soy, mirin, sugar, sake, garlic, and ginger 10 min, then thicken with the cornstarch slurried in a little water.
Marinate the chicken thighs in a third of the sauce 30 min.
Grill or broil the thighs skin-side down until charred and cooked through, 12-15 min, basting with sauce as they cook.
Slice the chicken across into strips.
Serve over rice with the shredded lettuce salad on the side and more sauce spooned over.
p: Seattle teriyaki is its own institution, sweeter and thicker than the Japanese original, served in hundreds of neighborhood shops since the 1970s with rice and a wedge of iceberg. Baste as it grills so the sugars lacquer rather than burn.

i: 1 geoduck siphon, blanched, skinned, and sliced paper thin
m: Blanch the geoduck 10 seconds in boiling water, then plunge into ice water; the tough outer skin peels away easily.
Slice the cleaned siphon as thin as you possibly can: thickness is toughness with geoduck.
Arrange the slices in a single layer on chilled plates.
Dress with lemon, olive oil, shallot, and chile just before serving.
Finish with flaky salt and chives and serve immediately.
p: The geoduck is Puget Sound's giant burrowing clam, prized in Asia and eaten raw at its best. Everything depends on the knife: sliced paper-thin it is sweet and crisp, and cut any thicker it is rubber. Dress it at the last second.

m: Toss the cherries with the sugar, cornstarch, lemon, and almond extract.
Roll the pastry into a rough 30cm round on a lined tray.
Scatter the ground almonds over the center (they absorb juice and keep the base crisp), then mound the cherries, leaving a 5cm border.
Fold the border up over the fruit in loose pleats, brush with egg, and sprinkle with demerara.
Bake at 200C for 40-45 min until the pastry is deep gold and the juices bubble. Cool 20 min.
p: The Rainier cherry was bred at Washington State in 1952 and is the sweetest of them all, yellow blushed with red. The layer of ground almonds under the fruit is the galette-maker's insurance against a soggy bottom.

i: For the glaze: 115g butter, 150g brown sugar, 60ml cream
m: Whisk the flour, soda, cinnamon, nutmeg, and salt.
Beat the eggs, brown sugar, oil, and vanilla, then fold in the dry ingredients; the batter will be very thick.
Fold in the diced apple and walnuts; the apples release the moisture that makes the batter come together.
Bake in a lined pan at 175C for 50-60 min until a skewer comes clean.
Simmer the glaze ingredients 5 min and pour over the warm cake.
p: Washington grows more apples than any state, and this dense, moist cake uses a great many of them. Do not add liquid when the batter looks too stiff: the diced apples will weep enough moisture as they bake.

m: Clean the razor clams thoroughly, removing the dark parts, and chop them coarsely.
Whisk the flour, baking powder, egg, and milk into a thick batter.
Fold in the clams, scallions, Old Bay, and pepper.
Drop heaped spoonfuls into 180C oil and fry 3 min, turning, until deep gold.
Drain, salt, and serve with lemon and tartar.
p: Razor clam digs on the Washington coast are a licensed, tide-timed ritual followed by thousands. Chop rather than mince the clams so you keep some texture, and do not overmix once they go in: they toughen with handling.

n: Penn Cove Mussels Steamed in Cider
i: 2kg Penn Cove mussels, scrubbed and debearded
m: Discard any mussels that stay open when tapped.
Sweat the shallots and garlic in the butter until soft.
Add the cider and bring to a hard boil.
Tip in the mussels, cover, and steam 4-5 min, shaking the pot once, until they open.
Lift the mussels out, whisk the cream and thyme into the liquor, pour it back over, and finish with parsley.
p: Penn Cove on Whidbey Island grows some of the finest mussels in the country. Discard any that will not close before cooking and any that will not open after, and never overcook them, since a mussel goes from plump to shrunken in a minute.

i: 2 onions, sliced and griddled until soft
m: Griddle the onions slowly in butter until soft, sweet, and lightly browned.
Grill the hot dogs until blistered.
Split the buns and griddle the cut faces.
Spread a thick layer of softened cream cheese inside the warm bun so it melts slightly.
Add the dog, pile on the griddled onions, and finish with sriracha or jalapenos.
p: A late-night Seattle street cart institution born outside the bars and music venues. The cream cheese sounds improbable and is entirely the point: spread it on the warm bun so it softens into a tangy sauce under the onions.

i: 3 large Walla Walla sweet onions, sliced in 1cm rings
m: Separate the onion rings and soak them in buttermilk 30 min.
Whisk the flour, cornstarch, baking powder, salt, and paprika, then add the cold beer to a batter just thicker than cream.
Heat the oil to 190C.
Lift each ring from the buttermilk, dip in the batter, let the excess run off, and fry 2-3 min until deep gold.
Drain on a rack and finish with flaky salt.
p: The Walla Walla sweet is so low in sulfur it can be eaten like an apple, and it is the state vegetable. The cornstarch in the batter is what keeps the crust crisp rather than bready: do not substitute more flour for it.

i: 1 side of sockeye salmon, about 1.2kg, pin-boned
For the cure: 150g brown sugar, 100g coarse salt, 1 tbsp black pepper
2 tbsp maple syrup or honey for glazing
m: Mix the cure and pack it over the flesh side of the salmon. Cure in the fridge 6-8 hours.
Rinse the cure off thoroughly, pat dry, and rest the fish uncovered in the fridge 2 hours until the surface turns tacky: this pellicle is what smoke adheres to.
Smoke over alder at 80C for 3-4 hours until the flesh flakes and reads 60C.
Brush with maple syrup in the last 30 min for a lacquered finish.
Cool and serve with rye bread, or flake into chowder.
p: Alder is the Pacific Northwest's smoking wood, used by coastal tribes for millennia. Do not skip the drying step after rinsing: without a tacky pellicle the smoke slides off and the fish takes almost no flavor.

m: Render the bacon; lift out the bits and sweat the onion and celery in the fat.
Sprinkle in the flour and cook 2 min, then whisk in the stock.
Add the potatoes and simmer 15 min until tender.
Add the milk and cream and heat through without boiling.
Fold in the flaked smoked salmon and dill at the very end, warm 2 min, and finish with lemon and pepper.
p: Pike Place Market has sold versions of this for decades. Add the smoked salmon at the very end: it is already cooked, and simmering it breaks the flakes apart and turns the whole pot muddy and over-salted.

n: Alaska King Crab Legs with Drawn Butter
m: King crab is sold cooked and frozen, so the job is reheating, not cooking. Thaw it fully in the fridge first.
Bring the salted water and lemon to a boil in a wide pot with a steamer basket.
Steam the split legs 4-5 min, just until heated through. Any longer and the meat toughens and goes stringy.
Melt the butter gently with the garlic, skim the foam, and pour off the clear butter.
Serve the legs on a warm platter with drawn butter, lemon, and crackers.
p: Bering Sea king crab is the great luxury of the Alaskan table. Because it is cooked at sea and frozen immediately, over-steaming is the only real way to ruin it: four minutes to warm through is all it needs.

n: Baked Alaska Halibut with Mayonnaise Crust
m: Pat the halibut fillets dry and season lightly.
Mix the mayonnaise, Parmesan, scallion, lemon, dill, and pepper.
Spread the mixture thickly over the top of each fillet, sealing it edge to edge.
Toss the panko with melted butter and press onto the mayonnaise.
Bake at 200C for 12-15 min until the crust is gold and the fish flakes at the thickest point.
p: Halibut is extraordinarily lean and turns to chalk if overcooked; the mayonnaise blanket is an Alaskan cook's insurance, sealing in moisture as it bakes. Cover the fillet completely: any exposed fish dries out.

i: 250g solid vegetable shortening or rendered fat, at room temperature
m: Whip the room-temperature fat with a wooden spoon or mixer until it is white, light, and fluffy; this takes real effort and is the whole technique.
Beat in the sugar gradually.
Add the water a spoonful at a time, whipping constantly, until the mixture is airy and holds soft peaks.
Fold in the berries gently by hand.
Chill until firm and serve cold in small portions.
p: Akutaq is a traditional food of the Yup'ik, Inupiat, and other Alaska Native peoples, historically made with rendered seal or caribou fat and berries and carried as high-energy food. Whipping the fat until genuinely light is the skill; rushed, it stays greasy and heavy.

m: Fry the diced potatoes in the oil until crisp and golden, 12 min; season and push to one side.
Brown the sliced reindeer sausage in the same pan until the edges crisp.
Add the onion and pepper and cook until softened.
Make four wells in the mixture and crack the eggs in. Cover and cook 4-5 min until the whites set and the yolks stay soft.
Scatter the cheese over, season, and serve with hot sauce straight from the skillet.
p: Reindeer sausage is an Anchorage staple, sold from downtown carts and served at every diner breakfast. It is leaner and slightly sweeter than pork sausage, so brown it in the potato fat rather than dry: it has little of its own to give.

i: 1 side of king salmon, about 1kg, skin on
m: Whisk the birch syrup, soy, mustard, lemon, garlic, and ginger into a glaze.
Season the salmon and set it skin-side down on a lined tray.
Brush a third of the glaze over the fish and roast at 220C for 8 min.
Brush again and roast 6-8 min more until the flesh flakes at the edge and reads 50-52C at the thickest point for medium.
Brush with the last of the glaze, scatter with dill, and rest 5 min before serving.
p: Birch syrup is tapped in the Alaskan interior and is darker, more mineral, and less sweet than maple, closer to molasses. Build the glaze in three thin coats rather than one thick one, or the sugars burn before the fish is done.

m: The night before, mix the starter with the flour and milk and leave covered at room temperature to ferment.
In the morning the sponge should be bubbly and smell tangy. Beat in the eggs, sugar, salt, and melted butter.
Sprinkle the baking soda over and fold it through: it will foam as it meets the acid, and this is the lift.
Cook straight away on a buttered griddle over medium heat until bubbles break across the surface, then flip once.
Serve with butter and syrup.
p: Alaskan prospectors were called sourdoughs because they slept with their starter to keep it alive through the winter. Add the soda at the last moment and cook immediately: the foam it makes against the sour sponge is what raises the pancake.

i: Pastry for a double-crust pie, or 500g yeasted dough
600g salmon fillet, skinned and cut in chunks
m: Sweat the onion in the butter until soft, then fold it through the cooked rice with the chopped egg, dill, lemon, salt, and pepper.
Line a baking dish or tray with the bottom pastry.
Layer half the rice mixture, then the raw salmon chunks seasoned well, then the remaining rice.
Lay the top crust over, seal the edges, cut steam vents, and brush with egg.
Bake at 190C for 45-55 min until deep gold. Rest 15 min before cutting.
p: Pirok came to Kodiak and the Aleutians with Russian settlers and remains an Alaskan church-supper dish. The rice layers above and below the fish absorb its juices and protect the pastry: build it in that order or the base goes soggy.

m: Dry the moose well, season, and toss in the flour.
Brown hard in the oil in batches: crowding the pan steams the meat and costs you the crust.
Sweat the onions and garlic, add the tomato paste and cook it dark, then deglaze with the wine.
Return the meat with the stock, juniper, bay, and thyme. Cover and braise at 150C for 2.5 hours.
Add the potatoes and carrots for the last 40 min and season again: game takes more salt than beef.
p: A moose fills a family's freezer for a winter, and stew is where the tougher cuts go. Moose is even leaner than elk, so the browning, the juniper, and a long slow braise all work to supply what the animal itself does not.

m: Melt the butter in a 23cm cake pan, stir in the brown sugar, and spread it over the base.
Arrange the rhubarb tightly over the sugar in a single close layer: it shrinks considerably as it bakes.
Cream the butter and sugar, beat in the eggs and vanilla, then alternate the dry ingredients with the milk.
Spread the batter over the rhubarb and bake at 175C for 45-55 min until a skewer comes clean.
Rest exactly 5 min, then invert onto a plate. Wait longer and the caramel welds to the pan.
p: Rhubarb thrives in the long Alaskan summer daylight and grows to remarkable size in dooryard gardens. Pack the rhubarb tightly, as it collapses in the oven, and mind the five-minute rule on turning the cake out.

i: Icing sugar or a lemon glaze
m: Whisk the flour, baking powder, sugar, salt, and cinnamon.
Beat in the egg, milk, and melted butter to a thick batter.
Fold in the wild blueberries with a light hand so they stay whole.
Drop heaped spoonfuls into 180C oil and fry 3-4 min, turning, until deep gold and cooked through.
Drain and dust with icing sugar or drizzle with lemon glaze while warm.
p: Wild Alaskan blueberries are small, dark, and far more intense than any cultivated berry, picked across the tundra in August. Keep the batter thick so the fritters hold their shape, and fold the berries gently: crushed berries bleed and weigh the batter down.
